messages.content: there we go that's the consent bit and then the interview there's only one question and the rest is just a
OK
a chat about it
yeah
so the question is do you feel like you use language creatively

I suppose it depends what you mean. I tend not to have a creative output for my language, so I can't really do writing or art or anything like that. But if I use it creatively in my day-to-day life, I'd probably say no, because most of my interactions are quite normal and just kind of basic, so there's not really an opportunity to use language in a different way or there's no benefit to doing that, so therefore I don't really think that I do, not on a day-to-day basis really.
I see, and what does the idea of creative language mean to you? How would you define that?

How would I define it? I'd suppose using language in a way that is expressive or is expressing something in a kind of—I don't want to use the word creative again—in a way that's kind of unusual and that perhaps indulges in representing forms rather than in a functional way.
I see, so
I suppose
does the language that you use perform a lot of the functions that you need it to do, and is that why you don't tend to use language creatively?

It's difficult. There's no opportunity. I kind of just have functional interactions, so the interactions I get involved in in my day-to-day life aren't really creative because I'm in quite a constrained environment—a supported housing project. And in my day-to-day care, from my twice-weekly depot, never is it really kind of creative, so I don't really have the opportunity to indulge my more creative side, I would say.
oh I see, so would you like to do more creative stuff with language?

I don't know, to be honest with you. I kind of think that I'd like to feel more that I can express myself more freely and that what I do is more interesting to other people, but because it's not and because it's kind of functional, then I don't have the opportunities. I suppose the answer is yes, I would like to feel that there was a reason for me to be creative or expressive.
so it sounds like—and correct me if I'm wrong—but it
no
like it sounds like there's a big communicative aspect about what being creative with language is, about what you talk about and what's going on in your life at the time, is that right?

Language to me at the moment is just kind of functional, driven by function and not really experience. You know, having room for expression—or I don't feel that people really want to hear me. So I suppose what I think of as creative is not indulgent, but it's using language in a way that I'd identify more with. So I suppose that I don't really have the outlets available to me to really be able to use language in the way that I want to, I suppose.
and do you mind telling me more about the way that you want to?

I suppose what I'd like to do is feel that my intellect is stimulated by the need to talk and that there's something about being heard by other people that kind of makes that important or makes that work. And I suppose when other people don't want to listen to you, then I have no reason to indulge that, then it just becomes quite functional and simple. But I don't feel like I'm in a terrible bind because of it, it's just how life is. So I kind of just get on with the day, try and get by, and that's kind of living one day at a time and just being normal in that sense. So yeah, it's kind of up in the air. I mean, I don't really think about it very much, but yeah, I don't know how to say it really. The use of language in my day-to-day life is just normal, and I don't know how I want to use my creative abilities. I don't really have a way of being out of the cycles that I'm in, and so I kind of just let it go by, just another kind of thing that doesn't happen or thing that doesn't work in my life.
when you say up in the air
mhm
I'd say that's a creative thing, like because it's like a
mhm
like an expression, like a—do you know what I mean? Like
yeah
like a figure of speech you know

yeah, well I mean I don't really have many people ask me questions. People aren't really driven to hear me, so I just get on with the day. I'm quite isolated in that sense, and I don't really have quality communication with people.
I see

and yeah, it's driven a lot by the social environment I'm in and what's demanded of me. There's no real demand on me to fulfil any function apart from basic communication, not really expression or artistry in language. It's much more designed to explaining the day-to-day running of my life in a small way. The use of language in my daily life is very normal, very poor in the sense of creativity.
I see, and like
mm
in terms of things you like, like hobbies and stuff
mm
I understand what you say about communication opportunities not being as available
yeah
but what do you like to do, whether it's creative or not, in your spare time?

I watch a lot of TV at the moment, I read the newspaper, I go for walks, and not much really. It's quite a normal, basic existence because I'm recovering from illness. I lost a lot of the outlets I used to enjoy—meeting with friends, talking with friends, playing pool or snooker, going out for a drink. I lost all that in the course of my illness, so a lot of my life is just TV and newspaper. Not really much else at the moment, trying to stay off drugs, which is important to me, and that's about it.
that sounds like a lot to handle in the middle of lockdown

yeah, I suppose lockdown is kind of the same as it was before to me. I feel like I'm on a bit of a lockdown anyway because I don't really have that social aspect. It's difficult to go without, and I'm getting used to it, but I'm not sure if it's me or my illness that makes me want to isolate myself—I can't divide the two. I feel the need to be alone and not communicate with people, and I find that stressful. It's always been a bit of a problem for me; I've always had that personality that wants to withdraw and finds communication difficult. So lockdown for me, I do miss seeing my mom because I saw her regularly, but other than that I'm used to being alone and not sharing things with people, just getting on with the basics of the day. It's OK to feel that way, it's just difficult dealing with not having that social aspect and not being able to want it. I still want it, but I have an aversion to it at the same time—like being allergic to something good. It's not ideal, but yeah.
I see, like
mm
is it nicer in smaller amounts then, the social stuff?
I don't know, it's not really—I'm not sure. It's very difficult to put a blanket over anything and say that's how it is, because
mm

everything can be different. I like the idea of it, and it doesn't go well or badly because it happens—sometimes things go well and sometimes they won't. It depends on the nature of the interaction, who it's with, and whether things feel right at the time or not. It's difficult. I still need that interaction with people, and dealing with it in small amounts should be easier, shouldn't it? But I'm just not geared up for it; it's not something I was born with. It's always difficult to interact with people, and even in small amounts it's hard to find the place in that for me that really works. Like I said, it's like being allergic—it just doesn't come naturally. It's something I've boarded out, like I can't draw from very well, I'm not a very good artist. I think that's part of my illness, you know.
I see, yeah. I'm mindful of what you're saying, that I don't keep you on the phone too long if this conversation is like
no, it's fine, it's
like

it's just—I struggle through, and I won't go to bed tonight worrying about what I've said or what we've been doing, so it should be fine. As long as there are good boundaries and I'm not forced into it too much, it's fine. This is just—I can say no, and it's just over the phone for one day, it's thought through, like half an hour, so that's fine.
So is it different if it's a situation like a birthday party where you feel you have to go and there are lots of people?
Yeah.
Is that the kind of situation where you're not too sure about it?

Yeah, the bigger the event, the worse it is. The more people, the more stress and the harder it is. I've been withdrawing from those things for most of my life. I'm trying my best to work with that and hoping to find something that helps me cope better with anxiety, but that's difficult. Anxiety is really hard to shake and get past. I'm trying my best to deal with it.
Mm.

But this feels alright, it feels controlled and not so difficult. We have a subject to talk about, whereas at a birthday party there would be no rules and that could lead to danger. I find people difficult, and if they're drinking they can be even more difficult. One-on-one interaction has worked best for me in my life. I can cope with talking to one person and make a conversation, but I can't deal with an open-ended interaction with lots of people. There are many occasions like birthdays and Christmas that I've missed out on because of that.
I was just going to ask if one-to-one was easier, because having a subject means you get to take turns more.
Mhm.
Like when there's...
Yeah.
...a big group it's harder to know whose turn it is.
That's true, yeah.
And yeah, like...
It's more balanced one-on-one, like tennis. There's an elegance to it, whereas with a big group there's more performance involved, which is harder. I'm not very able to perform on order.
I know what you mean.
That's a really good way of putting it.
Cool.

Do you mind if I ask whether there's a difference in how you feel about language, not necessarily how you use it, before you started to get ill and after? Like any question you don't want to answer, just say.
Mhm.
Like any question you don't want to answer, just say.

The problem is I don't really feel I've become ill recently or that there's been a particular time I got ill. I suppose with the schizophrenia, during the more florid parts, language is a lot freer. I feel like I have more rhythm and I can talk, but maybe I don't say much conversational. I feel more poetic and creative. Now I'm on the depot, I feel a lot more stolid. My mouth doesn't work as well and my muscles don't react the same way. There's a kind of romance to feeling florid, for want of a better term. When I'm ill, or what's seen as ill, I can be a lot happier, but I'm not necessarily so functional and I don't get tied up linguistically. Obviously hearing voices and stuff isn't so pleasant, and that part contributes to the other side. When you asked the question, I always think that when I'm ill I enjoy my language a lot more. I enjoy using language and the idea of creating language and being poetic. I'm on the phone, sorry.
Do you...
Yeah, and...
Oh no, sorry.
Yeah.
Please, carry on.
Sorry.
Oh, sorry, I said carry on because I was about to interrupt you and I didn't want to cut you off.
No, I think I'd finished.
I was just going to ask, are you happy to talk about how your language is in that florid state?
Yeah, totally. I'm open to discussion.
Because that sounds...
Ah.
It's just that it would be really interesting to hear more of your thoughts about what kind of form your language takes at that point.

I kind of make up poetry. I'm reasonably well-read and aware of poetry, prose, and theatre, and I come up with lots of ideas. I do a kind of mimicry of forms I'm familiar with and just create poems. Linguistically, I was interested in making things up and the quality that would bring to my life. Now that I'm not ill, that's gone, it's disappeared, and it's something I miss. I find it difficult that I have to be tied up to be well; being unwell is more romantic and easier on me. But it's very difficult because people don't really want to indulge that part of you, or see that it comes with difficult phases. Strictly to myself, I find it easier being a bit more ill because the medication is quite prohibitive. Functionally, it stops you from really being expressive and stops you from really being yourself. So yeah, I miss being creative, definitely.
And when you said that you sort of create poems and stuff...
Yeah.
In what kind of situations would you do that?
Really?
And I guess for what reasons as well?

Really in any situation. I feel like, to some extent, I was having a dialogue with the voices I was hearing and I was making up forms to deal with that. I also just felt I had that in me, like a little feeling or a voice inside me that I had access to at the time. So it would be all the time, but mostly I'd stick to myself and be in my own room and enjoy that. I was quite linguistically free at the time and I was really enjoying that, but I suppose there wasn't really a place for it to stick. It was just a kind of magic that there wasn't really a place for, and although I enjoyed it, there wasn't a formal future to it, so it kind of died. I'm regretful that it's something I've lost; it's something I mourn quite a lot.
I see, yeah.
Mhm.

Do you think it's something that's potentially compatible with treatment, like with more engagement with creative activities and more of an opportunity that you'll be able to re-explore it in a way that's compatible with the depot?

Honestly, no. The medication they put you on for the illness I had is just anathema to that kind of feeling. It's that feeling of lightness and ease, and I don't have that anymore. With the depot, my muscles become tight, my ability to move my mouth becomes a lot more difficult, and my brain slows down and becomes a lot quieter. The attempt to even access that again is really depressing because it doesn't work; there's nothing there. It's like something's blacked out a bit of the window and you can't see that way anymore. I miss that ability to look at the world that way. It's not that I don't agree with the medication, because I know a lot of people think I need it, but I just think the medication isn't ideal. The side effects are quite severe, and although it's helped me calm down a lot, I feel it's turned something off or blacked something out. If I'm honest, I don't think it's really compatible with medication. That's one of the struggles with the disease I have: I can't really change or influence that because I've lost all my credibility through the more difficult aspects of being schizophrenic, which is hearing voices and physically feeling a more bubbly, buzzy feeling rather than the heaviness from the medication. That buzzy feeling is not easy to deal with seven days a week, so it's difficult.
Yeah, it's really tough with the medication because it's...
Yeah.
One of those things that we just seem to find ourselves at a point in history where it works, but like you say with...
Yeah.
The side effects, it's at that point where it could still be improved.
yeah
and hopefully in the near future we can get it to the point where it works and there aren't as many side effects
yeah
that's the ideal
that would be nice
yeah
mm
it's really a fascinating area to talk to people about
cool
is there anything we haven't talked about that you'd like to discuss

not really, I think the main feeling I'm left with is about creativity, because when you ask that question it resonates a lot with how I feel. the inability to feel free or to express myself fully is a big part of my experience. the ability to be free and talk a lot and feel expressive was a big part of my previous experience before I was on medication. the difference between those two aspects, and what that means and how it's influenced everything else, is quite intricate and interesting. it means a lot to me but I don't know what to say about it. hopefully as the medication decreases and as time goes on I'll get better and things will feel better. certainly the medication I'm on now is not as bad—I was prescribed Risperdal at first and that was a lot worse. I'm on a different one now, I can't remember the name, and that one is having fewer side effects for me, but all of them kind of reduce what I think is called creativity. so yeah, it rings a lot of bells definitely
I see, yeah
mm
what happens to these interviews is I type them up
cool
and then they'll go into a big database that is searchable by researchers
cool
we're building an archive of interviews on creativity with people who have a diagnosis of schizophrenia
yeah
with that in mind, is there anything you want on that record—your record will be anonymous—but is there anything you'd like
yeah
to add to that record

not really, I think we've got the main overview of where I am. we've covered what I think happened and what I think's really going on with that question. the rest would just be repeating myself, I don't have a lot more to say about it other than that. I suppose you could ask questions that would trigger a different direction, but yeah, that's the main part really
yeah, no, that's cool. I can't thank you enough for your time
brilliant
Thank you for sharing that with me, it means a lot.
Thank you.
I'll stop the recording now.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that unstructured social situations, like a birthday party with no rules, could lead to danger.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant does not express doubt about this specific belief in the session, but contextualizes it within a broader discussion of social anxiety and difficulty.

case_summary: The participant discusses their relationship with creative language, describing it as largely absent from their current functional, constrained life in supported housing. They contrast this with a past 'florid' state of illness where they felt linguistically free, poetic, and engaged in a creative dialogue with voices. They express that antipsychotic medication has suppressed this creativity, causing a sense of loss and mourning, though they acknowledge the medication's necessity. Social interaction is described as difficult and anxiety-provoking, with a preference for structured, one-on-one conversations over large, unstructured gatherings.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

messages.content: So it's just a conversation about creativity in language and what that means to you. Do you feel like you use language creatively?

I do. I write song lyrics, and sometimes poetry, but mostly song lyrics—like every other line rhymes, with a chorus and two or three verses. Yesterday I wrote a poem called 'Tranquility,' but mostly I write song lyrics. I also write scripts, like science fiction and RPGs, space-based stuff. But mainly it's songwriting and lyrics. I also program, mostly in HTML5—HTML, CSS, and JavaScript—and sometimes Python. But with language, it's mostly songwriting.
That's awesome. How long have you been doing all of those things?

Well, on my computer mostly. I do websites as well, but it goes on. I've been writing songs for maybe ten years now. I used to write poetry, but I wasn't really into it—it's always been songwriting, with every other line rhyming like a song does. I haven't published my work, but I have it all saved on my computer. I wrote a poem yesterday for the first time in quite a long time, but it's mostly songwriting. Apart from that, when I blog on the website I build, it's just general prose, not poetic. I was inspired yesterday to write a poem, but that's the first in quite a while. So it's mostly been songwriting, and also programming and some graphic design—I create PNG and JPEG files and put code over them to make things interactive on the website.
Wow.
So that is about it really. I wrote a poem for the first time in a long, long time, but it is mostly songwriting that I get creative with.
What's the thing you like about the songwriting more than the poetry?

I used to struggle for ideas with poetry, whereas songwriting is more structured—every other line rhymes. I use WordPad on Windows; I need a word processor. I can write with pencil and paper, but I tweak and hone it constantly. Sometimes the first line has to be taken out and completely redone ten minutes later. What I do is make each line the same width across, so they all line up vertically on the screen—like constraints. That seems to be how I get it out. With poetry, it really is more songwriting. I should really start sending my work out, but I don't know. The main thing for me is programming and graphic design, but I absolutely love writing songs and poetry as well. Apart from that, I like photography—just snaps of architecture, like the Gherkin building in the City of London, that kind of thing.
Yeah.

Good architecture that I like, buildings and that. But mostly it is now programming that I do to be creative with, and it's all digital on the computer. I have USB pen drives and I save my data to those. I don't like using my laptop to go online because of hacking reasons.
Yeah.

I just use antivirus software, but it would crash all the time for some reason—people hacking me or whatever, I don't know. But mostly it is programming, though I like writing song lyrics as well. I've been listening to music for years and years, all day every day for years. So that's about it really.
No, it's that's—

I like photography as well, just taking snapshots of anything here in London. In the local park there's a moat, and the reflections are really good, really nice reflections, especially in the autumn with the leaves. So that's about it really.
That's so interesting. Because it sounds like you're involved in loads of different areas of the creative industries. Like, you said you put the code on top of the images and stuff?
Yeah. I— sorry.
Oh no, no, it's all good.

I build websites by creating a single large PNG file divided into areas, or sometimes multiple PNGs. I overlay a coordinate system using HTML and JavaScript so that when a user clicks or touches a hotspot, it triggers navigation to another page or shows/hides elements. I prefer using the JQuery framework over newer ones like React or Vue. Because of brain fade, I copy and paste code from a personal toolkit and then tweak it, adjusting positions for mouse clicks or touch events on mobile devices. In recent years I've focused more on programming than poetry, but I still write songs often and have about a hundred saved. I now write lyrics in a narrow format, only about a third across the screen, using a straight edge to line everything up.
And is there a lot of text lining up in the programming languages as well?

You can set a right margin so the software automatically wraps text to the next line without needing manual line breaks. I used to insert BR tags for line breaks, but I worked out it's better to just set a right margin and type the paragraph normally, letting it wrap automatically.
I see. Does having that constraint you mentioned feel important to the creative process?
Right.
For you, I mean, not like...

It definitely works for me. On a practical level, if you're doing line breaks you have to keep checking the code because I hand-code; I don't use a design view. I use Netbeans, which is freely available online. It's only a code view, not a design view like Dreamweaver or CoffeeCup. So if you're doing line breaks without the right margin point, you have to keep checking how it displays in the browser, because the entire thing is about the browser—that's client-side, not server-side. I do front-end. On a practical level, if you set a right margin, you can type as much as you want and the monitor will word-wrap for you. You can write an entire paragraph without line breaks; the right margin does it for you. It's usually important, and it works both for the webpage and for what I see on the monitor. So it definitely makes a difference. But compared to the poetry and songwriting, I don't know, because the songwriting just gets it out of me. With the pages, I put a straight line down the right-hand side and everything has to line up. I used to make the verses the same width as the chorus, then I went to a narrow format. It's definitely more zippy, more pointed—gets the point across better rather than rambling on for another four or five words per line. I used to use the same words quite often, but I like to be creative within the creativity, to make it a bit more ambient for people to read. With jQuery and JavaScript, I learned you have to put in a right margin and it does all the line formatting and justifying for you. You just have to make sure you don't overspill onto a plain piece of colour or another PNG, because it could go to maybe ten lines and that could be too much wording, too much content for the container it's created inside.
I see, yeah.
But the main thing is definitely writing poetry and writing songs. It has to be aligned vertically for me. That definitely does it.
And when you write poetry and song lyrics, are there specific techniques that you like to use more than others?

I don't know what's going on with my brain, but on a pragmatic, practical level, everything definitely has to line up. Sometimes I might use a couple of words from somebody else's song, like a popular song.
Oh, that's cool.

It's not like plagiarism, but it might be a phrase from a song—using a couple of words from it to make things more dynamic, maybe. I don't know. I definitely seem to like it when there's structure and confinement. I don't know if that's around me or in me. The main thing I really do now is programming. With HTML, you divide it—you've got the header area and the body area. I read that for people just starting out with HTML, building websites, it's a markup language, not a programming language, but it's still the most important thing on the internet. HTML creates and structures everything.
Yeah.
What I read was that people at the beginning put in loads of DIVs, dividers, and I read on somebody's blog that it is known as DIV soup.
Oh, OK.

So I decided not to put in that many DIVs, but it turns out you have to put in a lot of DIVs. You really have to divide the page up. You've got a wrapper that wraps the entire content of the body area; you've got the header and the body, and you have to work with the body. So now I gather up loads of DIVs. It's like structure and form, and when you're looking at it, it's easy to understand what's going on with the code. You've got DIVs, and inside them you have P tags for paragraphs—that's text and words—and IMG for images, which could be a photo, a JPEG, a PNG, a GIF, whatever people have. I really love HTML, and it's divided up into bite-size chunks on the page on the computer that I look at. So that could be more of the same thing. I don't know what's going on in my brain, but when it's organised and succinct, maybe, that definitely helps me being creative with it, I suppose. Alright.
That's—
Can I just—because it's been a couple of minutes, my computer's just gone into screensaver. I'll be back in a minute.
Yeah, yeah, sure.

Yes, that definitely sparks some creativity in me. On a practical level, it's easier to understand and nicely divided. For example, in JavaScript programming, there's something called scope. I used to put variables midway down the code, but it turns out they all have to go at the top to get full scope throughout the functions. There's also a tool called linting, which marks errors in red. I used to place variables as I used them, but now I prefer putting them all at the top. But the main thing is definitely with writing songs: everything has to be right-aligned and vertically aligned, each line across. I've done that for many years, and it's the only way I can do it. If I don't, it's the unknown, and I prefer the known.
I see.

In terms of structure and form, this is on a computer monitor. After that, like a former poet laureate, [PERSON], a line or so from one of his poems is in me as well, but it's mostly more music than anything else.
Yeah.
A line or so from one of his poems is in me as well, but it's mostly more music than anything else.

Do you think, or why do you think the structure is important? I don't know what's going on in my brain. I like where I come from, but I was abused as a child. That's what I used to hear in the voices in my head. But I was told I wasn't. When this first happened, when the mental condition I have, psychosis, started, what came back was that I'd been badly abused as a child and was tied up. Oh, I'm so sorry to hear that.

But I get told that I wasn't. So this is the schizophrenia, the psychosis I've been diagnosed with. I don't know what is going on in my head, but that definitely gets it out of me. I love writing songs and poetry, but all these years it's been music, popular music, contemporary hit music, adult rock. About eighteen years ago I was diagnosed with schizophrenia, and that's what I've been living with ever since. I thought it might be autism, but I was told no, it's definitely schizophrenia. I wonder if people with schizophrenia or maybe Asperger's are more creative. I took part in a walking group around 2014, and one of the guys there was also creative, doing websites. I asked him if schizophrenia makes people more creative, but I don't know. I've been told I was not abused, but when it first started for me, the first thing that came back was that I'd been badly abused as a very young kid, as a baby.
And the creativity, you said it kind of gets things out. Is it like...

I don't know if it's frustration or something. One of the hardest things I've always struggled with is trying to say my own name to people, like when going for blood tests for clozapine. Stuttering about saying my name has had a profound effect on me; it's absolutely terrible at times. So when I can do that kind of thing... I'm stuck here indoors on my own, and all I have now is my computer to express myself. The perfect thing for it is the internet, a website, in this day and age. I operate better when I'm confined, when there are limitations, maybe.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Does that have to do with focus?
Is that what?
To do with...
Sorry.
Is that to do with focus or like...
Erm.
Having almost like boundaries to work within makes it easier to be creative in that space, or...

I think if I hadn't had all this bad stuff, my brain used to freak out one-on-one with people. Maybe working in a job centre interviewing people all day would be great, but I can't really do that kind of work. Interpersonal relations are an absolute nightmare for me; getting on with people is absolutely terrible. I'm much better left alone to my own devices. So this stuff is in me for a reason. When I first had the schizophrenia, my brain was saying that had been done to me. How would it be my brain if it hadn't been done to me? But I say, well no, it's not real. Mixing with people is absolutely terrible most of the time. When I did the walking group, the bloke that was into computers as well, we hit it off straight away. It was about six weeks, once a week, and we went to the [PLACE] and all the way we were talking about computers and that kind of thing. So I got on really well with him, but that's all tech stuff, internet and Apple iOS and everything. I'm terrible at mixing with people until you give me something to chew on, like with him it was computers, then it immediately becomes OK. Without that, like at my father's birthday thing a couple of years ago, I basically spoke to two people all night. Everyone around me was chit-chatting, having fun, and I'm sat there with all that going through my head. So mixing with people is absolutely terrible, and conversation is, until I get to know somebody a bit and there's some kind of topic to go on. It's probably not just me, but that's what I've had. It would have been great to have been more confident when I was younger. It is an absolute nightmare for me to get along with people and to mix with people, until I get to know people. At the same time I've got almost like poetry going off as well at times, song lyrics and programming and everything, which most people are not really into, so that makes things difficult as well.

I see, yeah. It's almost like you're drawn to doing stuff that you can sort of chew on. Do you think that's because, I think that's something a lot of people find difficult, that the world is kind of geared toward being a bit more extroverted, but there are plenty of people who are more introverted and there's nothing wrong with that at all.
