delusion_points.summary: The participant reports a persistent belief that they were badly abused as a child, including being tied up, which first emerged during a psychotic episode. They acknowledge being told this did not happen and attribute the belief to their schizophrenia diagnosis, expressing uncertainty about what is real.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant states they are told they were not abused, identifies the belief as part of their psychosis, and says 'I don't know what is going on in my head' and 'well no, it's not real'.

case_summary: The participant discusses their extensive creative and technical pursuits, including songwriting, poetry, programming (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python), web design, and photography, with a strong emphasis on structure, alignment, and constraints. They describe a diagnosis of schizophrenia with psychosis, mentioning experiences of hearing voices, a persistent belief about childhood abuse that conflicts with what they are told, and difficulties with social interaction. They find that creative work helps them cope and express themselves, and they reflect on whether their mental health condition influences their creativity.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

messages.content: This study is really just a conversation. There's one main question, and then we'll just chat and expand on your answer. The question is: do you feel like you do creative things with language?
Can you repeat that?
Do you feel like you do creative things with language?

Yes, I do to some extent. I speak every day to fellow residents in the hostel and I talk creatively from time to time. I also write literature, which isn't spoken but is the written word, and I'm creative in that sense too. My main form of creative speech is with residents in the hostel, where I talk originally from time to time.
Did you say 'talk originally'?
Yes, I talk with residents in the hostel and I speak originally.
Can you tell me more about that?
I can't think of any examples at the moment. I said I can't think of any examples at the moment.
That's OK. But is doing something original with language important?
Is it important?
Yes, in the sense that is that one of the reasons you do it—because it's original?
I don't think so, actually. I talk to people anyway, whether I'm original or not.
I see.
But if I'm original, it can be a boon. It can make me feel happy. I have a sense of humour, a wit.
I see, that's really interesting. So have I understood right that it can sometimes happen by accident?
Yes, it's chancy, yes, unintended.
I see, I see. And what's that like?
It's quite pleasing. It gives me a fillip, a boon. It is pleasurable. I like to talk to people anyway, but if I'm creative as well with language, that's a boon.
I see, that's really nice to hear.
Good.

And I suppose in a day-to-day sense, I know you said you can't think of any examples and that's absolutely fine, but I'm really interested in what that process feels like—that involuntary process and everything else you've said as well. Do you mind telling me a bit more about the involuntary side of things first?

Well, as I said, it's unintended. If I make an original speech or use my sense of humour, that is unintended. But I can't think of any examples, which would be helpful. It would be good to think of an example, then I would demonstrate what I'm saying, but I can't think of anything at the moment.
Do you make puns?
Yes, I can make a pun, yes. Something like 'the pointless point'.
I see, yeah, yeah.
yes
erm yeah and and what about metaphors
sorry
and what about like metaphors
metaphors I don't know
erm when you talk about one thing as though it's something else
yes I don't know I can't think of anything there
oh OK erm and when it happens involuntarily, is it like a pleasant surprise then
yes it can be a pleasant surprise to have a turn of phrase or a point of wit it can be surprising and pleasing creativity is quite pleasing
yeah and what kind of literature do you like to write
er I write short stories
oh wow
about people going on holiday families going on holiday that sort of thing
that's brilliant and erm do you have favourite authors
yes one of my favourite authors is [PERSON] I love his novel [TITLE] which is about the great artist [PERSON]
oh OK I haven't read that but I will I want to that sounds good
very good novel that by [PERSON] very fine novel yes
what do you like about the novel like specifically the language

well it's about the stock broker [PERSON] who gave up being a stock broker in [PLACE] at the age of forty and went to live in [PLACE] where he painted beautiful women and had lots of sex so he broke free from the rat race and went to live in [PLACE]
I see
yeah
and are there things about the way that that particular author writes that you enjoy more than other writers
well it's one of my favourite novels I also like [PERSON]
ah and what is it about [PERSON]'s writing that you like
well you know [PERSON] writes mainly about sexual problems which is interesting
Yeah, could you tell me a bit more about how humour and creativity connect, or why humour matters to you in relation to creativity?
Well, humour is important as a way of expressing pleasure. It's nice to make a joke or say something original and witty, and that can be a real boost and very pleasurable.
Yeah, so originality is a big part of it as well?
Yes, it's important to be original.
Can you tell me more about that—why it's important?
I think it's important to create, and if you speak creatively it gives you a vehicle for sharing things with other people that can be pleasurable to you and to them—it can make you laugh.
I see.
If you crack a joke or make a witticism, it can make you laugh, which is a pleasure.
Yeah, is it about connecting with other people in some sense, then?

Yes, I might even make fun of some people in a good-natured way. I come up with phrases like 'wit and Wendy,' which is the wrong way round of saying 'wet and windy'—so if I say 'wit and Wendy,' I make a joke out of 'wet and windy.'
I see. Do you do that often—reverse the words?
Quite often I use a phrase like that, or a spoonerism.
Amazing. Is 'spoonerism' from Charles Dickens—Mrs Spooner, who used to…?
Well, there was a don at Oxford called Professor Spooner who invented the spoonerism, and he came up with phrases like 'erotic blacks,' which is a spoonerism for 'erratic blocks.'
I see. So do you enjoy spoonerisms in relation to humour?

Yes, a spoonerism can be very witty. You tend to get things muddled in the sound of the words, so you turn things upside down or opposite, but it's quite satisfying to make a spoonerism because it clinches your argument and gives you a point of wit at the same time.
I see. Is the sound aspect quite important, then—how words sound?

Yes, the sound is important because it's sort of musical, a spoonerism. It's the wrong way round, which musically you can work out what it means by swapping the words round—it makes spellings different. The main pleasure of a spoonerism is the wit of the inversion or the opposition; it is a pleasure to speak as a spoonerism.
And the spoonerisms that you speak—are they sometimes involuntary, sometimes voluntary?
It varies; sometimes they're unintended, sometimes they're voluntary.
I see.
It varies a lot.
And are there situations where it's more likely to be voluntary or more likely to be involuntary, or is it quite random?
Sort of random, I think.
I see. And is that the case with other things that might pop up in, say, literature—do they happen in your speech as well?
er
or is it mainly spoonerisms
well the spoonerisms are quite common there are other forms of wit like a play on words like a pun as you mentioned before
and is it so am I right in thinking that there's a mixture of voluntary and involuntary ways of speaking that involve playing with language playing with sound
yes that would be correct yes that's right yes

and do you do or which I suppose I'm wondering if one came first like did you have you always played with language voluntarily and then it started happening involuntarily later or have like were they both there or was one there first
well I can't remember exactly at what age I started to speak wittily but wit is important to me
yeah and do you mind telling me a bit more about that like why why it's important to you
It's important to make good-natured fun of things or people because it helps you get along with them better than if you didn't. Wit also makes you laugh, and that's its pleasure.
so would it be fair to say that some of these things are ways to connect and communicate with other people in a way that's also pleasurable for everybody involved
that's right yes
I see yeah and you mentioned the music of language
yes yes

how does how do you experience that like I realise that's quite a vague question but I don't want to influence what you say but I'm really interested in what you're saying so is it how words well I suppose actually the thing I'm trying to ask is when you come up with a witticism do you take inspiration from the sounds of the particular words that you choose

Yes, the sound of language matters to me. Words carry their own meanings and spellings. Sometimes two words with different spellings share the same sound, like 'pleasure' and 'pleisure'—not the correct spelling, but you can write it both ways. Letting the music resonate in the sound can be humorous, and you can get more than one meaning from each word's sound.
I see I see and does that influence the words that you choose when you're speaking to other people

Yes, it can affect my judgment. When I'm talking to people and want to be witty, I can think of two words with similar meanings, different spellings, but the same sound, like 'pleasure' and 'pleisure' as I mentioned.
and do you find that well how do other people respond to your wit do they like do some people not quite get it it takes them a little while to
yes they don't always understand my jokes but they laugh when they understand which is the main object of the exercise
yeah yeah but
yeah
it takes them a little while because they have to they almost have to sort of compare the words and see
yes they have to fathom my meaning from the sound of the word or the words and if they understand me they laugh which is a pleasure to me again
and is the process of other people fathoming your meaning part of what's pleasurable
yes it is pleasurable to make people understand and communicate and make contact with people and share an idea on a common basis that we both understand that is a pleasure
Yeah, and do you feel understood by other people?
Yes, when someone understands me, it registers in my voice and eyes, and we share and communicate together. That's important.
So the sense I get is that humor is a great way to communicate complex ideas in a way that's mutually enjoyable.
That's right, that's a good way of putting it. Yes, very good.
Oh, thank you. Do you—
Do you do it to communicate complex ideas?

Well, not necessarily. I don't like to be complicated, but every now and then I make a joke that's difficult to understand. I might make a joke like, 'What do you call a man with a stick in his leg?' and the answer is 'Rodney.'
Yeah.
That's the sort of joke I like. It's not completely creative on my part, but it is a witticism.
I see.
I like jokes like that, where you expect a double entendre.

That's really interesting. It seems to be about wordplay, communication, and connection. Is humor a good vehicle for communicating with people who may not experience the same things you do? Is it a good bridge?
I'm not sure. Sometimes if I crack a joke and they don't understand, I leave it there and don't press them on the point.
Yeah.
If they understand, it is a pleasure to share, and it can be a vehicle for pleasure and sharing.
I see. It's so interesting to hear not only what you like about creative language and playing with language, but also how it's related to connecting with other people.
Yes, that's right.
When you write creatively, is there a difference between how you write creatively and how you speak creatively?

Yes, writing tends to be more sustained, complicated, and logical than my everyday speech. I don't speak at great length, but I do write at length, which is one of the pleasures of writing. I get a sustained run of words and expression. I write with much greater length and complexity than I speak in daily life.
I see. In your experience, why do you think those things are different?
Sorry?
In your experience, why do you think those things are different?

Well, if you write, you have time to think to yourself more, and you can break up the writing and the flow into nuggets or bits of expression or creativity that you can take your time to think about. If you're talking to people and you take your time to think about it, you have to have a pause or a lull or a period of silence. It tends not to work very well for conversation.
Yeah.
So the beauty of writing is you can write at length and take your time about it.
I see. And something you said earlier made me think of another question: when you write, is there that same involuntary aspect?

Yes, it can be more involuntary to write than to speak. You have more opportunity to dig into your depths and come up with ideas, which is more possible in writing than in everyday speech. I think writing is more creative than speech. Oh, do you mind if I ask about that a bit more? Yes, go ahead.
Why do you think writing is more creative than speech?
All I would say is that writing is more involved and more powerful than the spoken word.
I see.

But if you are a lecturer or a speaker and you prepare long speeches to share and demonstrate, that's a bit like writing at length in your own domain. In everyday speech you don't have that much opportunity to plan a long speech; it can be quite difficult to speak at length, but it's much easier to write at length.
Yeah. Are there differences in the involuntary things that happen for you when you're speaking versus when you're writing?
I'd say there's more involuntary interest in writing than in speech, but speech can be very witty, which is one of the pleasures of speaking.
I see. What do you like about creative language, just in general?

My main interest in creative language is an exploration of ideas, the imagination, or fantasy, which communicates a deep interest in the material you're writing about. By writing you share this opportunity of thinking with other people who read your literature when you publish your books. Although I'm unpublished, I do get pleasure from writing on the basis that I can share at depth what I'm thinking and feeling. As I say, if you write you have more opportunity to share in depth than if you speak.
I see. What kind of ideas and thoughts do you like to use writing to explore in depth?

I like to explore relationships, including sexual relationships. I like to explore travelling, going to places, visiting places, going on holiday, going to famous buildings and sightseeing. My main pleasure is in studying relationships, which you can't do so easily in everyday speech.
Yeah, I know what you mean. Is it the interpersonal aspect of relationships?

I'd say it's about the feelings you have for someone else or the feelings you have as a partnership—partly sexual feelings, partly love, partly ideas, partly affection. One of my main pleasures of writing is to study a relationship between two people.
Have you always been interested in relationships and the sharing of ideas in relationships?

Yes, I'd say that's been a lifelong interest, not just as a writer but as a speaker in everyday speech. I like to get on with people, share things with people, and develop relationships, which is important to me.
Yeah, I feel the same. I agree, and I understand how writing can be a way to explore that.

That's right. Writing can help you to speak in everyday terms too, sort of as a point of research that trades off in speaking and conversation. The more you write about relationships, the more you make relationships in everyday life and share and communicate with other people.
That's—
So writing's important in that sense as a basis for research, a bit like a quarry out of which you hew interesting rocks and stones.

I see. Like the process of exploration helps you to—well, would it be fair to say, because you said a few interesting rocks and stones out of the quarry, that a lot of that exploration is looking for specific things?

As I say, writing and thinking about relationships feeds back into relating to people in daily life. The more you write and think about them, the better you communicate and try to form connections. Writing can help with that.
I see. Have you written for a long time, then?
Yes, for many years. I've been writing for thirty or forty years.
Wow, I see. What sparked your interest in writing?
Reading other authors, like [AUTHOR] and [AUTHOR], partly inspired me to write my own books.
And have you written a lot?
I've written quite a lot of short stories, a couple of books, and a few short novels.
Wow.
My output varies from year to year. Some years I'm very active and fertile, other years not so much. It's not a fixed thing; it varies considerably.
Yeah, creativity sort of does its own thing sometimes, doesn't it?
That's right. It has a will of its own. You can follow it and develop it in your mind with your imagination, entering into a flight of fancy which is fun to explore.
That reminds me of a line from [POET]: 'He who seeks to follow joy as it flies basks in eternity's sunrise.'
Yes, very good.
Like following the creativity without trying to catch it, just following it.
Yes, yes.
That's amazing. Thank you so much for talking to me about this. I need to head off in about ten minutes, and I'm really grateful you've given so much time to this conversation. It means a lot.
OK, well it's been nice talking to you, doctor.
You too, thank you so much. Is there anything that we...
OK.
...haven't talked about that you'd like to talk about?
No, I don't think so. I think we've been quite comprehensive.
Yeah, I think so. I'm sorry to ask so many follow-up questions; it's just so interesting that I want to know more.
That's good.
It's been an absolute pleasure to meet you. Thank you so much.
OK, lovely. Thank you very much.
Have a lovely afternoon, and the rest of the week, and beyond.
And you.
Thanks so much.
And you, lovely. Thank you.
Take care, thank you.
Bye now.
Bye.

case_summary: The participant, a resident in a hostel, discusses their creative use of language in both speech and writing. They describe using wit, puns, and spoonerisms in everyday conversation, sometimes voluntarily and sometimes involuntarily, as a pleasurable way to connect with others. They also write short stories and novels, primarily exploring relationships and travel, viewing writing as a more sustained and powerful form of creativity than speech.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant describes creative language use, humor, and the pleasure of social connection. There are no expressed beliefs about external reality that indicate a delusion. The discussion of involuntary wit is framed as a common experience of spontaneous creativity, not as a belief about external control or interference.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

messages.content: So, there's really just one interview question, and then the rest is a conversation about it. The question is: do you feel like you do creative things with language?
Right. Do I do creative things with language? No, I don't. I don't think I would say I'm creative with language.
Okay. Do you mind telling me a bit more about that and why you feel that way?

I mean, when I was quite unwell, I was thinking about language in a very different way. The way I was thinking wasn't always coherent and it was unusual, but I don't know if I would classify it as being creative.
I see. And thinking about everyday language use, what role does language play for you?
Currently?
Yeah.

The ideas I was thinking about when I was ill, I sometimes still think about them now, although I don't take them to be reality all the time. Those ideas stay playing at the back of my mind. I was reading about relational frame theory—I don't know if you've heard of that—but it was interesting because they look at the links between words and meanings. It reminded me of the way I was thinking when I was ill, although my thinking wasn't always coherent.
Are you comfortable talking about that time? I'm thinking about asking, if you wouldn't mind.
I'm okay talking about that.
Oh, okay. I just wanted to check. It would be really great to hear more about the links you were making, if you're happy to talk about them.

Well, I think I was just trying to understand things. I didn't really have an understanding of basic concepts in life, like how relationships work or the meaning of religion. I was thinking about all these themes. At the time, I thought, let me look at the English language and try to break it down to see if I can find anything that confirms my beliefs in my religion and how I live my life. I was just trying to break down the words and the English language out of interest, because I was ill and not doing much else. I was looking at links between words. One of my psychiatrists pointed out it was more about what a phrase meant to me rather than what it would mean to everybody else. So these were very personal interpretations I was making about language. I was looking at sentences and maybe rhyming in the sentences, wondering how many different meanings there are and whether you could say there's actually only one answer. But I think it's just one answer for that person, for myself, subjectively.
I see. And was it mainly rhyming then, or were there other things about words as well?

Well, I was looking at the words and the rhyming, trying to understand sentences and what they meant to me from the different words in a sentence. But I was looking at numbers too and wondering how that fitted in. So, the language and numbers as well.
Would it be fair to say that looking at language from different ways was part of a sense-making process?

Yes, I was trying to make sense of everything at that time. I was very confused and, to be honest, I wasn't very mature then. I've got more life experience now. Like I said, I was just trying to make sense of my religion, my relationships, my place in the world, just by trying to look at the language.
I see. Looking back on the ways you were looking at language then and thinking about how you look at language now, what things have changed?

I think I'm not so totally rigid. I was very emotional at the time and very rigid in my thinking. Instead of thinking of it as exploratory, I was taking it too personally and linking it to my religion too much. Now, sometimes if I rhyme something, I'll just think, oh, that's interesting, but I don't take it as being a hundred percent correct way of looking at the world.
I see. And—
So I'm not as rigid as I used to be when I was quite ill and thinking like that.
Because you said when you rhyme things—
Yeah.
Does that mean that sometimes you say things that rhyme without meaning to?

No, I don't say things like that anymore. I just think things like that sometimes, but I put it into perspective now. I just find it something that's interesting if I think of something that rhymes. I think about it and think, oh, that's interesting, but I don't really take that any further or think that it's reality or anything.
I see. So with rhymes, is sound an important aspect, or is it more—
I don't think it's the sound so much; I think I visualize the words more. When I think about something that rhymes, it's more visual than auditory.
I see.
yeah
like
So I'll see the sentence and I'll put in the rhyming words. It's more visual.
Do you mind if I ask for an example? I know it's very difficult to think of examples, especially when someone asks, but do any come to mind?
A couple do, but they're a bit personal. I'm just trying to think if there's anything that isn't personal.
sure sure
It's difficult off the top of my head.
no no that's fine
yeah
So if they tend to be personal...
The two that come to mind at the moment are a little bit personal, but not always. Sometimes it's just about generic things.
And do you think about them at specific times, or is it more random?
I don't really think about them anymore. It's just something from the past that I remember because it had a lot of meaning for me at the time.
oh I see yeah yeah so
yeah yeah
oh OK and which sounds quite... well I don't know, it sounds...

At the time, like I say, there was not much else that I was doing and I wasn't active, so I think most of the activity was taking place within my mind. Now I've got a lot to do and I'm living more in the real world, doing things a lot more rather than just sitting there and just thinking and thinking.
yeah
yeah

And in a broader sense about creativity and that sort of thing, because there's no right answer. I speak to lots of different people and some say yes, I think I do creative things with language, and some say no, not so much. Neither of those responses are correct or incorrect.
yes

to lots of different people and some people say erm yeah I think I do do creative things with language and some people say no not so much and th neither of those responses are are correct or or or incorrect erm
mm yeah
But in both cases it's really interesting to hear how people feel about creativity as well.
Yeah.
When you see creative language, like in adverts, puns, or very visual or poetic language in literature, books, and poems, what do you make of it?

I find it quite daunting to approach poetry, for example. I'm not particularly good at interpreting it. I think it's something I find difficult; if I read a complex poem, I wouldn't really get a hundred percent out of it. It's not a strength of mine.
I see, yeah.

I do get some poetry. I haven't really been exposed to much of it myself. I read a poem by T. S. Eliot that was strong and striking, so there are a few I've come across. But I find it difficult to read and understand poetry compared to prose and plain language.
And is that related to the fact that poetry uses language in such a way that so many different meanings are possible?
Yeah.
Is that part of it, that there are so many meanings?
Yes, I think most poems are very intricate, very complex, and very difficult to understand from my perspective.
And in terms of communicating with other people, just everyday conversation—
Yeah.
Do you find, when other people are creative with language, like with humour and such, how is that for you?
My sister is an English teacher, so—
Ah, I see.

She's more into using language like that to communicate sometimes. I think I keep up okay with my siblings when they're making jokes about anything involving language. It hasn't been a problem or a difficulty keeping up. I really just interact with my family, my siblings, and two or three friends, and I've not had any problems with the way they use language creatively. I do it myself as well; it's not been a big problem at all.
Is it more, then, that it's less about creative language being a difficulty and more about interest—that it's just less interesting?
I don't know. I admire creative writing, complex writing, and poetry, but I think you're right, it's probably not at the top of my list of interests.
I see, yeah, yeah.
Yeah.
And if you don't mind, do you mind if I ask about your interests and hobbies?

Yes, I've always been fascinated by psychiatry, even when I was young. Unfortunately, I fell ill and couldn't pursue a medical career, but thankfully I completed my master's in psychiatry from university and got a distinction. It was great; I really enjoyed doing the course. So I spend a lot of my time reading around psychiatry. I also like listening to the radio a lot—different programs, current affairs, and topics on history, art, literature, as well as psychology, medicine, and psychiatry. I have very broad interests.
That's— mm.
Most of my time is spent, I suppose, just reading a lot.
That's wonderful about the master's and the distinction, by the way. That's really nice to hear.
yeah
Has that course and reading about psychiatry played a role for you generally? I imagine it's been really helpful, but has it?

Looking back, when I was young I didn't really think about life, I just studied a lot and did very well. Then I fell ill and all I did was think about things in my head. After I came out of that period, I started focusing on real life and how everyone else functions, worked my way up, and did the master's. Now I suppose I have a more balanced, realistic view of life and don't think too much about how I was when I was ill.
I see. And with listening to the radio, the topics you like sound more like non-fiction, much more about information.
yeah
Do you choose the radio because you prefer it to, say, TV?
I can't afford, or I don't want to pay for a TV license at the moment, so I'm listening to the radio because I don't need a license for those programs.
Ah, I see. I don't have a TV license either.
yeah

I don't really want to pay for the TV license myself; we don't have one here. I don't know if you find this as well, but I find that sometimes not having the visuals makes me focus more on the information when it's just the sound. Do you find the same, or is it different for you?

At the moment, I fit in radio programs while I'm exercising, so I sometimes miss bits of it. It's a little difficult to focus on just the words, but the good thing is I can rewind if I really miss a big chunk.

I see. By the way, I'm finding this really interesting, but if at any point you feel like you'd like to end the call but feel you have to stay, you can always tell me you'd like to go now, and that's totally fine. It's really interesting hearing so many different perspectives about language and creativity. Do you find that creativity or creative language helps communication, or not so much?

I think being creative with language can be fun sometimes when we're making jokes with my siblings. My sister often puts in a creative joke here and there that's fun. I think creativity with language can be interesting and fun sometimes.
And do you find it fun?
Yes, I often think that just thinking creatively or laterally can give you a new perspective on things sometimes.
Yeah. Do you mind if I ask more about that? In what kinds of situations, or what do you mean by that?
It's difficult to say off the top of my head.

It's quite a vague question, really. I suppose what I mean is, in terms of where creativity could be useful, are there specific situations where creative language might be more useful or more fun than other situations?
For myself, I wouldn't really use creative language too much in my studies, but with family and friends and during recreation, I think it's a good thing to use.
I see. So have I understood correctly that it's maybe more appropriate in certain situations than others?
Yes, I think so.
I see. Is there anything about creative language that we haven't talked about that you'd like to discuss?
No, I can't think of anything off the top of my head that I would particularly want to highlight.
OK, that's fine. More generally, is there anything you'd like to ask about the project?
I'm just wondering about the size of the project—how many participants are taking part?
So, we have two parts: a creative language experiment part
Yeah.
and then an interview part. Overall, for the experiment there will be at least thirty people,
Yeah.
but probably more. Everyone who does the experiment will be invited to do an interview as well,
Yes.

but we're also interviewing people—especially now because face-to-face work is hard—who are interested in the interview but aren't available for the experiment. I think overall we'll probably be looking at between sixty and ninety people.
And would that be spread out throughout the UK, or...?

Yeah, yeah. We're working with an NHS Trust in the North of England and one in the South of England as well, so we're recruiting from both ends of the UK really, hoping to speak to as many people from different areas as possible.

Yes. Just one thing, probably on a tangent. I think when I'm writing something up, I've learned that I have to be really, really careful because sometimes my ideas can be a little bit illogical. So I have to work quite hard at going through it and making sure it does make sense. I don't think that's something that comes naturally to me. I don't know if other people have problems with that as well, but I work quite hard to make my written assignments logical and written in a logical sequence.
Oh, I see. Yeah, like...
Yeah.
I think that's something that—because one of the things about writing, and editing as well, is that it's very hard to decide in what order to present the idea, you know?
Yeah.
Because sometimes
Yeah.
presenting the idea in a beginning, middle, and end sequence
Yeah.
is quite helpful, but then sometimes presenting an idea in an end, beginning, middle sequence is also quite helpful—by saying, you know, 'because of this and this, this is what needs to happen'.
Yeah.
Then another way of saying it is, 'this is what needs to happen because this and this'.
Yeah.
And I think that's about style, you know, your style choices in some ways.

Yeah, yeah. Well, I just learn that I have to put a lot of attention into that to make sure it's correct. I don't know how I managed to get a distinction for my master's, but I was looking through some material on the difference between descriptive writing, analytical writing, and evaluative writing. It's quite new to me, the material I was reading about these three ways of writing. I think things are getting a bit clearer, but yes, I luckily have a natural style of writing that covers description, analysis, and evaluation—I suppose I naturally developed some skill in that. But to look through and really assess a piece of work and say which bits are descriptive, analytical, or evaluative, I'm struggling at the moment. It's something I'm working on so that I can read something and assess it really critically.
I see. Yeah, I think that's something that's very hard to do generally, like...
yeah
because evaluative writing can be descriptive and analytical
yeah
and the same with the others I think
yeah
it's one of those things we tend to overthink
yeah
is it evaluative because it has some descriptive bits? I think sometimes it's helpful to just think about what it's doing the most
yeah
like, is this section mostly describing, with some evaluation and analysis
yeah
but its main purpose is... that's just one way of thinking about it
yeah
like

I think that's analysing written work, criticising it critically. But I just went through a module that was describing how to critically evaluate an image. They presented a portrait of a woman who assassinated someone during the French Revolution. It was a picture of her having her hair cut before her execution. The task was to analyse the image and write a short essay on one's perceptions of the portrait. That is one of the best examples of something I would find very difficult—to look at a picture and then describe it, analyse it, and evaluate what's going on just by looking at an image. The module's description of how it should be written was very interesting but very, very difficult. I was looking at that assignment and thinking I would never be able to write something like that, just to look at a portrait and then describe it, link ideas together about it, and then link it to who painted it and the period it was painted in. That's probably the sort of thing I would really, really struggle with.

I see. Do you mind if I ask what the points of difficulty there would be? I follow what you've said about linking the ideas and the history, but from a technical writing perspective, what aspects of the writing in that task would you find difficult?

The ideas they were writing up are things I would really not think of. I think it's the linking together of all the themes that arise from that portrait—I would find it difficult to link it all together in a way that really flows. I'd also find it a bit difficult to make it... I struggle with the logical aspects of putting it together as well. I looked at the model answer and compared it to my ideas, and my ideas were very limited. I only came up with a few of the things they included. To get anywhere near the model answer, I'd have to spend a very long time thinking about it and trying to write it up. It wouldn't be something that would come naturally for me.
I see. Do you mind if I ask about the model answer and your answers—what was different between them?

I'm afraid I didn't spend a lot of time working on my answer. I think I missed a lot of the details. I knew it was about the woman from the portrait. They came up with ideas like this lady is quite wealthy because of her expensive dress, and she's having her hair cut, which possibly signifies some sort of humiliation for women to have their hair cut off. There's someone painting her picture—I did notice the painting palette but I didn't notice a picture frame. Then they talked about the quill pen on one side and a sort of knife on the other side and the implications of that. I wouldn't have picked that up. I didn't pick up the quill or the knife and the implications that the knife possibly relates to the fact that she assassinated someone. These things I wouldn't normally think like that.

I see. I wonder whether there's something in there about how the person who wrote the model answer might have been doing things differently—whether they might have been almost giving themselves license to talk about things they didn't actually have evidence for in the picture, do you know what I mean?
yes
like allowing themselves to kind of fabricate details
yes
erm

Interestingly, the way they were thinking in the model answer was interesting. But the thing it reminded me of was how I was thinking when I was ill, except that they were verifying it with facts and historical details, whereas when I was ill I was thinking about things but there was nothing to support any of my thoughts or ideas.
I see. Would you mind telling me a bit more about that? I think it would be really good to unpack in more detail, if that's OK.

Yes. I might have thought of a word, rhymed it, and come up with a concept. But the way they were looking at the portrait, they had historical details about it and knew the facts related to it. So the ideas they were coming up with, they could substantiate. For example, the palette knife—it does sound a bit strange that they're linking it to the fact that she's killed someone, but because of the situation, it's something they have supported. They've linked together an actual fact with an idea they've come up with. For example, they were talking about the fact that she's in an expensive white dress, and the white dress implicates purity. It is quite true that in our society, a woman in a white dress can be linked to someone who is quite pure.

I see. So have I understood right that the difference has something to do with the idea that the people writing the model answer were linking their ideas to a feature of the painting, and that the ideas you've had in the past weren't linked to features in the environment, but the mechanism was similar? Is that right?

That's right. I think the mechanism—the way I was thinking and the way they were thinking about the portrait—the mechanisms were similar, but mine was a little bit more erratic and there was nothing in reality that was actually supporting it. So although they're making creative assumptions, they at the same time have links to reality that support their propositions.
I see. That's really interesting, because it's interesting to hear that the mechanisms are similar in some way, or feel similar.
Yeah.
Or share aspects, maybe. In terms of images generally and visuals, how do you feel about paintings, songs, creative uses of non-language things?

At the moment with COVID I can't, but I did enjoy going to art galleries and looking at the paintings. It's very nice visually to look at some of these really good paintings. But I think it's more relaxation for me, something that just relaxes me. Music I'm not really into—music with lyrics, or music's not something that's important to me these days. I enjoyed it when I was younger. I think because I spend so much of my time reading, non-language things like paintings, watching films, or drama series—that's very much relaxation. I always chill in the evenings watching something and I find that very relaxing.
That's really nice to hear. Thank you so much for giving so much of your time to talking to me. I can't thank you enough, I really appreciate it.
That's OK. I hope that what I've said will be helpful to you for your project.

Yeah, everything everyone says is amazingly helpful. The project's interested in how people think about these things and what's important to people about them. So everything that everyone says is brilliant because it's what's important to them. I really appreciate your time, thank you so much.
OK.
Before I go, is there anything we haven't talked about that you'd like to talk about?
Yes, I would really appreciate getting a copy of the study results that you will be distributing to the participants.
Yeah, of course.
What would be the best way to get that, and when do you think it would be available?

In terms of when it'll be available, we're going to continue recruiting until the end of 2022, but we might collect enough data before then. So the results might be ready in the middle of next year, or they might not be ready until the middle or the end of 2022. In terms of the best way to get them, I can send them to [ORG] to distribute them. Part of the arrangement we have is that we handle the minimum amount of personal information possible, so I only have your phone number. I couldn't email them or post them to you directly, but I could ask someone at [ORG] to post them. The main thing is how you'd like to receive them.
Will it be possible for you to email them to me?
Yeah, if you're happy for me to have your email address, then I can totally do that. That's absolutely fine.
Oh, thank you. Have you got some paper?

Yeah, I'll just grab a pen. What we might find is that we might be able to share some results before some of the others, because we might collect enough interview data before we collect enough experimental data, for example. So we might be able to share some results earlier, or it might be that they're all ready about the same time. But yeah, I've got a pen.
OK, it's all lower case, so that's all one word at [CONTACT].
So [CONTACT]?
Yes, that's right.

Brilliant, awesome. If you're happy for me to have that on file, I'll just add it to a list of email addresses of everyone who's asked to have the results by email. Then it'll all go into an anonymised email, so it'll all be blind copied.
yeah OK
and you'll get an email with the results. I'm excited to share them.
ah OK

yeah, it's been so nice talking to people, particularly about creativity and language, but also everything else. I'm looking forward to discussing how we looked at the data and sharing that. I'd be very happy to share it.
OK, thank you. I look forward to reading that.
yeah, I look forward to sharing. thank you so much for your time today, I really appreciate it. it was a pleasure to meet you. have a lovely week and beyond. it's really nice to meet you.
you too. OK, bye bye.
take care, bye bye.
oh, bye bye.

delusion_points.summary: During a past period of illness, the participant believed they could find personal, subjective confirmations of their religious beliefs and life meaning by breaking down the English language, looking for links between words, rhymes, and numbers.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant frames this as a past state of being 'quite unwell,' acknowledges the thinking was not always coherent, notes a psychiatrist pointed out the interpretations were purely personal, and states they no longer take these thoughts as reality.

case_summary: The participant discusses their relationship with creative language, stating they do not consider themselves creative with language. They describe a past period of illness where they engaged in idiosyncratic, personal interpretations of language, rhymes, and numbers to find meaning and confirm religious beliefs. They now view this as a symptom of being unwell and have gained perspective, though some thoughts occasionally resurface without being taken as reality. The participant has a master's in psychiatry, enjoys reading and radio, and finds complex poetry and visual analysis challenging. They note a similarity between their past thought mechanisms and the interpretive work of art analysis, but distinguish their past thoughts as lacking factual grounding.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

messages.content: There's only one interview question: do you feel like you use language creatively?
Sometimes I think more colourfully than creatively—maybe that's the same thing, I don't know.
I really like that expression. Do you mind telling me more about what you mean?

Well, I heard voices for many years. To deal with them—since I live alone and nobody can hear me—I swear at them vociferously. But I find that using the same swear words all the time doesn't help, so I have to be creative in finding new swear words to react to them. That's what I mean by colourfully rather than creative—for example, turning the air blue, so that's like a colour.
I see.
Does that make sense?
Yeah, like in the metaphoric sense?
Yeah, yeah.
I see. Is that an area you'd be happy to talk about? I don't want to ask about things that might be uncomfortable.
No, I'm fine with it. To be fair, I've been involved in so many research projects over the years and run a hearing voices group, so nothing fazes me anymore. Please do ask questions.

Thank you. I'm really interested in all of what you said, but specifically the need to come up with different swear words and how that helps. That's really interesting and not something I've heard before.

I just find it cathartic. It gives me a little bit of energy in responding to them, though sometimes responding in any way doesn't help get rid of them—it doesn't always work. That's where creativity comes in, because you have to think of new ways to get rid of them or put them on hold. One thing our group members say is, if we're out in public and the voices are disturbing us, you don't have to say it out loud—just say in your head, 'Come back later at 6 p.m. and I'll give you ten minutes.' It's just a different way of approaching them. I don't know if that could be called creative or not. What do you think?
I think that definitely is. There are so many different types of creativity, and I think that's more than one happening at once—creativity around problem-solving, creativity around communication.
Exactly.
And do lots of people find that that helps?
Anecdotally, yes. I know a lot of people it helps. It's not a be-all and end-all for everyone—it's just one of many strategies we use, and it works for some people and may not work for others.

Yeah, definitely. When it comes to language in song lyrics, books, and films, are there particular ways of speaking or using language that stand out as interesting to you, or that you like to incorporate into your own use of language?

I'm not sure I completely understand that question. I read a lot, and I do find certain films and books helpful with voices. For example, one film in particular, A Beautiful Mind, is a lovely film about a true story and quite uplifting about someone who was clearly very distressed with voices but was an extraordinary mathematician.
[PERSON].
Yes, [PERSON], yeah.
Yeah, it's an amazing film, A Beautiful Mind.
That's just one of many. I may have gone off on a tangent—I'm sorry, maybe I didn't really understand the question.

No, no, it's—I was wondering if there are things you see and hear in terms of language, whether written or spoken anywhere, that are more interesting than others. For example, what you said about using language colourfully really stood out to me as a really inventive thing.
Mhm.

Doing something with language that allows me to understand what you're saying at a deeper level than if you'd used a phrase that's more common. I wonder if there are things where, when people say certain things, you think, 'Oh, that's really interesting.'

Yes, I think so. I hear many different stories from our members about their past, and it's sometimes very difficult for them to open up. We all have our own way of communicating our stories, and none of them are the same—we don't have one thing in common, they're completely different. It's a way of accepting everybody's story and the way they tell it. I don't think that's answering your question, sorry.
I think it does, yeah. It's really important to acknowledge all the individual differences in how we communicate.
Yeah.
And...
I'm sorry, but during this call I keep getting something incoming on the mobile which is distracting me somewhat.
You keep hearing something, sorry?
A friend has been phoning me during this conversation, leaving me messages, so I'm getting a bit distracted. Obviously you're not getting it on your end, but on my end it says incoming call.
Oh, I see. Do you want to...
No, no, she's gone off, it's gone off now. I'm just saying sorry, I was distracted a bit.
Oh no, that's OK. In the groups that you facilitate...
Mhm.
Does creativity come up a lot?
What, verbally or other forms of creativity?
Like as a topic that people talk about.

Yes, in terms of creative outlets that we do, like cooking or baking, or artists, drawing or colouring, or whatever creative artistic ways. But is this to do with language, or just other forms of creativity?
Do you mind if we talk about them? That's... yeah, I'd love to know more about how those creative activities that aren't so related to language...

Well, one thing that helps: in our actual group session, about half the group likes to do some colouring during the group, and it helps them relax, feel more comfortable, and actually open up. Many members are very talented and bring their talents to the group. One member makes delicious cakes she brings in, which helps us open up and adds a social, informal aspect. Another member designed our website years ago and now produces a quarterly newsletter, with other members contributing photos of their activities.
That sounds amazing.
Erm.
That sounds really nice.
Sorry.
That sounds amazing, that sounds like a really nice thing to do as a group and for the group.
Mm, it works.
Yeah, because that's a theme that's coming out of a lot of my conversations with people, is that having a creative outlet is really important.
Mhm, mm.
and do you

One thing that helps me personally is knitting. It really helps me relax in the evenings, knitting in front of the television. I find that for many voice hearers, concentration can be quite difficult, whether it's on TV, reading, or whatever. That's where creativity comes in again—having a different outlet to focus on when concentration is an issue. Sometimes it's easier to have a little project you're good at.
yeah

Going back to language, I think we have different ways of using it. Our group is very diverse, from many different backgrounds, and that comes across in how people express themselves. You have to tune in to their particular way of talking.
and what are those ways of talking like
Perhaps sometimes a bit disjointed. You have to pick the bones out of what they're saying and listen quite carefully.
I see yeah
yeah
and as a listener, how do you find that

Difficult, to be honest. But fortunately I don't run the group alone. I have a co-facilitator who has worked in mental health for over twenty-five years, and she's a much better listener than I am. She's great at getting our members to open up and picking up on all their points and reflecting them back.
it sounds like you're a good listener yourself, to be able to tell me about them
thank you
do you find you have to switch the way you listen, since people talk in different ways

Yes, I think you do. It took me a long time to learn not to pretend to understand but to say if I don't understand—to ask what they mean. Personally I find that difficult. I'm a people pleaser; I don't like telling someone I don't understand. But isn't it better to be honest than to nod and agree with something you don't actually follow?
yeah, that's a very difficult one. I totally agree it's better to be honest when you don't understand, but I've had experiences where I worry that saying so might upset the person.
Exactly, you've put your finger on it. That's exactly how I've found it—that's the reason I sometimes pretend to understand, but I feel like a fraud in doing so.
I see. But my interpretation would be that I wouldn't see it as fraud if you're still trying to understand.
right
you know what I mean
yes yeah
but yeah, it's a really tough situation
mm
and does that come up often in communication in the group
Yeah, I think so. More so with new members.
and then over time as you get to know them does that
yeah
get easier
yep yeah
well it sounds like an amazing group that I'm sure everyone there finds really helpful
I mean to be honest I love all of our group members they're wonderful human beings and we get on so well together we're very lucky
that sounds really lovely how long have you been doing the group
erm sixteen years
wow wow
yes a long time
and I'd love to know about how you started it

oh gosh well many years ago I was a patient in an old Victorian asylum called [PLACE] and I met a lady, a friend and fellow patient. when the hospital closed and they moved to care in the community, we decided, as both voice hearers, to set up a peer support group. to backtrack a bit, I had been involved in the psychiatric survivor movement in the late eighties and nineties. my friend and I went to specialised hearing voices facilitation training, and two of the trainers were the very famous [PERSON] and [PERSON], founders of the hearing voices movement. we set up a group, very small at first, in what was then a clubhouse. that venue closed, we got a new one, and we just grew over the years. our new cofacilitator has been with us over three years now and she's fantastic, because my original cofacilitator moved to [PLACE] to be with her family. so that's how we set up the group
wow that's amazing
so
and so do you does it run how often does it run
well during the pandemic we haven't been running it at all except over the telephone. we can't even do Zoom because most of our members don't have the tech for it
oh I see yeah

but yes, when we're back up and running we'll go back to once a week for two hours. there's a big social aspect to the group as well. we go on a lot of outings together, whether locally, boat trips, seaside trips, Christmas meals, bowling—you name it, we've done it. our members love that because a lot of them are quite socially isolated
yeah that sounds like just an amazing atmosphere to be in and
thanks

it's such a good thing to do and really inspiring, because it shows how much good can be done in a group setting and around group activities. I think it makes an example of the sorts of things that could be integrated into services a bit more, you know
so did you know anything about the hearing voices network while doing this research or is this all new to you

I know about it, I've heard the name hearing voices network. I know less about the hearing voices movement. I know about peer support groups and things like that, but specifically about what groups do, I know less about what happens in them. it sounds like the combination of doing activities together and having a place to exchange experiences and ideas—all of those things coming together—I just think that's
I don't know how this helps you with your research though
well it so the type of analysis I'm doing is about conversation
right
I'm analysing the conversations I have with people, the way we talk about things. I've discussed all kinds of topics—we always start with creativity—but then we might move on to other subjects.
Have I said anything helpful, or has it all just been a load of waffle?
No, not at all. Everything's been helpful. Do you feel like you haven't been? Because you have been really helpful.
Thank you, good. I don't want to turn it into a rant or something inappropriate.
No, no.
Anyway, yeah.
And I apologise if I've steered things in that direction.
No, no. Thank you, anyway. I'm going to have to go because it's driving me mad—someone keeps trying to get hold of me on the phone.
Sure, OK.
If we could...
Yeah, yeah.
...wind this down.
Yeah, well thank you so much for your time. I really appreciate it, thank you.
You're welcome, and good luck with your research.
Thank you very much.
It would be lovely if you could let me know how you get on.
Yeah, yeah. If you...
Shall I give you my email address?
Yeah, I can add your email to the mailing list and then you'll get updates on how the study's going.
That would be great. OK, so do you know my email address or shall I give it to you?
No, I don't have it. I'll just grab a pen, OK.
It's [CONTACT].
Yep.
Yep.
...at dot com.
Great, thank you. I'll add your email address to the mailing list now.
Great.
Everyone is anonymous to each other, so it's all blind copied. I'll send the publication of the results, but also less formal updates on where the project is and that sort of thing.
Excellent, that would be great. Thank you.
Thank you.
Like I said, good luck.
Thank you so much.
Alright, bye. Take care.
Take care, bye.
Bye.

case_summary: The participant is a long-time voice hearer and co-facilitator of a hearing voices peer support group. They discuss using creative, colorful swearing as a cathartic strategy to manage their voices, and describe various coping techniques used by group members, such as scheduling time for voices. The conversation covers the group's creative activities (coloring, baking, knitting), the diversity of communication styles among members, and the challenges of listening and understanding. The participant reflects on their own difficulty admitting when they don't understand someone, and the history and social aspects of the group they've helped run for sixteen years.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant describes the experience of hearing voices and practical coping strategies, but does not express any delusional beliefs about the origin, nature, or intent of the voices. The voices are discussed as a manageable phenomenon, and no fixed false beliefs about external reality are presented.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

messages.content: There's really just one question, and then the rest is a chat for as long as you like about it: do you feel you do creative things with language?
What do you mean by language?
However you define it, really.

So, yeah, I'm young, I'm twenty-two, so I'm very active and happy all the time. I like cheering people up, I'm always smiling. I used to play football, so I'm still a very energetic person because I did sport from a young age.
Oh nice.
I did boxing and played for a football club, so I've kind of been...
Oh wow.

I've kind of been a sport person from my teens, and then I had a bit of a mental health relapse, and now I'm at the best point in my life. I speak in a very upbeat way, I'm very happy, I'm always open to talk, and I think I'm good with my language, you know what I mean?
Yeah, yeah. And in terms of music or art?
Yeah, so I'm a rapper.
Are you?
Yeah, I'm a rapper.
Do you mind if we talk about that and about your process?
Yeah, of course you can.
That'd be great.
Yeah, of course you can, man.
Do you like to freestyle?

Well, I write music. I'm not really a freestyler like Eminem. I'm more like Tupac in the way he comes across and talks about the poverty he struggled with in the community, about his mum and how much he loves her, and about the wrong in the world. The way I talk, I talk about pain in mine, like my journeys.
Yeah, yeah.
So my music's all about pain and talking about real things. I don't talk about things I haven't done.
Yeah.

Everything's fact, everything's real. When I first started doing music, I wanted to do it at a young age, like sixteen, but I didn't want to release anything because I was so young and didn't want to ruin my career before it started. So I was building up, listening to music, working out how people move, seeing how it worked, and basically studying music and rap. I spent a lot of time listening to Tupac—there's not an interview, a quote, or anything I haven't watched.
Wow.

I've watched everything, and to be honest, I've done it with most of them. I was kind of like a bedroom artist, just listening to music and playing music, up all day and all night. Then it got to the point where I came into mental health services. I'd had lessons about it at fifteen or sixteen, but when I got to eighteen and came in here at the start, I wasn't that well and music wasn't on my mind. Then when I got to low secure, I kind of got that feeling back for music and thought, right, now I'm nineteen, it's about time I started writing my music. It was passing the time, and I've actually got something—I'll let you listen to one if you want.
That'd be amazing.
Yeah, I'll let you—when do you want to listen to it?
Um.
We'll have to do it after this.
Yeah, yeah. I have to—we can.
We can chat and organize that. That'd be amazing.
Yeah.
If.
Yeah.
That's.
Yeah.
Um, if you don't mind.
Yeah.
Um, when you write, what's the process like for you?

So when I write, what I do is I put down pinpoints, like dots. I don't just start writing; I write down what I'm going to write. I make points, so I'd put down words like poverty, struggle, pain, motivation, passion—words I want to use.
Yeah.
And then in rap it's about metaphors and similes. So I'd say something like, 'I wanna be free, Freddie Mercury,' you see what I mean?
Yeah, yeah.
And then I talk about—what else did I say? I always had 'green' or 'Grinch' in there, but that's talking about my previous life, not now. There's a lot of similes and metaphors.
Yeah, yeah.

There's a lot of similes and metaphors. It's like, 'I'm coming at you, shot you, notorious like Biggie Smalls.' They wanna see me fall but I'm gonna stand tall like the Statue of Liberty, you see what I mean?
Yeah, yeah.

So stuff like that is what I say in my own songs. And actually on my Facebook I've got people that are on TV and stuff. Like [PERSON], I've got [PERSON] and [PERSON], obviously [PERSON]—he's my inspiration. He got killed when he was eighteen from a knife crime.
Oh.

But he's been my inspiration for my whole journey in music. I actually speak to his mum and I got a couple of tops from her. It's a privilege. And then I've got all of the people he used to rap with, and they know [PERSON] and stuff. So it's part of a big thing. I'm just getting my music out there, man.
That's amazing.

Yeah, it's one of those things, but I'm getting there. Every time I write, I'm getting better and better, and you can hear the talent. It's not like when you hear someone rap and they just haven't got it.
Yeah.
I just know that I've got it. I know I can do it, so I just have to keep chasing it.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that a specific acquaintance with ADHD is making fun of them and discussing their intended actions with his friends, which the participant experiences as a 'strange thought'.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant labels this a 'strange thought' and earlier states 'I suppose everybody has peculiar thoughts now and again,' framing it as an example of odd thinking rather than a confirmed external reality.

case_summary: The participant discusses lifelong difficulties with reading and writing due to dyslexia, describing how they avoid long texts and rely on copying others. They explore their creative use of language through humor, including making up words and using a personal version of Cockney rhyming slang, often to annoy or get back at peers. The conversation shifts to their passion for carp and pike fishing, detailing specialized terminology, techniques, and experiences teaching others. They briefly mention being in a hospital setting, denying hearing voices but acknowledging having 'strange thoughts' about a peer mocking them, and feeling staff do not understand their humor.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

case_summary: The participant discussed their experience with a metaphor-based experiment, finding it annoying and confusing due to the lack of clear connections between words and the repetition of items. They reflected on their cognitive process, noting a strong preference for concrete nouns (like 'boomerang') which they can instantly visualize, over abstract words (like 'aromatic') which are harder to conceptualize. They also discussed the role of language in daily life, emphasizing that they need to form a mental picture or notion before speaking.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant's statements describe their subjective cognitive experience of the experiment and language processing (e.g., visualizing concrete vs. abstract words, feeling there must be a rule). These are reflections on personal mental processes and task difficulty, not expressions of fixed, false beliefs about external reality.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that other people see something good inside him and dislike him for it, taking advantage of his emotional numbness and weakness.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The interviewer reframes this as people taking advantage of his good nature, which the participant agrees with, potentially softening the persecutory framing.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that others are specifically upset by his listening and breathing, and that they focus on his shopping bag and stare at his face because they know something he does not.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: Acknowledges it might be part of his mental illness, but insists he is not stupid and knows what he is talking about.

delusion_points.summary: The participant describes himself as a very clever and successful man who does not take crap from anybody, and believes this is the reason others are jealous and try to prevent him from thinking.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes family members are hinting at a marriage he knows nothing about, suggesting they possess hidden knowledge about his life.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant frames this as a thought he has in response to their questions, but does not express doubt about the hidden knowledge interpretation.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes a specific woman has control and influence over his feelings and life situation, playing with his emotions and sanity, and that she is the source of his ongoing distress.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant expresses uncertainty about the woman's identity and motives, wondering if she feels embarrassed, but maintains the belief about her control and negative impact.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes he must pick up a case from a public toilet, the contents of which are unknown and could be a bomb, and that doing so will solve all his problems and allow him to get married to the woman who is making him suffer.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant states he knows this sounds crazy and acknowledges a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia, but insists 'it was true'. He also expresses a refusal to pick up the case until he knows what is in it.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes his emotions have been taken away from him, leaving him feeling numb and unable to breathe properly, which he attributes to the actions of a specific woman.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The feeling of being unable to breathe is linked to solving problems and a desire for 'fresh air,' which could be metaphorical, but the claim of having no emotions is stated as a literal fact.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that people's weekly mood cycle, from Monday misery to Friday happiness, is a deliberate act directed at him, including pretending to be happy and then treating him like a fool.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that others can hear him as he speaks to the interviewer, suggesting his private conversation is being monitored or broadcast.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that people in authority, including doctors, nurses, and prison officers, are corrupt, do not care about patients' feelings, and treat them as 'guinea pigs' by forcing medication on them for their own financial benefit.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes he carries the burden of the world on his shoulders and is to blame for global corruption simply by being born.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant shows some insight by stating 'I may be stupid, but I'm not that crazy yet,' which could be a form of self-doubt or distancing from the belief.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that a member of the royal family was murdered by the rest of the family, and that celebrities visit the hospital specifically to mock the patients.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes a specific girl has literally gotten away with murder and that this is connected to the problems and misery they are experiencing.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant frames this as a conditional statement ('if I get through this') and expresses a desire for answers, suggesting some awareness that the situation is unresolved.

case_summary: The participant, a 55-year-old man with learning difficulties and a self-acknowledged diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia, discusses his profound emotional numbness, anger, and feeling that others are jealous of him and take advantage of his weakness. He describes a complex, fixed belief system involving a specific woman who controls his feelings, a mysterious case he must retrieve from a public toilet to solve his problems and enable a marriage, and a world he perceives as corrupt and uncaring. He also discusses his passion for music and desire to write a book.

case_summary: The participant discusses their creative use of language, primarily through short, rhyming social media captions that accompany personal photographs. They describe themselves as shy but artistically creative, valuing originality and the capture of authentic, real-life moments over repetitive or artificial content. The conversation explores their views on photography as a personal archive, the importance of uniqueness in self-representation, and a preference for real-world experiences over digital or manufactured ones. They also touch on broader societal topics like lockdown, economic hardship, and a desire for genuine connection, ending the session by reflecting on the unusual feeling of introspective discussion.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant's statements reflect personal preferences, social commentary, and metaphorical expressions of economic or societal frustration. The candidate point about things being 'swallowed away by somebody' is a vague, non-specific lament about societal conditions, not a fixed, delusional belief about a specific agent or conspiracy. No other statements express a clear, specific false belief about external reality indicative of a delusion point.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

Before I go, is it sunny there as well?

Awesome, I hope you get a chance to get outside in the sun.
OK.
Thanks so much, and have a really nice afternoon.
OK, thank you for phoning me. Hopefully it's been alright.
Awesome.
Hopefully it'll go well with your research.
Yeah, I really appreciate your time. Everything everyone is saying to me is really helpful, so thank you so much.
OK, I'll leave you for now then. Nice talking to you.
You too, thanks so much.
Alright then, thank you, bye bye.
bye

case_summary: The participant, a 45-year-old with a long-term schizophrenia diagnosis, discusses their lack of creative language use, attributing it to social withdrawal and difficulty communicating due to their mental illness. They reflect on past creativity in art and gardening, but note a significant decline in these activities, largely due to their illness and life circumstances, though they express hope for improvement.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant describes social withdrawal, anhedonia, and functional decline consistent with negative symptoms of schizophrenia, but does not express any specific, fixed false beliefs about external reality (delusions). Statements about being sacked 'because of my mental illness' are presented as a plausible life event, not a delusional interpretation.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

messages.content: There's really only one interview question, and the rest is just a chat around that.
OK, OK.
Do you feel like you use language creatively?

When I came to this country at eleven, I went to infant school. I was so tiny for my age, I didn't look eleven. My stepfather sent me to school. I passed my eleven-plus because back home you had to learn; if you didn't, you stayed in the class. I went to a top high school. My teacher was Mrs. [PERSON]. But sometimes it's not good to shine. I went to [PLACE]. That man who used to do [RARE_EVENT], I think it was a biscuit, the professor, I passed everything. He told me to go and get dirt under my fingernails because I knew so much I'd have the boss's job. I never got hired. But I have lovely children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren. I'm not saying I'm stupid, but sometimes people don't want to hear your IQ; they just want to know you're friendly and homely. You don't take people for granted. Everybody's a gem. No man can be in two places at once. My fifty-year-old son, born in the same hospital, said to me one day, 'Mum, every man is born equal. Guess what? A sperm and an egg. We don't need two.' We're all equal, but it's what we do to each other to get up the ladder. You asked me a question. I'm in a one-bedroom with two of my sons, thirty-four and thirty-seven. I haven't moved. I don't have any money. Have I got savings? No. I win money, I've won premium bonds, but they don't give me anything. Just a bit of blood goes with the talking, it'll burn down the house. I'm not crying to you, but every time I get up I'm so glad, and all my sons are alive.
I think that's a really nice way to look at things.

Of course that's how we look at things. You phone me, not that you're short of knowing who someone is or where they come from, but we just want to hear. If I really told you how I got here, you'd say everybody cries. Even me phoning you is crying. But we know if we get it right with ourselves, we get it right with everybody. I don't have any money in my bank account, it's one pence. I'm waiting for some money. My grandson wants to borrow some, I don't have it. You say, 'Oh, you stupid thing, you got mugged.' I'm not going outside sweeping the road with bangs. So I help them out. Before you rang, my son said, 'Mum, my friend needs ten pounds until Friday.' Guess what I said? No. You probably say, 'Well, your son, you help.' No. That person, every time I need something, they don't phone for a week. But they get their money, and then when we get ours, they're here. I tried to work out why they are always here when we get money, and when they have it they don't come. I can't work it out.
I see, yeah.

I can't work it out. I can't work out everything. I became very ill, mentally very bad, my brain just went 'boop' because Dettol kills. I don't want to go into that because it's not what the language you said. I'm only a black man, them. I went to finishing school and they said, 'You're not like us, you're not finishing to courtesy.' I was a little tomboy growing up. There were no boys to play cricket or football where I was brought up, just girls. I was such a tomboy, when I had my first child everybody was surprised, they were like, 'Where'd that come from?' My leg shows it, I have so many marks from climbing trees and running. But that's just me to explain. Sometimes I'm glad when somebody talks to me, it takes the pressure off my brain. As a child growing up, I had a good social worker, an English girl called [PERSON]. When I told her the pain I went through as a child, she said she knew some of the black children told her. And you know what happened? She just cut off, she couldn't face talking to me anymore, she just left. I don't know where she is, somebody said she went into some home or something. Big woman, mixed-race kids. Some people say, 'How did you get away from the children's dad?' It didn't look odd. Funny fate. I'm like that girl in [TV_SHOW], skin and bone and starvation. I don't know, school with those people, somehow they look and the girl's face looks and I look like that. I don't make people dry me out. Yes, I've got kids who make mischief, but I'm good. Sorry, sir, it does me feel a release when somebody knows the pain we go through just to be big. The list, red rent man, my list, I don't know where my child is sometimes. It is sad. I think you in yourself could say a bit of a story about yourself, but where you are focusing, people like me, we're sad talking. I used to be happy until they came and told me my son was dead. How can he be? He was just a five-year-old. He was there in front of me, then he just disappeared. Yeah, I've had it. I hold on to the two I have here, I really hold onto them.
It sounds like you're all really close, that sounds really nice.

Oh yeah, yeah. You know, back home I was molested by a big man, left to die in the gutter. They know that's why they brought me out of there. A big man, five or six years old.
