Sometimes when you would have told me I can't keep a secret, I'd say, 'Who is that child? Who are all of them tied to? All of them got kids.' And then to go down, if he hasn't broken up or a tsunami hit it. So who is that happening to? I am a bit angry, and I know I shouldn't take it out on somebody who phones me just to ask a question, but it all comes up from my stomach. No, the injection they keep giving me every two weeks, saying I'm hearing voices and blah blah blah. They knew why people are scared. You jump on the bandwagon, 'Oh, she's hearing voices.' Oh yeah, and this man called 'big man' and all that load of rubbish.
That sounds... I can't imagine what that must have been like, but that sounds awful. I'm really sorry to hear that.
Well, sorry.
I thought you only made two ones.
Child, I thought you gave me two ones.
Oh, you sorry, gave me some change and only gave me one pound. Anyway, sir, go on, how long have we got?
As long as you'd like to talk. If you'd like to talk for a little bit, that's fine; if you'd like to talk for longer, that's fine.

I'm laughing. You know that thing I got off in your ear, like a flea? It was so inside me that even when I explained it as myself, I couldn't. I had to explain it from someone else's pain. It makes sense. I told you about me, but it was so painful growing up, certain times, so painful.
And has that...

And I didn't end up having kids, I don't know. I found it, I'm sure there's a lamb here. I have a son, he's fifty, fifty-one this year. And you might like the story of the virgin, the Adam and Eve, and then you tell me a story about my son, this and that, they were calling him a different name, but he's not stupid. Really, he turned up and he's no fool.
I see. Do you has...

Say it, you won't say it, don't be frightened. When he's worked enough he can't get hurt more, and there's no more to hurt. He's chucked it all in, whatever he is, or we're calling to him. And be a man.
How do you use language when you think about these things?

My son said when I talk it sounds childish and doesn't sound proper, so he said write it down on a piece of paper and then when I'm reading it I can see what I've written. But I've written letters to look over and it looks like I've written scratchy writing. Sometimes when I was growing up going to kindergarten with my teacher, she teaches charity, you have to pass your exam before you go into first standard. I came out of kindergarten, went into first standard, then second standard. Back home you have to go to a private school like grammar school, it was called Pilgrim School at first, then they changed it. I think it's a different school now. I think that late, I was getting old, they say being jealous, send his daughter to this school. I don't call them between, I don't know that word. But change on the street is that way and at the corner. I went home in [DATE], the social service, but you sent me to this. If you go, you came back, don't know what was, everybody say oh you're sick, you're sick. Then once a psychiatrist, a top Jewish man, he looked at me saying you're not sick, they have you living all over the place. When you know where you're living, you came back after what that man say, and you know where you're living, gave me a car. This one I bring, that one I bring, [PERSON] are great. I don't know, I'm here talking to you but I didn't hear about half of the talking at the same time. How old am I? Very old. I don't like flirting when I'm sweet or familiar. What was she that looked like an unmade bed, old, but I know I think I look a bit stable. It's not a laughing matter because it is a lot of pain. I was with the father and he said, oh she's a small island, that's my sister's blood that she's talking about.
I see, wh-
I didn't think you were still there.
No, no, I'm still here.
With me.
I'm finding it really interesting. I just wondered what you think about things like poetry and song lyrics.
You know what I do? Shakespeare, I read because I remember one of the Shakespeare from center. And [PERSON], and what's that one with the rowing boat, what she did, [PERSON], you know [PERSON]?
I th-

Where she rescued her from the rocks. As my teacher once said to me one day, oh well, I'd love to read the books you read. Do you ever know the books where one hundred at a blow, that's a tailor with the jam bread and he took the piece of cloth and he counted all the flies and he called it one hundred at the blow. And then the pixie and the shoemaker. You don't read books like that, Harry Potter, no, I don't know.
And what do you like about the books that you read?
They were very, very educated, those books, very educated, trust me, they worked very educated.
And did you like that about them?

Yeah, boy, educated. Like you, you'll have to be so curious when you tell certain people certain things, these are old-fashioned stuff, they are so old that you can just take your hand and wave them back or you die. One man's book that frightened me as a child was, you know that winky wonky thing, what was it called, with the hairy hair and the trees are hairy, what was it called again? So the little boy, the little girl, you know when that book came out, sorry, that turn up your nose like that news man on [ORG] and what's his name. I talk with my nose when I read, I hide, they mustn't talk me because we destroy us, so I will tone down.
Oh, OK.
Do you like the COVID, could we, do you like the COVID, are you there?
Yeah.

You talk about this COVID and corona. I remember when I was younger, I have it on voicemail. I recall living at a place with two names, the bottom part. I stayed with my papa because my mother left me. She was fifty when she had me, conceived me, I was born in December and she abandoned me. Some people took me in, not like in England, one I called papa, one mama. That's the story, like talking up my nose and going beyond. One day my family said why don't you write a book? I said it's not a book, writing is a transmitter and receiver, the sky, like us talking here. When you play your recording back it sounds nothing like what I say.
Do you mind telling me more about that? That's really, I'd love to know more about wh-
Oh well, you know your recorder, I did have a recorder I bought in an electrical shop, I think it's a [ORG], is it [ORG]?
Yeah, the, like the-

Might be [ORG], yeah, I might not. The old [ORG] in those days, how old are you? The old [ORG] used to have, is it [ORG]? I think it was [ORG] because we bought a television, one of my sons is forty-nine. We had Donkey Kong and all those things. It was so cheap and nobody really had the sight to see the television. You know sometimes it's not to destroy or kill, because Jesus said ask and it shall be given, and he would have said if you ask today don't give him, ask tomorrow. We thought we'd be judged, but nobody out there is fighting, half are starving and want to come here. I just say come to Britain and you feed them. You get homesick, I got homesick, I came in [DATE], a Jewish man lent me something and handed me my, I blew past, never seen it since I landed. Everyone knows I couldn't go back home, that's what's happening to them and they know because somebody is manipulating you. You get up, go to the office, come home to an empty house, your wife is there sitting, not smoking or drinking but she hasn't cooked. You've been out all day, no food, and she tells you some stupid story about somebody, oh did you know, blah blah, no, you needed a proper plate of food. Yes, I used to think with my partner, if I grew, I'd leave food cooking in the oven to save gas, a low cooker. I'd cook, leave it in the oven, wash, come home to a good meal. If I'm in the house it's happy, just make do. Then he'd drift off to somebody and tell a stupid long story, by then he'd come back with germs, he had prostate cancer. I'm not saying I'm good all the time, not every day God resides, you can't be. When you said to somebody get off my sand, they came, they killed you, chucked it away, especially if it's yours. You can't treat somebody like that every day, you have to have a good day sometimes.
Yeah.

I have a friend who's been married twice. The second man wanted to marry her, he'd check on her at lunchtime. She'd pretend to have a cold and jump into bed when she got home. She cooks, cleans, irons, works, and handles the bills. He calls himself the king of the place. I don't know why I became the way I am, maybe nobody taught me because I never had a close mother. You need to have somebody, but I've seen friends marry three or four times. I remember someone saying I looked too skinny and tiny, they didn't want to marry me. I'd say to my children, we're not King Kong, that big monster. They'd say, oh no, she's so skinny.
Why are you sorry? No, no, it's fine.
It's nice to talk.

You're an English man. When I came here as a little girl, I had an English friend called [PERSON]. He wanted to take me to meet his dad, but after about a week he said his dad said I was black, so we never got married. You could tell how old I was when I had my fifty-one-year-old son. Nobody ever gave me anything, and it destroyed my life. I have kids back home. Sometimes people look at you and say they like you, you go about your business, you don't borrow or cause trouble. They dig up a little bit, maybe she owes ten pounds to somebody, they get on the laptop and find out things about her. That's how it goes for me. I get PIP because they say I'm a good person, but I worked in this country, I worked in a laundry and never got paid, while I was eating so much I became sick. If you don't eat and rest properly you get mentally ill. Sometimes people come in and take things. Growing up in England as a black person, you don't have a real family. I had my grandmother and my stepmother, God rest her. My head is just mixed up. I had a half-sister in America, I think she's dead. They told me she had a stroke and bleeding on the brain, and I just cut off. Nobody knew why. This person I'm talking to has never ever rung me or spoken to me. They weren't poor, I am poor, but they never spoke to me. I don't understand why, so when they told me she had a stroke I just cut off.
I'm so sorry to—
Yeah, yeah.
—to hear that.

It's not that I didn't feel for her. When I first spoke to you, your voice was accusing when you talked to me. But because it's so near to your parents, your sister, your brother, to tell you they care, I'm telling you that your voice changed from the human voice to your brain talking to me. There's a thing with my kids when they were big, we used to say 'skimpy' and the brain. Your body is skimpy and your brain, you need both of each other to carry on. My kids used to say, which one are we going to do today? Skimpy says we're going to rule the world, and the next day the brain says we do the same thing we did yesterday.
I used to love that show.

Yeah, skimpy and the brain. My kids are big now, thirty-five and thirty-seven. They had their own flat, but when you're young and have your own place, everybody moved in there. Not mine, but everybody wanted to be there, they were boys. I have family in America, one is a housing officer and one is a teacher with two girls. But your mum, she's with this fool, you always worry about how that affects life.
Yeah, how do you mean?
Well, do I hang on? They have the extractor fan turned on.
They're cooking in a small flat, frying something. I think they're cooking corned beef and rice.
Oh, nice.

Yeah. I think about being gentle, but I'm a whinger. I know in a minute the phone will ring and they'll say I'm selling out black people by talking to you. At the end of the day, they listen to me. I have a friend I borrow money from, but I have to pay him back tonight. I used to say, one day the white man isn't going to do anything for us, because we're always on about the devil. I said to my son, who is behind the bank, who is behind the soldier? I know the devil aimed to pour dirt on my head, because at two or three o'clock in the morning the bin men are calling, walking with a purpose, somebody trying to do something on my head. That's a different story. They won't let me bring my kids up that way, they say she's teaching her kids rubbish. No, I know from firsthand. You say, how do you really look when you sleep? I tell the truth. We know what it is, but a bit of fear doesn't hurt. It's when things escalate. My eyes opened when I had my son in a boat hospital in England. I saw some things and know some things. I know one day, walking home from A to B, somebody handed me a Jehovah's Witness leaflet. I go to every church, I just go and sit down. I was reading it and it said—now don't think I'm on about this general business, good or indifferent—it said the devil said to God, I don't deny you being God, but you've damaged the people so much that whatever you do to bring them back, they won't look normal, they'll line up. I did read it. By the time I read it I was back in [PLACE]. I think I told a lady called [PERSON], married to a guy called [PERSON], he's a preacher now. She died of cancer, leukemia or something. He's their pulpit preacher. I think that's why I said I'm so glad I've probably reached my limit and can't go any further. So that's it, that's me. There's a lot more, but I wouldn't tell you because you're a human being and you don't want to say it's corny, you want to research it for yourself. It's not easy being a woman, especially if you have a lady to face. I remember a researcher and her husband in a sports car. I had fun with my friend, we called them people you look up to. Her name was [PERSON], she took me to the [PLACE] and I became one of those ladies out with their baby, doing business. I didn't even know, she said three pounds. I was running around with those English girls, an adventure you do when you're young. But when you get older you look back and think, those were foolish days, and you can't change anything because people look at you as being that person. But I had my boys, they're very clever. My two granddaughters, one grandson, and one great-granddaughter. Didn't do too bad for myself.
It sounds like you have a lovely family around you.

They're wonderful, but I worry about them. One of them would give away his heart if I wasn't there. People have asked them what they'll do when I die, and they say they'll just get on with it. I worry about them. I don't worry about how the world is going because I don't want to take God's job away and turn to the devil. My son has a tobacco habit and people ask if he owes money. I never borrowed money growing up. Once when I was young, I was working at [PLACE] and they declared me bankrupt without me even knowing I had money. I'm not crying to you, but it hurts. We get through it. If we just sat and talked, we wouldn't have mental illness we can't work out. I was watching a program where some Englishman let off a cracker in the dark in Africa with night vision, and the animals made me laugh. That's the end of us now.
How do you mean?
In the dead of night in the jungle, they let off a cracker. It was too dark, but with the night vision light you could see the animals darting around.
Oh, I see.
That made me laugh. I said what naughty people could do that, like a bit of fun.
I see, it scared all the animals away?

No, not away. They let it off in the middle of the night in the jungle when it was dark with no moonlight. The animals, like the donkey, were just running and bumping into each other. There was no lion; I don't think they eat enough carrot to see in the dark.
Oh, I see. Is there anything we haven't talked about that you'd like to talk about?
It's nice to talk because you can work things out when you sit down and you're not telling a lie. It really says a lot about a person. Anyway, your beep went off, so I'm going to go now.
Oh, okay. Thank you so much for your time and for talking to me. It's been so nice to talk to you.

It's not so much the question you can't answer, it's what's behind it. A friend lent us some money because my son got into trouble with his bus fare for not paying the right zone. They fined him one thousand two hundred and sixty-something. I don't have that kind of money, so I borrowed it and we have to pay it back. That's how life is, but I'm not complaining because at the end of the phone there's somebody who listens and cares. Not everybody is out there hurting each other every day. Somebody had my food in the cupboard anyway. Bye bye.
So nice to talk to you. Thank you so much. Take care.
Bye bye.
Bye bye.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that when a recording of her voice is played back, the content is completely different from what she originally said.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes that writing functions as a 'transmitter and receiver' connected to the sky, similar to a telephone conversation.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes she must hide how she talks because 'they mustn't talk me cos we destroy us', indicating a fear that speaking openly will lead to harm or destruction.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes people are monitoring her online to dig up information about small debts and that she will be accused of betraying her community for speaking to the interviewer.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes the devil has personally targeted her by aiming to 'pour dirt on my head', and interprets bin men calling at odd hours as evidence of this.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: Acknowledges it is a 'different story' and frames it as a personal belief.

delusion_points.summary: The participant perceives the interviewer's voice as changing from a normal human voice to their brain speaking directly to her.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: None expressed.

case_summary: The participant, an older Black woman who immigrated to England as a child, discusses a wide range of life experiences including childhood trauma, sexual abuse, the loss of a child, financial hardship, family relationships, and her history of mental health treatment. She reflects on themes of equality, social judgment, and resilience, often moving between topics in a tangential and emotionally charged manner. She expresses distrust of mental health services, feeling her trauma has been mislabeled as 'hearing voices', and shares several idiosyncratic beliefs about communication, technology, and persecution.

provenance.source_citation: Delgaram-Nejad et al. (2023), Discussing Abstract Ideas in Schizophrenia Corpus, UK Data Service, doi:10.5255/UKDA-SN-855021.

messages.content: Okay. I'd like to start by hearing about the people you see socially and consider friends. Can you tell me about a current friend?

I don't have many friends. I moved to [PLACE] about a year and a half ago with my girlfriend, who is now my best friend and like family. I've met a few others since, but work kept me busy. The friends besides her are people I met after my illness, in the last couple of months. One is [PERSON], from an English course I took while recovering. Another is [PERSON], who is also [EASTERN EUROPEAN] and now my boyfriend. My flatmate [PERSON] is also a friend. So there aren't many. I know plenty of people from parties or around, but I wouldn't call them close friends.
Okay, so there are three or four people you'd consider good, close friends?
Yes, yes.
What sort of things do you like to do with them?

With [PERSON] we visit museums, the park, or [PLACE] nearby, see movies, and spend time at home since we share a room. With [PERSON] I go to concerts, get a drink, or mostly just meet to talk. We also cycle together; we both like bikes.
So you do lots of activities, seeing things and doing things together?
Yes.
What's the important part of those friendships? Is it having someone to do things with, talk to, listen, or support?

I think it's all of those. Before my illness I felt lonely because [PERSON] was my only real connection here. I had no one else to talk to about my relationship with her. I needed people I could share things with, where we have common interests, and I can support them too. Now I don't feel so lonely.
Yeah, so they give you company, a sense of belonging, and are like family since your own family is far away?
Yes, definitely.
Okay. Thinking back to before you were ill, it was just you and [PERSON], right?
Yes.
And even before that, before you moved here, did you have many friends? What were those friendships like?

I used to have quite a lot, mostly from high school. I still see some when I visit [EASTERN EUROPEAN COUNTRY]. Even after months apart, we still have things to talk about, which is nice. I also have two or three really good friends from university. So I have more than four people who are truly important to me.
So it's a small, close group.
Yes, exactly.
And your older friends from home—if you saw them now, is it different since you've been ill, or is it the same as always?

In January, right after I was ill, I didn't want to see them. I lacked confidence and didn't want them to notice I was different, because my behavior was peculiar then. On the phone they said I seemed sad and strange. But when I visited about two months ago, I met them and felt no difference. I had returned to my old self.
So in January you avoided them because you felt they'd see something different about you?
Yes, and I didn't feel valuable. It was just after the illness, so I didn't want to be seen in that state. I wasn't myself yet.
That's understandable. Thinking about [PERSON], since she was here before, during, and after your illness, is anything different in that relationship?
I think our friendship grew stronger. She was with me every day in the hospital and took care of me afterward. Now I know I can rely on her no matter what. It's really nice.
It's a very strong friendship?
Yes.
Okay. Now that you've been through your illness, when you look to make friends, do you look for the same things you did before, or do you think it's different now?

I think I'm always looking for the same things, because I always look for people I can trust, rely on, and have things in common with. I'm not a very wild person; I never look for party people. I prefer calmer people, and I don't think that changed with my illness. The only thing that might have changed is that I need closer people now, not just acquaintances, but someone I can trust. That's the only difference, but I always wanted people like that, so I don't think it's changed much for me.
So trust has become a bit more important, but it was always important to you?
Yes.
Do you think having [PERSON] around affected how you coped with your illness? Did it change how you saw things?

Yes, because if I didn't have her, it would have been very difficult, I'm sure. Right after I was ill, I went to [PLACE] and saw my family, and they took care of me. But I don't think it would have been good if I didn't have her here and I stayed in [PLACE] so my family could look after me. It wouldn't have been good because my environment and my life is here. I wouldn't have come back to my normal life as fast as I did. I spent one month in [PLACE] and then told my mum I wanted to go back to England because my life is here and I wanted to start doing things. So I came back, and at that point she was the only person with me. She gave me support every day, and that was really important for me to get well enough.
She was a constant for you?
Yes.
And when you came back, is that when you started your English classes?
Yes, a few weeks after that.
And how was that experience for you, going into a social setting with lots of people you didn't know?

Well, the class wasn't big. If there are a lot of people around, I get more quiet, but a group of three or four people is easier for me to make friends. The class was just me and three others, so it was really good. From the first day, I became really good friends with [PERSON]. We realized we read the same books, like the same music and films, a lot of the same things. So we started talking and meeting up after class. It wasn't that difficult for me to make new friends there because I met [PERSON] right away.
And the other two people you mentioned as friends, were they in your English class too, or from somewhere else?
Yes, they were in my class as well.
And as time went on, they became friends? It started with [PERSON] as your close friend in the group—how did the other friendships develop?
I don't know. The rest of the people from the class didn't become friends. One girl wasn't there very often, and the other was a lady around 50 years old, so she wasn't like me.
There wasn't much in common with her?
Yes, exactly.
And how about the other two friends you mentioned—where did you meet them?

[PERSON] is a flatmate; she moved into our house. I don't remember exactly when, maybe two or three months after I was ill. She's [NATIONALITY] as well, the same nationality as me, so it was much easier for us to connect and talk about friendly things. She's very talkative and easygoing, so we started to like each other. [PERSON], my [NATIONALITY] friend, I met him about two months ago at a picnic organized by [PERSON], so that was very nice. There were some other friends [PERSON] invited, and I met him there.
And was it easy for you to start talking to him, someone you didn't know?

Well, no, it wasn't that easy. He's [NATIONALITY] too, but I was a bit quiet at the picnic. But because the others saw that we somehow liked each other, they just left us alone, so I was forced to talk with him. They went for a walk for an hour, and we stayed alone. It was very nice. That way we could see if we liked each other, and in the end we did, so it's nice.
Do you talk to any of these friends about what happened with your illness, or if you have any worries about it?

I don't tell them exactly what happened, because I know it can be a bit scary for people, so I don't want to scare them. I say that I was ill and had a very hard time, and because of that illness I had to leave my last job, but I never give much detail, I would say.
Do they see it as a mental health problem or a physical illness?

No, they think it was more like a difficult period, depression or something. They don't think it was physical. They know I had problems and it was stress-related; a mental health problem, not physical.
Is talking to them about your illness and what happened important to you, or would you rather not discuss it with friends?

Apart from [FRIEND_4], because she was always there, I prefer not to talk about the illness. I have her to speak with about how I feel and how it was, and I can share everything. With other people I prefer not to discuss my illness.
[FRIEND_4] stuck by you through the illness and your friendship stayed really strong from beginning to end. Was there anyone you lost touch with as a result of your illness?
No, because I didn't have friends here. There wasn't anyone I could have lost touch with.
You stopped working, is that right? You had a job before. Did you go back to it afterwards?

No, I didn't. My care coordinator and I thought it wasn't good for me because my illness was job-related, tied to the job and its stress. It was a decision we made. I need to find a less stressful job, so I didn't return to my previous work.
Was there anyone at your previous workplace you were friends with or got on well with, or was it strictly professional?

It wasn't strictly work-only because we used to go out together on Friday nights or something, but they were more acquaintances. I didn't really have any friends there. We got along well with each other, so it was a good environment.
When you finished there, you didn't see them or speak to them again?

No, I only saw them a few times because I had to go there to drop off my doctor's certificate. Sometimes when I was there we would chat, and I would visit them, but afterwards, outside of work hours, I didn't see them.
Was that because you didn't want to, or because it just didn't happen?
I don't know. I didn't feel like I wanted to.
Ok, that's fair enough.
Is there anything you'd like to change about your friendships at the moment?

Not really. The only thing I would like to change is to have a few more friends, because when [FRIEND_4] is busy with someone, [FRIEND_1] goes away somewhere, [FRIEND_2] has something to do, and [FRIEND_3] is busy, and I have a day off and would like to spend it with a friend but everyone is busy. Sometimes it happens that everybody is busy, so I would like maybe one or two more friends just so I'm not lonely. Sometimes I feel lonely.
What sort of things would you like to do with those two friends, or if there were more people around?

If there were more people, I would like to go to museums, the park, cycling. Sometimes just meeting and talking would be nice. It doesn't have to be a specific activity, but I like discovering things about another person. So if someone likes, I don't know, flowers, and wants to go to [GARDEN_NAME], I'm happy with that. It's always nice to discover new people, very nice.
Have you got any ideas about how you might make some new friends?

Last time I was at weekend BBQ parties, that's a good way to meet new people. If someone invites me to a party, I should go. I don't like going out specifically to a pub or club to make friends; it's not a good idea. I prefer to look within the circle of friends I already have to find new friends, that's better.
Why is that, do you think?

I don't know. I think I'm not open, confident, and brave enough to just go out alone to look for new people. If your phone rings and someone introduces you to someone—this is [PERSON], this is [PERSON]—then it's easier for me to meet that person, I think.
So having the support of your friends there makes it easier?
Yes.
Is there something about meeting people who are already friends of a friend that makes you think they would be a good friend, rather than a stranger?
Umm
Does that make sense?
I'm not sure what you're saying.
Let me say it again.
I guess I'm wondering, if somebody is a friend of a friend, is there something good about them that means you'll like them as well?

I know what you mean. Somebody who is in my circle of friends but not my friend yet, why I would like them to be my friend… I don't know. I think I used to look at whether we have things in common, or of course if the person is nice—usually the person is nice too. But I look at how I speak to them, what we speak about, if I like the way the person is, then it's easier to become friends. But I have to see something I like in them. Sometimes it's things in common, but sometimes it's somebody who likes really opposite things because it's something different. So I don't have one particular thing that I think should be the case.
Ok. Does anybody at the EIS ever talk to you about friendships?
Yes, I speak with my care coordinator about things related to my friendships.
If you had any worries about your friends or friendships, would you talk to your care coordinator?
Yes, last time was yesterday.
Is there anything that services here could do to help with friendships, do you think? Anything to help you with it?

I think my care coordinator is the person I can speak with about everything. I am honest with her about my problems, my worries, everything. It's helpful that I can speak to her if I have worries related to my friends as well. I can tell her all of it. I think it's very important because she's not from my circle of friends or my family, she's someone outside who can listen to me. It's very important to have someone to speak to about important things. I think it's just helpful.
So aside from your care coordinator listening and talking, is there anything you'd want the service to do, organize, or provide for you regarding friendship?

Maybe some more… It would be nice if there were more groups to meet people from EIS or people we can meet here. For example, I go to a badminton group; it's a place where I can meet people. Yesterday there was only one other person and me, but usually there are more people. If there were more groups, we could meet and go, it would be nice. But anyway, now I'm working so I don't have loads of time for this, but for other people who have more time, for other clients of the EIS, I think it would be nice.
Some people want to make friends who have also been here, and some people don't. What's your position on that?

I don't mind. It's nice because we were almost in the same situation, so I don't have to hide anything. With my other friends I don't like to speak about this, but with people from EIS I can ask or say something about how I felt or how they felt. So it's nice to have people who were ill with the same thing as me.
The same experience?
The same experience, yes.
Thinking about your friend being there for you when you were unwell, can you give me an example of when having a friend around really helped you?
For example, when I was in the hospital I was feeling a bit bad, unsafe, especially in the beginning. It was important that she was there every day to see me, someone to speak to and to hug.
Someone you could trust. It seems difficult for you to remember that time. It was a hard time for you. Talking about it now shows how far you've come, doesn't it?
Yes, yes.
Let me pass you a tissue.
Thank you.
Which part is upsetting you? Remembering the hospital or thinking about [PERSON] helping you?

Both. It's sad that it was so bad, it involved very strong emotions, and even now remembering it makes me feel a lot. I also feel a lot for her, that she did all these things for me; it was very important to me.
What she gave to you?
Yes. As a friend and as part of my family. She's like family to me.

And you've been through a very difficult experience together. Do you think there's anything missing in your friendships at the moment, or are you happy that everything you need is provided for in your friendships?

Well, firstly with [PERSON] there is nothing missing for sure. But with the other people, I don't know. They are my friends but I'm not sure if I could speak about everything with them or if I could rely on them always like with [PERSON]. They are good friends and I like to go out with them and talk and everything, but I'm not sure if they would be there if I was ill again. I'm not sure about this. I don't know if they are such good friends. There may be something missing, because if somebody is a really good friend they would be there for you and I don't know what would happen. Maybe I've known them for too short a time to know that. Hopefully I will not have to find out that part of the friendship.
To be able to talk about what happened to you and the difficult time you had, do you think you would need to know somebody for a long time and know them very, very well?

I think so. In my case, to open up to another person I need to know them much better. I can go for walks and have fun, but I need to feel I can trust them and tell them everything. Without that feeling, I won't speak about it.
Have you always been like that since you were a child, or is that new?
I think that somehow I was always like that, because in childhood I was ill with epilepsy and none of my friends knew about this, so I think I was like that before as well.
So you'd keep some of that to yourself rather than talking about it with anybody around you?
Yeah.
Another question about [PERSON] really; I'm wondering what it is about the friendship that helped it to be such a good and strong friendship?
What was so good?
Yes, what was it about you and [PERSON] and the two of you together that has meant it has survived?

I don't know. I think it's because, firstly, we were in love with each other, so even though we aren't now, we love each other like family. That's very important. If you love someone you can be there for them. Also, at the beginning in [PLACE] we didn't have anybody else, so I just had her and she just had me. Now it's different because I have some friends and she has someone important in her life too. Because we were so attached, our friendship was very strong from the start. And the difficult experiences must have made it stronger.

Thinking about the people you lost contact with who were more acquaintances, what would it feel like to get back in touch with them now? Would that be hard to do, or would it be that you didn't want to do it?

I don't really want to do it, I think. We were acquaintances but I didn't feel like I would like to spend much out-of-work time with these people even when I was feeling well, when I wasn't sick. They were nice people to have a drink with on a Friday evening after work but nothing more. I wouldn't like to get back with them now.
So they weren't really people that you would pursue more time with?
No, no. And with your friendships that you have at the moment, the friendships that you've described with [PERSON], [PERSON]... I've forgotten the names of the two other friends?
[PERSON] and [PERSON]
What sort of role do you think you play in these friendships? What's your part of the friendships?
I don't know, what kind of roles can there be?

For example, some people say that they are the one who listens, or they are the one who speaks, or they are the one who organizes things, or they're the one who looks after somebody. Do any of those roles resonate for you?

With [PERSON] we both look after each other. I help her with everyday things like meals or housework, but she's very disorganized, so I often have to sort things out for her. Like last week she lost her bank card, and since her English isn't as good as mine, I called the bank to cancel it. For her that's really difficult and scary, but for me it's nothing, so I'm the organizer too. With [PERSON] she's more the organizer because she likes to arrange parties or outings, and I just ask what we can do and she suggests places. I also listen and talk with her. With [PERSON] we don't really discuss deep things; we just enjoy chatting about everything and nothing. It's about enjoying speaking and listening to each other. With [PERSON] I'm sometimes the organizer, giving ideas for what to do and where to go, and if he needs help with something I can assist in some ways.
Is there anything that he helps you with?
That’s a good question. He hasn’t actually helped; he hasn’t had a chance yet to see if he can help me with something. I think so.
It’s a new friendship.
Yes, I think I hadn’t realized that before.
I’m happy with my friendships now, but I’d like one or two more. That’s the only thing. I’m happy with the people I have.
Ok, thank you.

case_summary: The participant discusses their social life and friendships following a period of illness. They describe a small, close-knit group of friends, including a former partner who is now like family, and others met through an English course and social events. The participant values trust and common interests, prefers calm social settings, and is selective about whom they confide in regarding their illness. They express a desire for one or two more friends to avoid occasional loneliness but are otherwise content with their current relationships.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant's statements reflect ordinary social preferences, anxiety about social perception after an illness, and a desire for deeper trust in friendships. There are no expressed beliefs about external reality that indicate a delusion or reality-boundary disturbance. The content is consistent with typical post-illness social adjustment and personal boundaries.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I'd like to hear about people you see socially, people you consider friends. Do you have a specific friend in your life right now?

To be honest, when it comes to friends my parents always told me growing up to keep your enemies closer than your friends, so I don't really have many friends. I'd say my mum is one of my nearest and dearest, and I've got a two-year-old son so I'm working on our relationship so we have as good a friendship as a relationship. I'd say one of my best friends is my mum.
Ok, has that always been the case?

Yes, definitely. Since having my son I've wanted to build a stronger bond with him, so he can talk to me like a friend. I want the same kind of relationship with him that I have with my mum. I look up to her and always go to her with any problems. We speak very regularly, often daily, so she's one of my closest friends right now.
So the important thing about your mum being your friend is that you talk regularly. What else makes it such a good relationship?

If I have any personal problems or questions—about sex, or anything, not abuse—anything I'm concerned about, I always go to mum. She's in her forties and pretty experienced, so I can look up to her, ask her a lot of things, and get a good response.
So she gives you some pretty good advice?
Yes, lots of support. And she phones me pretty regularly so I know I'm on her mind and she cares for me a lot.
Is there anybody outside of your family that you would spend time with?

Socially, I have an auntie. My son is in local authority care right now, but if he were with me I'd definitely say he's my best friend, even though he's only two. He's like a teddy bear you can cuddle. Someone you can teach a lot, who looks up to you—he speaks two languages at two and a half. My auntie, who lives in [PLACE] and is my mum's half-sister, is also a very close friend. I'm in a relationship with my baby's father, and he's more a friend than anything, so he counts as a good friend. After I left school I lost contact with most of my friends. If I speak to any old school friends it's on social media, that's it.
Why do you think you lost touch with those friends?

I moved far out from the area, a good few miles, so I lost contact unless I visited my grandparents and occasionally saw them. It's a good thing you've brought this up, because I'm quite interested in this whole topic of friends. Friends come and go. If you want a good friendship, you have to take it upon yourself to get to know that person, or you can miss the opportunity. Friends come and go, but not very regularly.
So if you see a chance you've got to grab it?

Yeah, it's very hard to come by a friend. There's a big difference—someone you can call a friend but you don't really know if they're a good one. You don't come by that often. You don't just meet someone and think 'you're my friend'; it takes a lot of tests before you can say someone is a really good friend.
What sort of things would those tests be? What would you be looking for in a friend?

Someone very smart and intelligent, who puts you in a positive direction, not negative. Someone good. It's best to have friends in your own age group, not older or younger. Someone you can relate to, and if you need a break, someone you can meet for a chat or lunch. But friends are hard to come by. A lot of my old friends are younger than me. I was an offender a couple of years back, so many of them are offenders, thieves, and weed smokers. I choose to stay away from them because I'm older and more responsible now. They'd probably steal from me. They're not good friends, so I don't have those kinds of friends anymore.
What happened to stop you being friends with them? What changed?

I was given an ASBO and kicked off my estate. My mum and I had to move out because of a big ASBO for graffiti and robbery. I was known by the police. The whole estate signed a letter saying my friends and I were making it an unpleasant place—graffiti everywhere, smoking on the blocks at night, people being robbed. We were basically voted off, and I got the ASBO. After that I had a six-month curfew, then a 16-month supervision order with an advocate, like probation. I was sent back to court after 16 weeks to check my progress; if there was none, I'd have gone to a young offenders' institution because I was uncontrollable. I had no positive friends to rely on, so I had to break away. I'd be in jail by now if I'd stayed with those same bad people.
You made the decision for your own future that you were going to stay away from those people?
Yes, and not long after I gave birth to my son. Getting in trouble with the police and all that was five years ago, so I've made a big difference since then.
Yes, big changes.
Big, big changes. When I see those people now they can't even remember me, so it wouldn't make a difference. I look so different.
Thinking back to before you used the services here, do you think there's any difference in your friendships?
It's brought me and my boyfriend a lot closer, because he had to come and see me in the hospital and things. It's brought us to have a better friendship, a better relationship.
What was it that he did or you did that meant that relationship survived?

He showed he was there for me by visiting me in the hospital twice a day. It really showed me who my real friends are, because not even my mother, who I considered a close friend, came to see me once. My boyfriend came every day. When you go through something like that and end up in hospital and no one visits, you realize who your real friends are, the ones who go out of their way to see you.
Do you think what you look for in a friend now is different from before, because of all your experiences?

I don't know, it's hard to say. If I were looking for a friend, I'd just look for normal things, like as long as you're not getting into trouble with the law and you're doing things legitimately, then I'd be interested. If you're a bad person getting into legal trouble, I have a child so it's not in my interest to associate with that sort of person. I'm not on that wavelength. I'm on a more positive vibe, so if a friend suggested robbing someone, I'd refuse. I have a two-year-old son who looks up to me, and I don't want to let him down. He's in local authority care, so it's even worse.
So at the moment there's a lot of pressure on you to keep being positive?
Yeah, positive.
With the friends you have around you already, is it important to be able to talk about the symptoms that brought you here, to talk about your experiences, or do you prefer to keep that inside?

I keep that to myself actually. I have a friend who's 26, a few years older than me, and I find that even though she's older, she looks up to me because she lives in a hostel and I had my child before her. We can relate on a lot of things because I can look up to her regarding work. She's in college and works, so if she ever wanted to come to me about children, I can give her advice, and she can give me advice about work.
It's important in that relationship then to be able to help each other?
It's good to have friends in different age groups, someone older and someone your own age, so you can see things from different points of view.
What sort of things do you like to do with [friend 1], or your partner?

With [friend 1], I don't see her that often, but most of the time we go for walks because she has three dogs. Usually I'll come over and walk one of the dogs while she walks the other two, to help keep them under control.
So when you're out you can have a nice walk, some exercise, but you can also talk?
Yeah. We used to be on the same estate, but things are a lot more distant between us now.
Ok. She was somebody that you'd known for quite a while?

Yes. I used to be pretty close with her cousin, but because I moved off the estate we don't see each other as much anymore, so it's a lot of phone contact. If we do make phone contact, we might meet up that day, but it used to be that we lived on the same estate. Things have changed.
You said that you'd lost contact with a lot of people off of the estate, but [friend 1] is somebody that you managed to stay in touch with?
Yes, because she's not like that. She's always been in college and university. Very positive girl, African girl.
Because she's focused and working hard..
I always choose to stay in contact with her. I did lose contact with her when I was pregnant, but I got back in contact after I had the baby.
And during the time that you spent in hospital, did you lose contact with anybody then?

I didn't really intend to tell anybody because it was my own personal business. A lot of people knew what was happening, like my mum's sister, aunties, cousins—I have a very big family—but people like [friend 1] didn't notice that I was in hospital.
So as far as they're concerned, they don't know about that at all? You kept that separate?
Yeah.
Did you find it hard to start friendships up again when you came out, or did it work quite well?

Yeah. I even made a friend inside the hospital, actually, who was going through the same thing. An [Asian Nationality] boy called [FRIEND 2] that I've stayed in contact with since last year when I was first in hospital. I met him there and I've been in contact with him ever since.
What is it about him that has worked out?

After I was discharged, he stayed in for another six months. We kept in touch—I'd call him at the hospital and bring him lunch, the way my boyfriend looked after me. I wanted to make sure he had visitors, because it's hard when no one comes.
What did that do for you? I can see that he got a visitor and somebody to see..
It made me feel proud of myself for caring. When I was in hospital, I kept hoping my mum might visit. I was there for two months and didn't see my son once—that was really, really bad.
That must have been really difficult. So you were thinking that you knew what it was like to be waiting there and no one comes, so you've been doing that for [FRIEND 2]?
Yeah.
Is he still in hospital or is he out now?
No.
Have you stayed in touch?
Yes. I've known him for more than a year now.
And what sort of things do you two do when you see each other?

I've never met him on the outside; we just make phone contact since he's gotten out of the hospital. He went to [Asian Country] because he's [Asian Nationality] and he's been in [Asian Country] for about a month now so I haven't had contact with him for a couple of weeks now. He's on holiday.
Yeah.
He only came out of hospital early January so he was in there for just under a year. He was sectioned.
Ok. So we've heard about your mum, and your aunt and your partner, and [friend 1] as well, and [FRIEND 2], is there anyone else who's really important to you?
My son.
Of course, yeah, sorry.

Yeah, my son. When you have children it's more, it's a different relationship. You can ask a lot of parents who's your best friend and they're going to say my son or my daughter. Its hard to say because my son's only 2, so right now like, everybody, my mum, my dad, ask everybody, my son is my best friend, because he's someone who that, out of all the people in the world right now there's one person that I can say really needs me, and that's my son, and he's in local authority care, and the carer always tells me that 'he always asks for you'. I'd say that's my best friend right there, I'm trying really hard to get him back.
And it sounds like your friendships with [FRIEND 2] and also with your son it's important for you to be needed and to be able to give something to those people, is that right?

Yeah. I love my son very much and because he's 2 I'm finding it very hard right now to explain to him what's going on. I see him at this contact centre for 3 hours a week, 2.5 hours twice a week, and when it's time to say goodbye he starts crying, and it's pretty sad because he always leaves me in tears as well but I don't know how to explain it to him. Because he's only two he's learning words and stuff but I sometimes sit down and speak to him and say son don't cry, mummy's going to be back on Thursday, today it's Tuesday and its an hour and a half but I've got to go. I'm finding it very.. I'm getting very caught up because since I've got out of hospital my son's.. I haven't had my son and I've got the house and everything, and my son's on the tenancy agreement and sometimes I feel like what's the point in me being here if my son ain't here? Very bored. I feel like my parenthood has been taken away from me. I've had a very bad two years, back and forth to court and social services.
Have you felt supported in that time? Have you felt that there's people around you?
Yeah, I guess so.
Is there anything else anybody could have done to make it less stressful for you?
Not really, no.

We've covered a lot about your friendships, and I want to make sure nothing is overlooked. We discussed your current friendships and what you appreciate—conversations, giving to others, and feeling supported. Before your hospital stay, was there anything you valued in relationships that matters less to you now?

Not really, because I didn't have time for friends when my son was with me all the time. It wasn't that I was unhappy; I chose to be a full-time parent instead of going out drinking on weekends. Now that my son isn't around, I'm looking for more friendship because I have so much time on my hands.
And would you want to be doing those sorts of things again? Going out?

Not really, it doesn't interest me. I planned to be a full-time parent and that was taken away because my son is in local authority care. I don't really think about friends unless I have nothing to do. It's not because I want to be with them since my son's not around, it's because I'm bored.
Ok. And is there a gap in what you want from friends at the moment? Is there something missing?
No, it's not really in my interests. I'm just trying to do my best to get my son back.
So your attention is on that, you're not noticing the other things apart from when you're bored?
My baby's father is around a lot of the time. He works during the day, so by 5 or 6 I'm alright.
It's the daytimes when you're by yourself. Do you think having those people around affected how quickly you got better? Or do you think it made no difference?

It didn't make any difference. My privacy, me and my son, is personal. Sometimes my baby's father might think I'm being a bit soft, but he's not on my tenancy agreement. He doesn't help me with bills, and I don't ask. My son is on the tenancy agreement, he's not. He doesn't live with me. I think sometimes I could say I'm being a bit selfish, but I keep myself to myself. Everything is me and my son. And because my son's not here right now, my baby's father has maybe pushed himself onto me a bit more because he knows [SON] isn't around, so he gets more attention from me. Before, I was a 24/7 mother to my son and I didn't really plan to have more children.
So before there wasn't anything missing in your life because it revolved around looking after your little boy, and now your life is still about that but there's this extra time until it's resolved?

It's not just that. The reason I say my son is my best friend is because I had such a difficult childhood. I was never taken on holiday by my parents, so I planned on giving my son everything I didn't have. Right now I've been decorating his room for when he comes back. I've got a car bed and a new TV and everything; he's only 2 now. I plan on traveling with my son, taking him to [PLACE] and [PLACE], that's why I think I can relate to a child a lot because I'm very young-acting and I like to have fun. I think me and my son can relate; I can be really close to him. He's only 2 now and we're already close. I think as he gets older he'll be able to come to me and speak about anything because we'll have such a bond. It's not only that I plan on making time for my son; I plan on going places, taking him abroad.
So you're putting a lot of time into thinking about how that's going to be at the moment?

I want him to say that his mum gave him a very fun childhood. I never had that; I witnessed a lot when I was younger with my parents—violence, they split up early. I don't want that for my son. I want to be best buddies with him.

Just thinking if there's anything anybody here could have done? It sounds like the time you were in hospital didn't have too much impact on the people around you because you managed to keep it private and when you came out you could start your friendships up again quite easily?

Well, the first time I was ill I was there for three months and the last time for a month. I used to sleep a lot; time flew by in there. I got discharged. I was sent home for the weekend, went back on Monday and was discharged, and I haven't been back since. That's how I lost my son initially, because I was hospitalized. I never want to return to that place because it doesn't help.
Do you think there's anything that friends around you can do to help with that?

No. My friends are a lot younger than me, so they've never paid a bill in their life. I can't really relate to any of them. They don't have a clue. They all live with their mums. Even [PERSON] still lives with her mum and she's 26, so I'm a lot more mature. A lot of my friends come to me with problems because I'm the one with the 2-year-old. I've lived by myself since I was 14, so I've gone through a lot. I could relate to other people who've gone for counseling. I've been through so much.
All these people come to you for support and you give a lot to all these people. Where do you get something from?

My baby's father. And I get a lot of cuddles from my son, and my son shocks me every day. He comes and tells me 'I love you,' and he's only 2 years old. I know that no matter what happens, I've got a son out there and he loves me very much, and he doesn't have a clue what's going on around him. I've got so much to make up to him. I might end up going to a temporary mothers and baby unit so I can be watched over, and I'm willing to do whatever it takes right now, because me and my son have never been separated before and it's really hard for a woman to go through that, when your child's been taken away from you. I believe that I'm doing pretty well for someone that's supposed to be mental. Know what I mean?
Who told you that you're mental?

Well, I'm on this medication called olanzapine, and I think I'm doing pretty well for someone who's supposed to have all these mental reactions and stuff. I think I'm doing pretty well. I can't see the mental in me at all.

From what you said, it sounds like you're somebody who from an early age became used to looking after yourself. You're kind of independent, so you don't rely on friends or people around you much. You deal with things yourself. Have I got that right?

Yeah. That's why it's killing me right now. My son's with somebody else and he keeps getting flu and stuff, and okay if you foster a child, but do you love my son like I do? Are you going to check his temperature every 2 minutes? I'm just worried right now that even though he is learning, this person caring for him isn't giving the full attention a 2-year-old needs from his mother. So you're finding it hard to rely on someone else to do something for you?
Yes.
With your baby's father, can you rely on him?

I can rely on him and trust him, but he's in local authority care now, so neither of us has a say. Social services handle everything, and I can't make any decisions. I asked if my son could stay the weekend with me, but they said no because he doesn't have a bed there. That's why I'm spending a lot on decorating his room right now, so when he comes back everything is ready for him, his bed and all.
Does it feel like hard work to be the one who has to give?

It probably will feel like hard work because every time I seem to be making progress, I get set back several steps. Like I'll just start decorating and then the police and nurses come to my house and I get taken back to the mental health hospital. After I lost my son, I've been set back, and I'm having to go to court. Before, he was in local authority care for a month, and now he's with a complete stranger. So you could say it's going to be hard for me, but I'm not finding it hard taking care of him; I'm finding it hard that he's not with me. If it weren't for my son, I wouldn't have that house—I'd be living in a women's refuge. When I got pregnant with him, I got that house, and now I'm living there and he's not even with me, even though he's named on the tenancy. I'm getting vouchers for healthy food and buying all this fruit, but my son isn't here to eat it with me, so I'm finding it a bit lonely at the moment. I don't really feel like a mum. To be honest, it feels like my motherhood has been taken away. I see people on my street and they ask where my son is. I don't feel it's their business to say he's in care, so I don't say anything. None of my friends really know because it's pretty serious. I don't sleep at night sometimes because I don't have my son. I feel like my motherhood has been taken away. I was happy up to six months ago; I'm not happy anymore.
This is something you find hard to trust anyone with, to tell anyone about if you don't trust other people to know. Would you like to be able to trust someone with this?
I speak to my mother, my social worker, and my solicitor. I do speak to people, but there's only so much help I can get. It all comes down to the judge really.
So people around you, you don't want to trust them into your life?

I do trust them into my life, it's just that there's only so much they can do. It's in my interest to either get involved with these people, or if I just sit and wait for them to phone me, it'll go quiet. If I don't show them that I want to get my son back and ask what they can do to help me, then I won't get him back.
So you're taking a very proactive approach. We've talked about a lot of things, and you've given me some useful things to think about.
I've got to be home soon, I think it's a bit late now.

case_summary: The participant discusses their social relationships, defining close family (mother, son, aunt, partner) as friends. They describe a history of antisocial peer groups, an ASBO, and a deliberate break from those friends to focus on a positive future for their son, who is currently in local authority care. The participant expresses deep distress over the separation from their son, feeling their motherhood has been taken away, and is focused on regaining custody. They also mention a hospital stay, keeping it private from most friends, and maintaining a supportive friendship with a former patient.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant's statements reflect distress related to real-life circumstances (child in care, past legal issues, social isolation) and personal values about friendship and parenting. There are no expressed beliefs about external reality that constitute a delusion point. The statement 'I can't see the mental in me at all' is a reflection on their perceived wellness, not a fixed false belief.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I'd like to hear about people you see socially—your friends at the moment. Do you have a particular friend right now?
Yes, but he's at college. He's the kind of guy who goes to college and all that.
Ok. Has he been a friend for a long time?
Yeah, I used to go to college with him. I went college with him for about four years.
Ok, so you've known him for a good amount of time?
Yeah.
What sort of things do you like to do together?
We sort of go out like, occasionally, maybe down to a shopping district or somewhere like that.
Do some shopping?
Yeah
Can you think of a recent time you've done that?
It's been a few months you know.
And would you phone him or who would organize it?
We organize it out on the street, sort of thing.
What's the good thing about this guy, in terms of being your friend? What do you like about him?
He's an honest guy really.
So he's somebody who says what he thinks?
Yeah.
Is there anything else about him?
No, not really.
What sort of role do you think you play in the friendship? What do you think it is that he likes about you?
I don't know, just.. I'm just a normal guy really. Natural, that sort of stuff.
So in the same way you like it in him that he's quite honest and he might like the same things about you?
Yeah.
Are there any other friends in your life at the moment?
No, not really.
Just this guy.
Yeah.
What sort of qualities do you look for in friends? What’s the important thing about friends for you?
Just for who they are really. Being honest, a natural instinct about them I’d say.
Anything else?
Not really.
And if this person, what’s his name?
[PERSON]
[PERSON], would you consider him somebody who you could talk about anything to? Or would you keep, tend to not talk about personal stuff?
Not really, no.
You wouldn’t?
No.
Would he know much about the symptoms that brought you to this service?
No.
You wouldn’t have talked to him about that?
No.
Is there anybody you would talk to about that stuff?
My cousin, my mum and dad and my cousin, the rest of my family.
So in terms of that sort of thing you’d rely more on your family?
Yeah.
Is your cousin someone who you’d do social stuff with?
Yeah.
What sort of things would you do?
Just go out, go to the shops like, go shopping, that sort of stuff, we’d go out for a drink or something.
And your cousin, presumably you’ve known him a long time if he’s in your family?
Yeah.
Is he in the same age group as you?
Yes, but he’s eight years older than me.
Can you tell me about any friendships you had before you started coming to the service? Or before the symptoms that brought you here began?
Yeah, I had a friend when I was in high school, his name was [PERSON]. I used to hang around with him.
What happened to that friendship?
We just stopped contact sort of thing. I dunno why.
Did he come to college with you?
Nah he went somewhere else.
Ok, so you went off and did different things after school?
Yeah.
What sort of things did you like to do with him?
We used to go out and all that sort of stuff. All the same stuff really.
Give me an example.
Just going out and socializing and all that sort of stuff.
Ok. Do you think there have been any friendships that you’ve lost because of your illness, the symptoms that have brought you here?
No not really.
So your friendships have stayed the same?
Yes
You said that [PERSON] didn’t know that you’ve not been well. How have you managed to keep that from him?
I dunno. I haven’t seen him for a while. He goes to college and is probably on his holidays. I see him at work though, he works at the same place as me, [PLACE].
So you see him there?
Yeah.
Do you have any other friends at work?
Yes, there are some I see at college as well.
Did you used to go to college?
Yeah.
What led to you stopping?

It was the end of the year. I was supposed to go to university but I didn't get enough grades, so I had to go back to college for another year or two. If I can get the grades up, then it'll be university.
I see. Is [PERSON] doing the same thing?
Yeah.
I'm just thinking about the symptoms that brought you here and the effect on friendships and possibly college?
No, none.
And it didn't stop you working?
No.
That's good, keeping those things up. Your friends, the people at work, the people you know from college wouldn't be aware of what you've been through?
No.
Ok. So who would you, if you wanted to talk to someone about any of this stuff, who would it be that you would talk to?
My cousin really.
Your cousin first. Your parents?
I'd sort of tell my parents. I'd tell my cousin as well.
Ok. Do you think your experiences, having the symptoms and not being well, have changed the way friendships are for you?
Not really.
They're still the same?
Yeah.
Has the way that you would, what you'd look for in friends changed?
Not really, the same stuff.
Much the same?
Yeah.
Do you do any different social activities now? Is there anything you used to do that you don’t do now, or vice versa?
I wouldn't go out socializing as much with a person. Not as much.
Why do you think that is?
We're just doing other things, that sort of thing.
What sort of things are you not doing?
Like socializing. I'm quite busy, sort of thing.
So it's more because you're quite busy, or because you haven't been well?
No, just been busy.
When you've been busy, what have you been doing?
Finding work, looking for work and all that sort of stuff. Finding a permanent job.
Do you think friendships in your life, or the people around you, have impacted how well you've coped with your illness?
Yeah, definitely.
Who would you say has made the biggest difference?
The biggest...
Yeah, who's helped you to cope with your illness?
My mum and dad mainly, and my cousin as well.
Do you think having them around helped, or did it not make any difference?
Yeah, it helped a little bit. I don't know really. I remember that time. I was on my own really.
On your own from friends. Why was that?
I don't know really. It was just a weird time, how I got ill. And then, I don't know.
Do you think it would have been different if you hadn't been on your own?
Yeah, could have been.
Do you still feel like that now, that you're on your own, or does that feel different now?
What do you mean by...
You said that when you got ill you felt on your own. I'm wondering if you still feel like that now?
No, not really now.
What changed so you don't feel that way anymore?
I try to stay positive and push it out of my mind.
Do you think you have more people around you now than you did back then?
Yeah.
And those would be your mum, your dad, your cousin, and [PERSON]?
Yeah.
Do you think anything could have helped with friendships—any extra support that might have helped you keep people around and stay social?
No, that's about it really.
So you didn't feel there was anything anyone could have done to help with that?
No.
Is there anything about your friendships right now you'd like to change?
No, not really.
Do you feel there's anything missing in your life when it comes to friendships or relationships?
No.
You feel things are how you want them?
I'd like to be closer to [PERSON], but we don't see each other as much as we used to.
So if you could change something, you'd want to be closer to a friend you already have?
Yeah.
What gets in the way of that?
I don't know. He's pretty busy with college and stuff like that.
So you find it hard to catch up with each other?
Yeah.
Does anyone here ever talk to you about friends—your care coordinator or other staff?
Yeah, [PERSON] does sometimes.
What sort of things do you and she talk about?
Just about whether I'm socializing as much as I used to, that kind of thing.
And what would you say to that when she asks you?
I would say that I do see my friends but not as much.
Which you feel is because everyone's busy rather than because of your illness or what happened. Is that right?
Yeah.
If life were perfect and you were completely satisfied with everything, would there be more friends or the same amount?
Same amount.
Have you ever been somebody who's had a big crowd of friends or have you tended to be a small group of closer friends?
Small group really.
That's always been the case since primary school?
Yeah.
Has there been anybody who has helped you to keep up with friendships and stuff?
Not really.
You've done it yourself. And in terms of you and [PERSON], you're both really busy but you're still friends. What is it about that friendship which has meant it's kept going?
We're sort of close. We're on the same wavelength as each other and all that sort of stuff.
So you think the same way? Are you interested in the same things?
Yeah.
I think that's everything.

case_summary: The participant describes a small, stable social circle consisting of one close friend from college, a cousin, and immediate family. They value honesty and a 'natural instinct' in friends. Social contact has decreased due to both parties being busy with work and education, not due to the participant's health. The participant relies on family for emotional support regarding their health and prefers to keep that aspect of their life private from their friend.
no_delusion_point_reason: No belief about external reality expressed by the participant meets the criteria for a delusion point. The content is limited to descriptions of social habits, personal preferences for friendship qualities, and practical reasons for reduced social contact (busy schedules). There are no statements indicating persecutory, referential, grandiose, or other reality-boundary distortions.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I’m interested in hearing about people in your life who you see socially, people who you consider to be friends. Do you have anyone like that you can think of?

I have a few people I can go and see, but I think a few of my friends haven’t really changed. They’re still the same people from about 7 or 8 years ago. I find that I don’t really go out and see the few friends I do have that often. I’m normally alone. I don’t go out and see my friends as much as I would like to.
What sort of things would you do with those friends if you did see them?

I might have a few beers or a couple of joints, listen to music, watch TV, just talk. I haven't really told my old friends about my problems. They knew I was hospitalized but never understood it was mostly due to alcohol and being stuck at home. Honestly, I don't get out much, but yesterday I went to [PLACE] for the day with a group, the EIS. I'm finding I can make friends through that program too. If you count them, then yes, I have some friends there.
What sort of things would you look for when you’re making friends?

What I look for in friends.. Maybe just.. I like people to be really down to earth, and just be themselves, be polite, be nice, and that’s about it. Friends that are not full of it, you know? Not arrogance.
Do you think what you look for in friends is different since you had a period of being unwell?

Yeah, I think so. I used to look at people like maybe they’re objects, not human, you know? But now I’ve got to realise that human people, what we are.. My attitude.. I don’t know really. I’m a bit puzzled.
That’s ok. You feel that there is something different?

Maybe I sort of think that the other person is special, not because they’ve got mental problems, just that they carry themselves well, they like to be treated how they would treat someone else. You would like to be treated that way too.
So you’re sort of looking for respectful?
Yeah, respect for each other.
Since you’ve had that time of not being well, do you think it would be easier now to make friends with people, like from the EIS, than it is elsewhere?

Yeah. I can make friends outside, but some of them might have mental health or alcohol issues themselves. Most of the friends I grew up with had problems. I grew up in a tough estate where everyone knew each other—it was a tight community, but you could see everyone's struggles: alcohol, smoking, aggression, that kind of thing.
And with that in mind, why did you decide not to tell people about being in hospital?

I didn't want to explain what I was in for. It was all tied to my past. I had a falling out with one of my best friends when we were younger—a fight—and I never really spoke to him again. So that's a close friend I don't see anymore. I do miss a few of them, but I worry we'd have nothing to say. It would just be silent. I don't want to talk about my problems because it feels selfish, like I'm only talking about myself. That's how I feel with friends now.
Is that what would stop you phoning someone up?

Not really, no. I haven't thought about getting their numbers because I feel stuck in life right now. I have a flat but I haven't properly moved in yet. Once I do that, I'm sure I'll get out more, make new friends, and socialize a bit.
So you think that once you get into your new place it will seem easier?

I think so, yeah. I'll feel more independent and happier in myself. I won't have to say I live with my parents—I'll have my own place and can invite someone over to watch a DVD. In the past, all I ever did with friends was get high or stoned. Nothing else.
Being at home with your mum and dad is limiting what you can do with friends?
That’s right, yeah.
Do you think there’s any friends that you lost touch with or have fallen out with because you weren’t well?
Maybe just one.
What happened there?

He was judging my weight, calling me fat, saying I looked pregnant when I was ill. It made me paranoid around other people in case they judged my appearance—my size, my weight. I don't like him anymore. I'm not angry at him for what he said, but I found it out of order. We grew up together, he was a good friend, and he was judging my weight. I've never done that to other friends—never judged their weight, personality, or how they dress or look. I find it a bit heartbreaking. I didn't like it, so he's one friend I don't really see.
It sounds like that was your decision not to see him anymore, because you felt judged?
Yeah, that's right. He was disrespectful.
The friends that have been around, what do you think it is about them that has meant your friendships have carried on?

Because of my past, my background, having good teenage years, growing up, having a good life—enjoying life, partying, getting out every day, hanging out maybe five hours a day with a group of friends.
A shared history?

Yeah, we all have that close bond, like you would with a brother or sister. That's why I would find it difficult to talk about any of my own problems to them—I don't think they would understand what I went through.
In your friendships that are still going, that you see from time to time, what sort of role do you think you play?

I think I play like... my friends used to call me big [NICKNAME]. I used to like it. I felt, not powerful—powerful is not the word—I felt strong. I felt that I played a strong role. Physically, mentally, I'm there to listen to them, to understand them. What I've realized by making a few new friends from this early intervention group is I can ask them for help or they ask me about their problems; I can talk to them more easily than old friends about my problems. They're on the same sort of medication that I'm on. I can understand them, they can understand me. I find it easier to talk to someone who has mental health problems than talking to someone who hasn't had them or won't get them.
So before you had quite a strong role, would you still play that same sort of role now if you saw those mates?
Maybe, yeah, I would.
And I might have got this wrong, but it sounds as if you talk to them about your problems that would make it seem less like you were strong?
Yeah, that's right. It would make me feel really different.
We'll come to friends from here, from the group, in a minute. But these friends you've known for a long time, what sort of thing do you like from them?
They value my friendship, my presence.
What do you like about them?

They make me feel good about myself. That's why when one of them commented on my weight and said I looked pregnant it did hurt me, because I've never been judged like that.
