I thought surely he can't be talking about me but he was. If I saw him again, the guy who disrespected me, I wouldn't even look at him. I couldn't be bothered to talk to him about anything. With some friends I had, they're really close, like family, known them for years. What I do miss sometimes is going to see some of these old friends and maybe just driving about together, maybe going out on the town for the night. Enjoy [CITY] a little bit more. I've noticed now I'm older that [CITY] can be a really lonely place if you're by yourself.
What do you think stops you from going out on the town and doing that stuff?

When I see my reflection, I sometimes think I'm overweight. Some days I look and feel good, other days not so much—that's probably universal. I think being around my friends constantly might bring out a more egotistical, wild side of me.
And that stops you from wanting to do stuff?

Yeah. Mostly not doing things with them because I'm not really happy with my physical appearance. I find that, if I liked a lady or a girl and she would look, and if I did like her and she wouldn't like me because of my size, I feel like I get problems like that sometimes.
So you're not feeling very confident about yourself. Do you think that's since you were unwell or have you always felt like that?

No, since I was unwell I think. When I was ill I was really slow. When I came out of the hospital the first thing I did was get some drink, which I shouldn't have done, and went and sat up in my friend's house, one of my best friends called [PERSON]. After that I haven't really seen them much because I don't want to go there and start drinking around them again. We got violent towards each other after a few drinks. We wanted to fight and he thought I was flirting with his girlfriend but I wasn't, and I hold a grudge with my friend. I didn't want to fall out with him; I thought he was genuine, nice, and just good company. The same friend whose company you enjoyed, it turned to aggressiveness and anger, we don't enjoy each other's company anymore. I miss going to see friends, I really do, then I think but I can make new friends, as I'm older now you know?
It sounds like since you were unwell, some of your old friends wouldn't have been that helpful to keep you well?
Yeah, that's exactly how I felt as well.
You've mentioned some violence but also a lot of drinking, which you were perhaps trying to avoid?
Yeah, that's right. I didn't like always going out drinking, smoking, and getting high with my friend. It just got boring after a while, doing the same thing over and over, going round and round.
With the friends, or the people you've met through the EIS, what sort of role do you think you play with them?

Sometimes I feel like I'm the dad role, the role model, someone to look up to. Someone to show that everyone has problems but they're not all the same, so if I talk to someone about theirs I'd share about mine. I think there's more of a bond, or a different sort of bond, than I had with my old friends. I find with the EIS people, I feel like I could be the dad model because I'm the oldest. They're all a bit younger, early twenties, and I'm almost 30. More responsibility on my shoulders. Not to look after them, just to lend a hand. If they need anything or to ask how they feel... I feel like a doctor or like the relationship a doctor has with a patient. I feel that sort of bond with these people from the EIS.
Protective?
Yeah, protective and that sort of thing. I feel like I protect them, my friends. I've always had that side to me.
Is that a role you enjoy?

I do in a way, I really do. I know that—without talking about violence—I can look after myself and handle myself well. If anyone wanted to hurt me I could really look after myself, but some of these EIS people can't do that, so I find if I walk down the road with them, I'd be like a bodyguard. I feel that role sometimes. Only with friends from this EIS though.
So they might seem a bit vulnerable?
Yeah, I'd protect them.
It sounds like, perhaps not to the same extent, but with your old friends you were the strong one, and that's important to you?

Yeah, my character, full of life, enjoying everything—that's how I used to be with my old friends. There's not much I miss about them, except maybe their company. Not what they have to say, just their company from all those years we grew up together. I don't see them, I very rarely see them. That's what I miss, just their company, or maybe just to see them. But then I wouldn't like to have any comments again because that was really downgrading and I didn't like it. It made me walk down the road thinking everybody was judging me or looking at me and thinking I'm overweight or getting big and fat.
Is there anything that could happen that would make you want to get back and see them or be out and about?

If I joined the gym, which I have done but don't really go—I should, it's just round the corner from where I live—if I used the gym I'd start feeling better in myself. Then if I saw them again, the guy who said I'd put on weight would say I'd lost weight and I'd feel a bit better. I'm still up to here in my brain with him telling me I look pregnant and stuff. It's not right to talk to people like that, not in this day and age.
So if you raised your confidence a bit...
Yeah, getting out and seeing people.
Is there anything anyone could do to help you with that, do you think?

Myself really, just myself. A bit of willpower. I'm really surprised how many people suffer from mental problems. In [PLACE], or [PLACE] especially, or [PLACE] in general, who suffer from mental health problems. I'd feel better if I could slim up a little, lose a few pounds. I don't want to turn into a big muscle man, just be a bit slimmer so my clothes fit and hang better. I carry my weight a bit more instead of thinking old friends are disrespecting me. I'd feel better if I could start using a gym. Even just one hour a day. In a few months the first thing I'd do is knock on a few old friends' doors and show them my new look, my new body. That's what I'd want to do. I don't think I could do that now. I think they might still be judging me. A few of my friends used to say I had a crazy side to me growing up. I would never harm anyone, maybe crazy but nothing to hurt anybody.
Is there anybody, apart from in the EIS group, that you've talked about your mental health problems with?
Not really, no.
Do you talk with your family about that stuff?

No, I don't. I don't really talk to them about my problems. I've done a path with [PERSON], of my past, future, and present, with pictures underneath of all my problems, and she's really good. I don't think my parents are interested. My dad has diabetes, he's been diagnosed with diabetes, and I suppose they're looking after themselves a bit more, they're getting old now. Fifties, not old but older than me.
So you use the professional people here to talk to instead?

Yeah, but when I want to talk, I'd talk about my problems but then I think anyone who drinks quite a lot or smokes a lot of weed, it's going to affect their body, how they talk to people, how they feel. They get really tired and don't really want to talk about their problems. It just numbs your pain. Alcohol and smoking, just get rid of everything. Just keep high and stoned and don't care about anything. That's what I do sometimes. I know I shouldn't. I shouldn't really be drinking. I don't drink on top of my medication but I don't think the two mix together. All the problems I had in the past when the police used to come round my house and get me off the streets drinking a can of beer and bring me home—after a while, I think they always used to see me on my own, so they thought I didn't have friends around me. That might be why they stepped in and helped me and put me in hospital, because they saw no one was around to help me and I was in a right state mentally, my head all over the place, felt really bad, depressed. They looked after me like they were friends at the time. They were friends to me, the police, helping me, seeing I had problems. My old friends, they didn't really ask why I was in hospital or what I was in there for. It doesn't really interest them. I suppose if I saw a few old friends again I wouldn't mention my mental health problems. I'd say I was in hospital and that was it. I wouldn't mention how I used to feel and what I used to do to make myself feel better.
The time you were in hospital, your friends weren't around, were they? Do you think things could have been different for you if they were? Would it have changed you getting better?

Towards the end of my seven-week hospital stay, around week five, I really wanted to see a friend. I needed to. But no friends were around then. The only friends I could make were the other patients on the ward, there for similar reasons.
What sort of people were they? Did you stay in contact?

No, I never stayed in touch, but when I've run into a few of them on the street they're really happy and cheery, glad to see I'm okay. Maybe we'd have a drink, then I'd go home, or we'd talk about how my problems are now, whether I'm still on medication. They give me advice, and I appreciate it. They understand mental health struggles. When I was in hospital I really listened to them instead of just hanging around. I understood what they were saying, that everything would be okay. When I was first admitted, it all felt like one big dream, and that's when I really needed a friend but no one was there. None of my friends visited me in hospital. I think it would have helped.
In what way would it have helped you?

I think it would have helped me mentally, to stop thinking about problems, thinking negative all the time. Instead of focusing on the positive things, the good, simple things in life. That's what I'm missing right now. I want to get all that back: a girlfriend, my own flat, a car, a job. Just a simple life. Once I have that I'll feel better in myself. I'll keep it, and I wouldn't feel like everyone's watching me or judging me or telling me I'm overweight. It's simple, it's just around the corner. I think my life will be a lot better. I'm at a point now where I don't really need friends. I feel I don't need support from any of them. I feel like I'm my own adult now, a fully grown young man. I'm 28. I don't want to get old before my time; I want these next two years to be the best for getting back on track, getting off medication, mixing with people. That's what used to get me down, being alone all the time with no one to talk to. I couldn't understand myself, so I couldn't be around other people. So I wasn't talking, and a friend would probably keep asking what's wrong, which would get annoying, and then I wouldn't see them for months. I haven't seen my best friend for about nine months. It would be good to see him, but I don't really have anything to talk about. That's why I was talking about joining the gym, because I'd feel more toned up and confident. Even having a job. When I was growing up I worked quite a lot, earning good money at 16, saving, going out, having drinks, enjoying life with a girlfriend, just normal. That's what I miss. So friends are maybe second, third, or fourth on my list. First is getting a job, second is sorting out my flat, third is being more sociable. I know that when I was in [PLACE] yesterday I thought, look at all these people, but none of them were looking at me badly. I felt at ease. No one gave me bad eye contact, just normal. That's what I really miss; I miss getting out.
It sounds like it's important to be independent, to know you don't need those people but to have them around for socialising. It's a want rather than a need?
Yeah.
So the kind of things you'd like to do to socialise now sound different from what you would have chosen before?

Yeah, a lot of them are different, for the better I suppose. There's nothing really good about my old friends. It's just that we were all from the same area, and it was really nice. I enjoyed growing up and not worrying about stuff. When my mental health problems started, I stopped being sociable with my friends. That's when I used to lock myself away and have bad dreams and nightmares, and my friends would be in some of them. They still are, which is pretty strange.
If life was good, you talked about having a job, a flat, some money coming in. What would your friendships be like in that ideal, perfect situation?

Seeing them twice a week, going to a bar, having a couple of beers. Maybe bringing them back to my flat to watch a DVD, then saying goodbye and going to bed. Or just the normal thing, which would be best: get a mobile phone, and if you don't want to talk to them, switch it off. Simple. That's still the best way to keep in contact with people. There's nothing easier. I'd get more phone numbers from people I meet at the bar. Speak to them, mix with them. I'd like to meet new people. Not people with mental health problems or old friends, just people in general. Reality people, I'd call them. People who are real to themselves and real to life, who have respect for life and just get along. That's all I miss right now, which is better than my past problems of not mixing with anyone at all. Even if I'm indoors at home, I'm still mixing with my parents. There are people in the house, so I'm not completely alone.
Do you not use a mobile at the moment?
I do, but I don't have any credit. I need to buy some. I have a mobile back home. I'll get some numbers down. I got some from the [ORG] group, numbers to talk to and stay in touch with.
Is there anything you think the service here could do to help you with any of this – friendships and socialising?

Not really. It's up to me, I think. I've had all this help, going to badminton, museums, cinemas, playing pool, bowling, doing everything. I've really enjoyed it, but I've realised now's the time to get on with my life. My mental health problems are getting better – with each day I feel a lot better. I really do, I'm not just saying it. I feel better in myself. I can be around people now without thinking they're thinking, look at that, you know? I think it's really bad to judge someone who's had mental health problems. You should just leave them and let them get on with their life. And if they are having problems, come and talk to the people at the [ORG]. If you're having problems with your family, talk to them. I've done it before; I've talked to the people here at the [ORG] about loads of things, all my problems. Whenever I have talked to them, they're good listeners. They know how to listen. I think it's really arrogant not to listen, use your ears, that's what they're there for.
Is there anything you want to add that I haven't asked you yet about friendships?
No, not really. We've covered a lot, done really well.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believed that after a friend made a derogatory comment about his weight, strangers on the street were also judging him and thinking he was overweight.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant frames this as a past feeling that has since improved, stating he can now be around people without thinking they are looking at him negatively.

case_summary: The participant discusses his social life, describing a small circle of long-term friends he rarely sees, a falling out with a friend who commented on his weight, and new connections made through an early intervention service (EIS). He reflects on how his mental health problems and past substance use have affected his friendships, expressing a desire for independence, a job, and his own flat before prioritizing socializing. He notes an improvement in his mental state and a reduction in feeling judged by strangers.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: So what we’re interested in hearing about is people you see socially. Can you think of any particular friends that you have in your life at the moment?
Yeah.
Can you tell me about somebody?
Well just about them or..?
Who have you got in mind? Are you somebody with a lot of friends?
I have a decent number of friends, though not a huge amount. Most are from university or from after I relocated to [PLACE] roughly a decade back.
Who would you say you see the most often?

I see someone once or twice a week, but it varies who. Others I see monthly or every couple of months. Most now have children, so it's harder to meet regularly—evenings are taken up with bedtime routines, so they're tied to their schedules.
Okay, have you seen any friends in the past week?

Not this past week, mainly because work has been busy and I've had a lot of weddings. I saw friends the last two weekends for weddings, so I've just been working, eating, and sleeping. I am seeing work friends tonight for wine-tasting on [PLACE]. I've known them about five years. They just returned to the UK from working in [PLACE], so it's been good seeing them more now they're back.
What sort of things do you do with these friends then? Wine-tasting is unusual. What sort of stuff do you do normally?

Usually lunch, since we all work—it's easier. We used to go to the pub. With these two it's mainly lunch and the pub, plus wine-tasting about once a month. There's a nice place in [PLACE] I used to go to—free and pleasant.
Is the sort of things you do with those friends different to what you do with your university friends or new friends?

I think so. With university friends, I go to their homes because they have babies and can't travel easily. We have dinner, chat, maybe an evening walk, or a weekend picnic in the park. So it's a bit different.
People play different roles in friendships - what sort of role do you think you play in friendships generally?
I don't really know. Some friends come to me for advice when they need to talk. With work friends it's more about fun or gossiping about mutual acquaintances. I'm not sure what role I have.
It varies perhaps.
Yeah.
Okay and instead of what you do for them, what are the important bits for you in those people?
People I can talk to about things, but also have a laugh and be silly without worrying about what I say or do. Like [PERSON]—he's really funny, jokes and laughs most of the time.
Okay, so quite light-hearted?
Yeah, but he can also be serious when needed and talk about serious things if you're not feeling right or need help.
Do you think that the things that you look for in friends now is different to what you looked for perhaps before you had symptoms that bought you to the service?

A little, but not really. My friends now are mostly the same as before my episode. One friendship changed slightly because of how she reacted when she first heard what happened, but she's still a friend. Communication was difficult then, and she's only recently talked more openly. I think it affected her—she hadn't realized what happened. What I look for hasn't changed much, but I'm more aware of mental health issues now. I might challenge things people say that I'd have ignored before, which has probably strengthened friendships. If someone I don't know well talks about 'crazies,' it might make me reluctant to befriend them. I try to challenge it.
With the friends rather than those people that you don’t know, would you talk to them quite openly about what had happened to you?

Yes, I try to be as open as I can with colleagues. All my friends know what happened, even if they don't know every detail—they know I was in hospital. It helps that they knew I was on medication, and I even had a small celebration when I stopped taking it.
Was there anyone who was particularly present during the time you were unwell?

Yes, especially afterwards. While I was in hospital, it was mainly my family and my fiancé who were around, not really friends. I have one friend from work who now lives in [PLACE]. She was around a little at the time. She knew what happened—she was one of the first people I called when I was in a terrible state just before I went in. I don't see her now because she's in [PLACE], but we speak regularly.
Do you think having her available by phone made a difference to how the episode progressed, or do you think it would have been the same? I know it's an impossible question, but in your opinion?

I'm not sure. I think she did help. She was the one person I trusted while I was having paranoid thoughts about everyone else. There weren't many paranoid thoughts, but I don't remember having any about her, whereas I did about other people from work. Speaking to her helped, and she tried to calm me down and understand what was going on, but it was so confusing I don't think she really knew. It helped afterwards too, because she used to be a solicitor's clerk at a firm specializing in mental health cases, so she understood a little of what I'd been through.
Okay. So, as you say, perhaps her and your family while you were in hospital. Did friends play much of a part when you came out?

Yes. One friend, who is coming for dinner tomorrow actually, was pregnant at the time and is an ex-flatmate. Because she was pregnant and not working when I came out, I spent a lot of time with her. She lives just down the road, so we'd do things during the day—go swimming, see exhibitions, chat, hang out, listen to music, bake. I'd see her two or three times a week, and then it gradually became less as I went back to work.
What do you think it was about that time that was helpful?

Just being with someone. Being on my own was really hard. My boyfriend works during the day, so he was out, and at the beginning my mum stayed... Sorry, it's getting a bit hard for me to... [participant tearful]
It's okay, it's remembering a difficult time, isn't it?
Yeah, my mum, sorry...
It's okay, that's okay. I'm sorry, I'm not sure we've got any tissues in here.

I've probably got some. My mum is retired, so she spent quite a lot of time with me when I first came out of hospital, but then I kind of asked her to just go home. I wanted things to go back to normal, but when I was on my own it was really hard. So it was good to have someone who wasn't my mum, or my sister, or related to me—just my friend.
Why do you think it was better to have someone with a bit more distance?

I think you always feel—not so much now—but my parents and my sister were always trying to tell me what to do. When I came out of hospital, it was a lot of very well-meaning advice: 'you should do this, you should do that, you should think about talking to this person.' My friend was just like, 'do what you want!'
A bit of company but without crowding you with advice?
Yeah.

Okay. Was there anyone when you were in hospital or afterwards—I think you mentioned one friend already—that didn't understand, or found it difficult to be around to talk about things? When did that become apparent?

Well, I went into hospital really suddenly and was there for the full 28-day section, though by the end I was coming home on day and overnight leave and was practically at home. The first time I talked to this friend after I came out, I hadn't seen her for a good month. It had been my birthday just after I went in. She asked how things were, and I said I was getting used to being back home and not having to go to hospital. I told her I'd been in hospital for quite some time, which was why I hadn't returned her calls. She said, 'Oh, I thought there was something wrong when you didn't return my calls.' It really hurt, because she seemed more worried about me not returning her calls than about me. When I did see her and tried to talk about it, I could tell she wasn't comfortable. She didn't want to talk about it, didn't ask any questions, just let me talk, and I felt she didn't really want to listen. I just left it at that and felt like, doesn't she care? Now I don't think it's that she doesn't care—she just didn't know what to say, or it was too difficult. That was the one. Everyone else asked questions, had a laugh about it—some things that happened were funny in retrospect. A lot of my friends were there for my boyfriend too, phoning him, but she didn't. Maybe she didn't feel comfortable doing that. She knows him well—I've been with him 10 years. I think it was difficult for her, but at the same time it made me angry, because if it's difficult for you to talk about, what's it like for me?

Thinking back, you had a good number of friends who were there, were supportive, wanted to talk about it, and supported your partner as well, and then this one friend who didn't. I'm wondering if there's some characteristic or quality in the friends who were around that helped them to be there, for the friendship to survive? Do you think there's anything about them or about the friendship?

I think they're much more open about things in general. If I think about that one friend, since she got married and had a little boy, it's very difficult to talk to her about anything when she's with her husband. On her own it's much easier, but even then it's sometimes like I'm asking all the questions. I just think maybe she doesn't want to tell me, and that's fine to a certain extent. For example, we went for dinner with her and her husband, me and my boyfriend, and I hadn't seen her for a couple of weeks. I suddenly found out she'd set up this whole website that's been running for about nine months—it's her website that she runs and gets other people to comment on. I thought, that means she's done research and all this work, and she just didn't say anything to me about it. Whereas with all my other friends, even if I don't see them that often or talk to them every day, I feel I know most of what's going on in their lives. Not in detail, but I have some idea.
Do you think that friend has always been a bit more detached, or is that since you were unwell?
No, I think since she got married.
Ok.
It was before I went into hospital, a couple of years before, so she's been married about six or seven years.
So you'd relate it more to that than to when you were unwell?
Yeah.
Do you think the way she was when you came out of hospital had any impact on your recovery?
Not really. She was one person, compared to a lot of others.
Okay. Can you tell me if there are any friends you've made since you were unwell? More recent friends?

People at work. Even though they're not friends as such, we socialise outside of work—drinks after work or lunch, that kind of thing. I see them every day and you kind of feel like they're friends even if you might not see them socially.
That's interesting. You said they were from work but weren't really friends—I wondered what would make them move over into the friendship box?

Yeah, I guess it's if I start seeing them socially outside of work, at the weekend. The people I see every day at work, I talk about the weekend or things with them, have a ten-minute chat in the corridor, but I wouldn't call them friends as such apart from a couple of people. My landlady actually works in the same department as me now, and I would say she is a good friend even though I live in her house, so it's a slightly different relationship.
Is there anything about that sort of acquaintance-friendship that's different from people you've known for a long time?

Yeah, I guess people at work don't know me as well, and to some degree I think you maybe put on a bit of a front at work regarding how much you want people to know—you aim to be professional. There are some things you might never discuss in detail with certain colleagues, whereas with my friends you go into detail. With people at work I try to be open about what happened with my illness on a need-to-know basis. My line manager knows I need to leave early for medical appointments at least once a month, and she knows I have occupational health check-ins to see I'm coping with work. There were days I was off sick, and when I first came back my performance wasn't very good. She knows the history. I don't think she knows exactly why I wasn't at work, but she's never asked and it's never been an issue.
So when you were unwell you were off sick; did you go back to the same job afterwards?

I did, but then I changed jobs shortly after because the job I was doing before was just far too stressful, and I think that was part of the reason I got unwell. I moved into a different department—same kind of group but a different team, completely different kind of work. A lot of the people move on quite regularly because you have two years in a job then move to another, so a lot of the people who were there when I went sick are no longer there, or are about to leave.
In that first period of going back to work and being around those people again, do you think the way you were around them was different to how it was before?

Yeah, I think when I first went back to work I wasn't as communicative. I found it very difficult to talk to people and engage in conversation. It wasn't that I wouldn't talk at all—I would say hello and make small talk—but I found I couldn't engage in conversation the way I could before or can now, in terms of making the links. It was very much they talked and I couldn't think of how to progress the conversation; it stagnated, whereas now it's proper dialogue.
Sort of back to normal conversation? And how do you think you've got from there to here? What's been the important bit for you, do you think?

So many things. Accepting what happened, trying to understand what happened and why, and how to avoid it happening again. Learning more about myself in terms of my limits, and what to do if you think it's too much—even just recognising it is too much. And then just perseverance, really: getting up in the morning and putting yourself in that situation. On the bad days, going 'ok, it's a bad day, just get on with it'; scream and shout and cry and it'll be better tomorrow.

A lot of people say that actually; that afterwards it's difficult to be around people socially, but kind of keep putting themselves in that situation makes it start to feel normal again, almost like getting back on the horse. Is there anything about your friendships and the people in your social networks at the moment that you'd like to change?

I kind of wish I could bring them all together, because I have friends from university, friends from work, friends of friends, friends of my boyfriend, and I see them individually or with their group of friends. But I'd quite like them to be all friends together in one big group. For birthdays and things like that, I think 'are they all getting along?' because they don't really know each other apart from through me. So yeah, if there was one thing I could change, it would be that they had all been friends as long as I've been friends with them.
Is there anything you think is missing, or that you would need from friends that's not always there or that's difficult to come by?

Sometimes I think—especially now they've all got children and their priorities have changed—I kind of think that maybe you need to come to me for once, and why do I have to travel just because you've got a baby. So maybe that's something for me to accept, that their priorities have changed, but I don't know.
You would like your needs to be put equal to their needs?
Yes.
I'm wondering if there's anything the service could have done or did do to help you socially; did you attend the groups or anything like that?

Yes, before returning to work I attended bowling once. Was that the only time? They also held an odd meeting I didn't fully understand—a client or service user feedback session. A staff member was there with snacks and drinks, asking our opinions on the service. This was quite a while ago. I thought many other service users would attend, but it was only me and one other person. He later told me his whole story was fabricated and he didn't actually have psychosis. Another individual briefly entered, took some crisps, and left. I only made it to bowling that single time; other sessions conflicted with my schedule. The bowling itself was enjoyable.
I was wondering if there was anything in particular you got by coming here and meeting people through the bowling that you wouldn't get from your friends in your normal situation?

Yes. It was challenging since I only attended once. I genuinely wanted to discuss my experience with someone who might comprehend it. After leaving hospital, I spent excessive time online, even during work, reading mental health forums and others' personal accounts. Hearing those experiences, even virtually, and discovering support organizations and their published leaflets was reinforcing, even when I already knew the information. Regarding the bowling, there wasn't really an opportunity to socialize despite the shared activity. The group was mostly men; I was the sole woman. It wasn't unpleasant, but the dynamic centered heavily on the game and winning. Our brief chat afterward remained superficial small talk, not a sharing of deeper experiences.
Would this have been something you would have been more interested in?

Yeah, I think it would have been good. Actually, my friend's sister had a psychotic episode a few years ago, about seven years ago now, and I only found out through my friend when she found out about me. She was like, 'Oh, my sister went through this a couple of years ago.' I was in email contact with her for a while because my friend said I should email her. I really kind of enjoyed it and liked talking to her through email. But I guess if I'd had more of that, it might have filled a need in me; I wouldn't have surfed the internet at that time.
Has anybody here talked to you about friendships or asked about your social support or anything?

When I come to see my care coordinator, she always asks, 'How are things going?' and 'How's your family?' She doesn't really ask about friends as such, but she always kind of asks what I'm up to. I go to yoga as well, and she always asks how the yoga is going, if I'm going regularly, but nothing ever in detail. It's always quite general, and as long as I'm healthy, I think she's quite happy.
And how about you? Would you like to be talking more about that, or are you quite happy that it's meeting your need?

Yeah, I think it's okay. I now think sometimes when I come here, I wonder why I come here because I'm like, 'Oh, I'm just going to have my small talk with my care coordinator.' But then, you know, I think it's important to check in. But then I'm well, I'm working full-time. At the beginning, coming here twice a week gave me structure because when I wasn't working, it was very tempting just to lie around the house in my duvet. So it kind of helped and gave me structure.
Is there anything else about friendships or social stuff that you think is important over the last couple of years?

I think my friends who are really aware of mental health issues, like I've got a friend who used to work for a mental health charity, I think the people who are more aware about things, it was much easier to go to them for help if I needed to talk about something more. If I just wasn't feeling right, it was much easier to go to them and say, 'Oh, can you come and help me?' or 'Can you spend the day with me?' That sort of thing. At the same time, the friends who weren't necessarily aware about mental health issues, it's not essential, but it helps. Even at work, because where I work we look after people who live, work, or travel overseas, and there's a huge issue with travelers who go overseas and have an episode or get mentally ill and get stuck in a foreign country in a mental hospital. We have to try and get them back to the UK where it's safe. So within the department, there are some social work advisers who advise specifically on mental health issues, so the people at work have got quite an awareness about mental health. I think that has really helped because it makes it easier to talk about things. You know, somebody says this guy is in a mental hospital, it makes it easier to talk about my own experience and say, 'Oh well, you know, when I was in hospital...' and people are like, 'Yeah?' And because we're talking about it all the time, it kind of helps. Okay, that's helpful, thank you.

delusion_points.summary: During a past episode, the participant held paranoid beliefs about some colleagues at work.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant states the paranoid thoughts were not numerous and that she did not have any such thoughts about one specific trusted colleague.

case_summary: The participant discusses her social network, which includes university friends, work colleagues, and friends of her partner. She describes how friendships have adapted to life changes like parenthood and her own mental health episode. She reflects on the varying support she received during and after a hospital stay, noting one friend's difficulty in discussing the event, and emphasizes the value of openness and mental health awareness in her relationships.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I'm interested in hearing about people in your life you consider friends or spend time with socially. Is there anyone like that at the moment?
Yes, there are a few people. So it's not about family?
I'm more interested in the friends side, but we might come to family later. Can you think of an example of someone you've seen socially in the last week?

Yeah, I went out with three people from school yesterday. We just went for a drink, but it was the first time in a few months. I think since I've had serious mental health problems it's become more difficult. I've lost some motivation to call people. I used to drink quite heavily when I went out, and I've tried to cut down. I found drinking helped me socialise, so maybe cutting down has made it harder. It's a combination of things.
Do you think drinking helped you socialise because it was an activity to do together, or more because it gave you confidence?
Yeah, I think it was more that it gave me confidence, but also when I see friends it often tends to be at the pub. It's something to do with that as well.
Thinking about these friends you've known from school, how long has that been?
I'm 26 now and I've known them since I was about 12 or 13.
So quite a long time, and you hadn't seen them for a while before this week. What prompted you to meet up?
I'd texted people asking to meet up and for whatever reason it just hadn't happened, but eventually we managed to organise a date.
It was just everyone finding a suitable time?
Yeah, I think so. At least one of them definitely knows about the problems I've had. Sometimes I feel like a bit of a burden, like friends are looking after me more than just socialising.
Do you think your role in your friendships has become different now?

It's weird, because only two or three people know about the problems I've had. Others may have been told, but I'm not sure. I feel like people are looking out for me a bit, particularly those who know about my problems.
What was it about the people you told that made them the ones you chose to tell?

When I first went into hospital, my sister chose the people she thought I was closest to and informed them of what was going on. I may have told two people myself, and she told a few others. I don't really talk about it much, so I don't know what they know or how much.
What makes you decide not to talk about it?

I think I'm a bit embarrassed about it. It just feels easier to talk about normal things. I spend most of my time at home with my parents, so I talk about it with them. With friends, it just doesn't really come up. Nobody asks, and I don't volunteer it.
You mentioned you might still go to the pub but drink less. What other things do you like to do with friends?

I play football quite often. In summer, a friend who lives near [PLACE] and I go to the park in the evenings and join in games there. I also play every Saturday during the season with training once a week, which is good for routine. I see those people regularly, but we don't socialise much outside football, just a quick drink after a game. I also like going to the cinema, but I find it hard to just sit and chat without an activity to focus on. I find small talk difficult. If there's no activity, I'd normally go to the pub. I have one friend who visited me in hospital; I can talk to him about personal problems, but generally I don't go out for coffee or things like that.
Has that always been the case, or is it recent?
I think it has always been the case.
I think that's quite common. I was thinking about the friend who visited you in hospital and is around more if you want to talk. What is it about that friendship that has survived through everything?

Partly he's quite different to me. He's very mature, and he's a strict Muslim so he doesn't drink or have sex with women. He's just finished his training as a doctor, so he knows about the area. He's also separate from my other friends; he's met them but doesn't really know them, so it feels natural to talk. He made quite an effort to visit me in hospital. I didn't really like having visitors, and he didn't force his way in but didn't give me much choice either, which was good because it meant he spoke to me while I was in the middle of my problems. He's the only person outside my family who visited me. Others offered, but I discouraged them without saying 'don't come'.
You discouraged him?
Yeah.
Having this guy around.. What was his name?
[PERSON].
Having [PERSON] around, do you think that made a difference to when you came out of hospital and your recovery since, or do you think it was more your family and other people?

It helped a bit, though it was strange—I actually saw him more while I was in hospital than I normally do. Knowing someone made a real effort to visit showed they cared. With family you sometimes feel they're obliged, but friends aren't.
Was there anybody during that time who you lost touch with or who's no longer a friend?
I wouldn't say it was because of the hospital stay. It was more gradual—I've lost contact with people over quite a few years, not just since being admitted.

After leaving the hospital and starting to resume everyday life, some people found the first few visits with friends tough but then things settled into a routine. Did you experience that, or was it different for you?
I think so. They seemed to know what was going on, but I didn't really talk about it. It was hard at first and I had to force myself to meet up.
And how did that get easier? What happened to make it easier?

Partly I started feeling more normal again. I've been in hospital twice—the first time was much worse because it was completely new and more unpleasant. Since then I've got used to dealing with my symptoms and they're integrated into everyday life now, so I'm not held back as much.
Thinking about making new friends; Have there been any new friends since your symptoms?

Yes, especially recently. The first admission I was really scared of the place and the people. The second time I met someone in hospital and we saw each other regularly for a few months, but I lost contact when his phone stopped working. I also come here weekly and have met nice people through activities like film club and football, though I haven't seen them outside those groups. There's also a housing project, [ORG], running a football group with [ORG]—I'm going after this. I've met someone there I might see later this week. It's good meeting people with similar experiences; a lot of mental health services help with that.
What is it that's good about spending time with people who've had similar problems?

You have things in common and they're all trying to get past their problems. It's nice knowing others experience the same things. We haven't really talked about symptoms—just knowing they've had problems too helps.
I was wondering with those people if you still feel that role of other people looking after you that happens sometimes with your other friends?
Yeah. Yes it's different definitely.
What sort of person do you think you are with people from here or the other activities at [ORG]?

People from these places don't judge you like others do. I feel more comfortable around them than with my school friends. I think I just have less in common with my old friends now, so it's good to meet people I share things with.
And if you're making friends at the moment, what sort of things would you be looking for in new friends?

I'm not sure. I'd want shared interests, and maybe someone I can look out for as much as they look out for me. With old friends, I think some are looking after me, and I don't always like that—it makes me feel fragile, like a bit of a failure.
So redressing that power balance would be important to you in new friendships?
Yeah, that would be nice. But I'm not meeting that many new people, so I'll decide what I want when the situation arises.
Is that something that you would like to be doing more of? Do you think there's something missing in terms of friendships at the moment?

I often feel quite lonely. I'm thinking about applying to university for next September—if that goes well it'll be a good chance to meet new people. I've started part-time and voluntary work, but I haven't met people there I'd see outside work. Still, it's nice being around new people.
And if you were able to strengthen those friendships or meet new people when you start university, what kind of things would you want to do with them? What feels missing?

Well, the idea of having a girlfriend has pretty much disappeared over the last couple of years since being in hospital, so that's something I definitely think about. I'm quite close to my sister, but apart from that I don't have any female friends, so it could be good to meet some women.
Has that always been the case, or has it changed recently?

I think it has changed. I had female friends at school, but since leaving I've gradually lost touch with them, so I don't think it's because of being in hospital. I think university would be good because it's nice to have people doing the same thing as you, so you have things in common. I feel I have less in common with my school friends now than I did a few years ago.
Everyone's kind of grown and is doing different things?
Maybe I've become a bit cut off from them because of what's been going on.

And do you think if you hadn't had that time in hospital, things would have gone a similar way for you as it has for them? Or do you think you are different sorts of people and would have done different things anyway? That's a hard question to answer, isn't it?

I think I would have been more similar to them if I hadn't been in hospital. I feel that hospital was the big hurdle that got in the way of things. I feel I've become closer to my family since being in hospital, but further away from my friends.
And if you had to think about why that is, what would you say?

Partly I feel I'm spending more time with my family, and they also saw first-hand what went on. In a way, times of crisis bring people together. I've definitely seen my friends less since being in hospital, but I think it's for a number of reasons, not just because of going into hospital. And if I'm seeing them less, it means I'm seeing my family more.

We touched on what you might seek in a friend and how it's hard until you're face-to-face or in the moment. Do you feel your current approach to finding friends or what you desire in one has changed since before your hospital stay, or would it be similar?

I think it's similar things, like having things in common. I'm quite into football, so it's always nice to talk to people about that. I've never really been fussy about the people I hang around with, and I've had friends who are quite different from each other. If I'm with someone, I wouldn't normally think I don't like this person because of what they've just said or anything like that.
So you're an easy-going sort of person?
Yeah, I suppose so.

Okay, and lastly, thinking about the service here—I know you've come to some of the activities—is there anything else they could do, or could have done, or could do in the future for other people to support friendships when people are getting better?
What, the friendships they've already got?
Yeah.
I don't really know, because I'm not sure if people would really want them interfering in their friendships.
Is there anything they could have done to help, to sort of support you from the background, if you see what I mean?

Well, I had some CBT which was quite helpful. We looked at my drinking, because I used to drink and I still drink quite heavily but less often, and that was helpful. I think I don't need it as much now to socialise, so that was good. I've been really happy with the help I've received. I think they could offer to bring friends in to inform them, but personally I really wouldn't have wanted that. Maybe some people would want close friends to come.
To come in here with you and hear about what the service is?
Yeah.
I think that's everything actually. Was there anything you wanted to add, or anything you think about friendships that we haven't touched on?
Not that I can think of.
No? Okay, thank you.

case_summary: The participant, a 26-year-old, discussed how mental health problems and two hospitalizations have affected his social life and friendships. He described feeling like a burden to old school friends who know about his issues, leading to a sense of fragility and a preference for friendships with people who share similar mental health experiences. He maintains some long-term friendships and engages in structured social activities like football, but often feels lonely and hopes university will provide new social opportunities.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant's statements reflect common social anxieties, feelings of being a burden, and a realistic assessment of changed social dynamics following a health crisis. There are no expressed beliefs about external reality that qualify as delusional. His perceptions are grounded in his actual experiences of hospitalization and social withdrawal.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I'd like to hear about people in your life you see socially and consider friends. Anyone come to mind right now?
Yeah a few people. They've all gone off to uni, but there's a few people in my life.
What sort of things did you used to do with those people?
Just like go out with them to clubs and maybe go to their house every so often, just like sort of talk about anything, like random stuff, girls and stuff.
What were the bits that you liked best about those friendships?
Just that I could go to their house at any time, we'd just be able to talk about anything, and laugh about anything, that sort of thing.
Did you talk to them about the symptoms that brought you here?
No, I haven't talked to any of my friends about that yet. Some don't even know. One person knows, but I haven't really discussed it with anyone.
Why's that?
It's not something I want to share with my friends because it was such a bad time. I'd rather let it pass and hopefully things will get back to how they were.
Okay. And in your friendships what sort of role do you think you play? Like someone's a joker maybe, someone's the planner..
I'd say I was the joker. People say I'm funny. I'm the one who cracks jokes all the time and doesn't take life too seriously.
And in terms of your friends, what sorts of role do they play? What sort of people are they?
One friend is good with girls. Another goes to church now, he's become a Christian, wasn't like that before. There's another one but I can't really think right now.
And do you go to friends for different things? Like is there one friend you could go to if you want talk about one thing, somebody else..
Yeah I think so. I'd go to the one good with girls for that topic, another for more serious stuff, and another for work or assignments.
And what about your friends coming to talk to you - what sort of things would they want to talk to you about?
Yeah, well really the same thing. Not anything specific. It's probably the same thing about girls or work or something like that.
And these are friends that you've had for a long time?

Yeah. I've had like these different sets of friends: university friends and my friends in [PLACE]. The ones in [PLACE] I've had for a long time, and then the ones in uni I'd had for seven months by the time I left.
And the friends from uni, are you staying in touch with them now that you're not there?

They phoned me a few times, but since I likely won't go back, I don't see the point in keeping in touch. If I go to another uni I'll probably never see them again. It's a shame but that's how I'm thinking right now.
And is that a direct result of the symptoms that brought you here?

Yeah. What triggered the psychosis was smoking cannabis at university. When I stopped, I went home before term ended to get off it. When I went back, a friend came round with cannabis. I thought I'd have one toke, but it was stronger than usual so I stopped. I went back home for the last two weeks of the holidays. When I returned, that's when things changed, little things started happening, and I ended up in the mental home. That's what triggered it. I've forgotten the question.
I was asking you, is that what led to you not talking to your uni friends?

Exactly. I'll probably try to visit them this year or next, but since I'm going to a different university—because I feel like I can't go back, like there's a label on me, the guy who went sort of crazy—that's why I feel I can't really return. It's a shame because I liked it there. I was close to people, even for a short time. I don't know if I can go back because of that label. A fresh start at another uni. I'm still not sure what I'm doing, so I'm back and forth.
And your friends here—when you came back from uni and things started to happen, you started not feeling quite right—were you seeing your friends from home then?
Yeah, I was. When I came back. No, actually, when I came back the second time, I don't think I was. It was my family, I think.
Are you close to your family?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
So when you went into hospital, did anyone visit you there?
No, it was family. They were the ones who knew I was in hospital. Yeah, it was my family.
And was there anyone in hospital you made friends with?
Yeah, there was this guy called [PERSON]. He was a good friend. He basically got me through it. He'd been there a long time, so he'd seen people come and go. He was a good friend.
What did he do that helped?

Well, he was only two years older than me, so I could talk to him about anything, like any of my old friends. The same things—girls, or life in general. We were on the same wavelength, more or less, because he had smoked cannabis too, and he'd been on it longer than me, so we could talk about that and different stuff. So yeah, he was a good friend.
So it helped because he knew what you were…
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
And when you left there, did you stay in touch with [PERSON]?
No, I didn't, because near the end we sort of drifted apart a bit, but I think he lived on my estate. If anything, he'd probably knock for me or something.
And when you came out of hospital, did you start seeing your friends around here straight away, or…?

No, because I wanted to be by myself for a bit. I turned off my phone. I didn't talk to any of my friends for nearly two weeks after I came home, and then I turned my phone on eventually. I think one time my friends rang me to go to a club, so I thought I'd just go out. But when I went to the club, I didn't feel myself for some reason—not myself. I wasn't joking as much as I usually would. I wasn't enjoying myself. So I left quite early in the evening, said I'm going home now. That shattered my confidence a bit; I thought, 'Why wasn't I enjoying myself?' So after that, I started not really picking up the phone to my friends. I didn't want to talk to them because I knew it would all be about going back to uni, and I didn't want to talk about it because it would remind me of all the good times I'm missing out on. If they wanted me to go out, I was worried I wouldn't be the same person—I wouldn't be the joker anymore. Even now it's the same thing: I'm not really answering my phone to my friends. Maybe my uni friends, I'll say, 'Yeah, I might be coming back,' just so they know I'm alright, because I had no contact with anyone for about three months. So sometimes I answer my phone to my uni friends to say, 'Yeah, I'm alright.' But my friends in [PLACE], they want to go out, but I think there's no point because I probably won't be the same person, like joking, for some reason.
So now you're seeing friends a lot less than you were before?
Yeah, a lot less, yeah.
It sounds like you were pretty sociable?
Yeah, yeah, I was. Yeah, I was.
What do you think needs to happen for you to be able to start doing that again?

I think I need to get my confidence back, but without having to be in contact with my friends. Maybe getting a job; my brother's telling me about a door-to-door salesman job. He did it before and was telling me it increased his confidence. It increased his confidence because you have to go door to door, and you can't really get stuck or get an attitude. You can't take a no to heart; you've got to carry on door to door.
You get quite a thick skin?

Yeah, yeah, so I think something like that would just get my confidence back. Just something to get my confidence back to get in contact with my friends. I can't really tell them why I don't want to go out or anything, because it's not really the sort of thing I talk to them about. It's only my family really I can talk about that with.
So you could talk to your family about that?

Yeah. Before I wasn't really saying anything, I kept everything bottled in. But when I came back the first time and admitted to my family I'd been smoking cannabis and was trying to quit, that's when I first had a chance to talk to them about anything—how I feel, emotions and everything. I'm not the sort of guy to talk about emotion, but I had to.
So do you think your family and you are closer now than you were before?

Yeah. That's a good thing that's come out of it; my family are closer now. The only bad thing is I've reached a stage where I'm sort of low, borderline depressed. That's the only bad thing. I mean, I wanted to say I regret it. If I had known this would be the outcome I would never have touched it.
It takes a little while to get back on your feet.
Yeah, it takes a while, a long time.
If you were in a situation to meet new people and make new friends now, would you seek the same qualities you valued in your old friends, or would you look for something different?

That's the thing about meeting new people. My friends at uni, we were all on the same wavelength, just funny guys making each other laugh. That's what makes me want to go back to my old uni, thinking I'd meet the same kind of people. With new people, you never know what you're going to get. I'd go for the same qualities, but if there was something else, I wouldn't mind that either. As long as they're alright, not idiots or fools, just normal and on my wavelength, then they're alright.
If you made a wish list for a friend, it sounds like a good sense of humour and being fun would be major. Are there other traits you'd consider really important?

Just being a joker, joking about, not taking things too seriously. I don't like people who take things too seriously or judge others too quickly. You need to have a laugh at any time really. That would be the only thing.

Thinking about the friends that you've got, you mentioned how you're not so much in touch with them as you were before. Is there anybody you've stayed in touch with completely throughout, the same as before?
No, I don't think so.
What do you think would have to be different about any of those people for you to still be talking to them lots?
What do you mean?
Well if you'd had a friend who you were still in contact with, I wonder what they would have needed to be like?
Probably just someone I could talk to about anything, maybe someone like my brother, not necessarily a joker. That's a hard question, I can't really explain what the person would have to be.
You're doing well. You said someone who's a bit like your brother and I'm wondering whether your brother is someone who you've got a lot of trust for?

Yeah, my brother. Sometimes I have to tell him some stuff, because I'm not used to talking about stuff like that with him—we usually talk about girls or unimportant things. The crucial thing is somebody who wouldn't see me in a different way. If I told my friends all this stuff I'm talking about now, they'd see me in a different light. So maybe someone who wouldn't see me differently.
So one of the reasons you haven't talked to your friends is that you don't want them to see you differently?
Yeah. I want them to see me how I was before, just a joker rather than all this stuff, because it's long and serious.
It's too much?
Yeah, it's too much.
Okay, since you started coming here have you been to any of the groups or the social stuff here?

Yeah, I went to the football thing once. I haven't been to any of the stuff up here because coming here is like a reminder of what happened before—psychosis and that. Coming here for the social thing reminds me of all the bad stuff that's happened. I'd rather just come here and talk to [care coordinator] and then get out than socialise. It sounds kind of bad, but the only good thing is everyone here has problems similar to me. I'd rather just talk to [care coordinator] and then go do something else like go to the gym. It might change, but for now that's how I'm thinking.
Regarding how you currently spend your free time, if you want to socialise or get out of the house, is the gym your go-to?

Even then, I sometimes avoid the gym because it's local and a lot of my friends go there. I don't want to run into someone and have to explain why I'm not at university or make up a reason for taking a break, when really I wanted to go back but couldn't because of what happened. So I tend to go for a quick workout and leave.
Is there anything else that you would do?

No, not really. The gym is the main thing. When I was smoking cannabis I got kind of skinny, and after I went into the home I put the weight back on, so the gym would be the perfect way to lose it again. That's the only thing really.
But then you haven't been able to go there as much as you might have wanted?
Yes, that's the thing, that's sort of annoying.
Do you think if you had had someone around, a friend throughout you could have talked to, it would have made a difference to how you're feeling now?

Yeah, definitely. If I had a friend I could talk to about this, it would definitely be different. At least there would be one person around me who knows everything. Because there's no one to talk to, it makes you regret what happened more. Right now it feels like I'm a shadow of who I was before. It makes you think, why did I smoke my first spliff? If I was at uni everything would just be normal. If there was at least one person it probably would be different.
Why would talking to somebody like that be different to talking to your family?

Well, with family you sort of have to be open about stuff, you can't really keep things to yourself. They keep asking you what's wrong and there's no escape from family. But with friends you have the choice to keep it or not. If I could, I probably would share it with one of my friends, but I can't. Does that answer the question?
Yes. Do you think there is anything anyone could have done to help you stay in touch with your friends better or any help you could have got?

No, I don't, because the way I was feeling I just wanted to be by myself, even from my family. Sometimes they'll tell me to phone my friends or something, but if you don't want to do it then you won't do it, so I don't think so.
If you were thinking about people in your life at the moment, what's the biggest thing that's missing for you in terms of friends? What's the thing you miss the most?

Just a laugh, cracking jokes like before, not having to think about all this heavy stuff. My life's become too serious now. Before it was just about jokes and maybe getting some girls. Life wasn't serious, so that's the thing I miss, just not taking life too seriously.
Let me see if I have any remaining questions. If you resumed socializing with friends now, would you return to your previous activities, such as clubs, or prefer something else?

I probably wouldn't want to go to a club. Maybe just go to someone's house or something like that. Maybe in the future when I'm in a better mood, feeling a bit better about myself, then maybe I would go back to clubs and all that.
So your aim is to get back to how things were before?
Yeah.
Okay, let me just check here. I think that's everything. Is there anything else you wanted to say about friends or how things have worked out?
Yeah, no I think that's everything.

case_summary: The participant discusses their social life before and after a cannabis-triggered psychotic episode that led to hospitalization. They describe previously being a sociable 'joker' with close friends from home and university, but now avoid contact due to low confidence, fear of being seen differently ('the guy who went sort of crazy'), and not feeling like their old self. They are closer to family now but feel isolated, regretful, and like a 'shadow' of their former self, hoping to regain confidence through work and eventually return to their previous social functioning.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant expresses social anxiety, low self-esteem, regret, and a fear of being stigmatized or judged by friends, but does not describe any fixed, false beliefs about external reality. Their concern about a 'label' is a worry about social perception, not a delusional conviction. No candidate reality-boundary points were identified.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I am here voluntarily to share knowledge for the research [PERSON] is doing. I do not wish to sign anything or be legally bound; I am just a natural person sharing what I know. I am happy for any information to be used for research, played publicly, or shared, as long as there is no damage to me.
Thank you. I'd like to hear about people you see socially and consider friends. Do you have any friends in your life right now?

Yes, definitely. Since I became so upset—losing my job and ending up on my own without parents—I felt totally unsafe. There isn't much help out there; everyone needs someone looking after them. When I told my GP I was unhappy, I got antidepressants straight away, and they just knocked me out of my normal state. I was crying about my mum and losing my job at [Previous Employer], where I'd worked about four years since uni. It drove me crazy, and I started asking what life is about. I need meaning, and it's not in shopping or books. I'm more spiritual; everything I read I feel I already know from my own spiritual knowledge, but that part of me was dead before I lost my job because I was busy with success and running around. Suddenly I started asking what the point was. Even with money to shop, I didn't want to anymore. I became more alive inside and dead to the outside. Going inside, you see something affects you subconsciously—something that drives the information we collect from life, something that chooses what we think about. We don't really choose our thoughts; they just come. When everything fell apart, I stopped wanting anything because I thought, what's the point? I worked hard for things that mean nothing; no one cares about your career, and they can stab you in the back anytime. My friends struggle too—one works at a bank and says people aren't nice in the corporate world. It really affected me. I like working with nice people, not those just there for money. When I got here, nothing mattered. I started asking deep questions, and something deep inside decided for me to find out what life was about. I was fed up with religion; I know there's a true meaning related to God, but that assumption makes it difficult because there's so much hate towards religion, and I have that hate too. I lost everything and stopped caring, so I decided to take hold of the last thing that might give me meaning: I went to church to pull apart how ridiculous religion is. That was my last meaning. I went, and I found my own meaning, so deep it plays with your subconscious and makes you so different and better. It's like the strongest drug; your mind starts to alter, and you think differently and see things you've never seen. It gives meaning to why you lost your job, why things happen in families, why there are wars and children dying. It's all politics and the spiritual world—100% related, the absolute of the physical world. What brought me here was realising the corporate world is a big con, fake success that eats your soul. This realisation is so strong and absolute you can't stop it; once you let it in, it shows you unbelievable things about the world and changes you. But before, because you're a human mind with so much collected information, it needs to be put right, so you become really emotional and start thinking about stuff that's happened. I'm letting it all out. I came here before I was 18, living on my own; my parents left me. Friends are just people like you with their own problems; they don't know any better. They can spend time with you, but no one else can know your life. When you're emotional and miserable, it's hard for them, and you don't want to let anyone in. You're ill; they can bring you food, but they can't just walk into your mind—that's your house. A psychologist tried to walk in and did help, but it's a spiritual house. Unless psychology understands the spiritual house, it tries to walk in through drugs and chemicals blindly, and that's a challenging road. When I started counselling, I was out of my mind, really emotional, not knowing what was real anymore. How can you work so hard for years and then 500 people are made redundant while a company head gets a million-pound bonus? It's a paradox that plays with your mind. People ignore it because they want the money too, but someone who doesn't want money, like me, starts questioning. The true conscious of a human being is to know that at the same second a transaction goes through for an expensive cream, a child is dying. You can choose what to think about, but when you choose to know both, you ask what the world, money, and these things are about. They're about lives lived this way and a lot of pain going round and round. That's why I was so upset—all that anger that lives in people.
These are big issues to deal with aren’t they? Is there anyone that you talk these things through with?

Yes. I talk about these things with my mum, but they're global issues. That's why so many friends… People don't want to hear this, they just want to go shopping. My friends just want to shop and enjoy life. I find it very false and I used to buy a lot – I never knew why but now I know – and I find things very pretentious. I'm not living on the surface any more, I am living on truth. I'm standing on truth, walking every day and seeing things as a real human being, the true human being I was always supposed to be, the one every true human was supposed to be: wanting to know that right now someone is suffering and being so good in heart they would never want anyone to suffer. No other soul suffer, that is the true human being, but we're dead in our souls. We're dead. That's why we pay no recognition. We have no knowledge, and we don't recognise the truth in time and it's an eternal truth because suffering always existed. That's why we're dead eternally a lot of the time. The knowledge I received from reading the twisted word of the son of god, because it got totally twisted – the people who wrote it probably weren't even the people said to have written it. Who knows who wrote what was written, but the truth about it is that truth, even if turned upside down, hidden, re-written, twisted, it still stands. It's like one of those dolls – if you push it that way, that way, upside down, it still turns the other way up. That's what truth is. It doesn't matter what happens to it. It can be written in a lie; it will still be truth because the true meaning is not the word but the message behind the word. So I read the word of the son of god. It is twisted, that's why people think it's foolish, but if you ask for the truth to be revealed and know there is something there, it will be revealed. This is what happens when you read it, it's like a pill. You know the film Matrix? When they swallow the pill? You have to actually swallow it, so an apple isn't actually an apple, it's a message. An apple is food, there are two types of food: one physical. The only way the truth can be told is in the context of this world. That is why apple was used but it's not actually an apple, it's a metaphor. The truth can only be told in a metaphor, so the apple is actually a message – she ate an apple. She had a message; she had a life, so the reverse is the pill in the Matrix. It's very hard to understand this, so what I'm saying is very deep and complicated. But why I ended up here and lost some friends and started making new friends: because the word of the son of god – although twisted – when you read it, and if you understand it… It's like power you need to plug in. If you read it and plug it into the source, that's when it'll light up. You can't just hold a pill in your hand, you have to swallow it. You can't just hold the appliance, you have to plug into it and then it will light up. You've got to plug into the source. So if you have the son of god in your mind you've got to plug into god. That's how it works and it will light up. That's what happened to me. I did it. I read the word and no matter how twisted it is, I read it, and it's amazing. What happened after that cannot be told in human language. It can only be told in the language of heart because you start seeing unbelievable things. Psychologists and staff who have never gone through it don't hear it at all, so they just end up wanting to go shopping. In the beginning when you haven't found people who have experienced what you are experiencing, you need someone to speak to, but at the same time I became so emotional because I was so upset. I was on my own. It was scary, having lost my job, having no money. I had money and then I ran out. I went shopping. I went crazy. I went shopping and it was like, it will all be fine, and then I kept going to interviews and couldn't get a job because I couldn't believe the way things are. To be honest, in [PLACE], on my own, I met some people who weren't really concerned with me, they were just concerned with money and that made me alone and unsafe. I had really weird interviews with other companies. They would ask me questions that literally knock you out. For example, I was once asked at an interview if I could say no. It's a trick question; it's a psychological question, but when you're upset and emotional, you really get so upset about people asking you trick questions. Can you say no? Imagine going for an interview, you've just lost a £30,000 job, you worked for it for 4 years, 2 years at college before that. You were at high school working really hard, your parents telling you to get on with it, you've done everything you were told to do, you've achieved things. You've got a job and suddenly they're like, we don't want you any more because you're just an animal, just labouring for us. You and many other people, goodbye now, we don't really care. We paid you money, and that's all you were there for, to get money. What was I talking about?

You were saying how all of that realisation led to you not spending time with the same people; realising their interests were just about money and shopping while you were thinking of something deeper. Can you tell me about the new friends you've found as a result of your discovery?

Yes. The new friends I've found are people in the truth movement. My experience opened my eyes to how the world works: government control, corporate connections to political campaigns, everything inter-connected. I now see how people are controlled, how much pressure I've felt since being made redundant, especially on my own. From my spiritual self, I've caught onto political events like UN globalisation and 'depopulisation'. I was 'depopulised'—my dad brought me here and put me in boarding school, then left. I was already used to this country; going back to my country of origin made me feel alien. I was 10 when I came, so I absorbed everything as a child. I couldn't go back to the beginning. Because of this immigration, I was completely alone. The truth is immigration manages population. I'm now 'depopulised' and fully dependent on the government. I have no family home to go to for help. I'm afraid the council will demand money I owe them for housing benefit overpayments. I've made an Excel table of what I owe. I'm afraid they'll demand it and I won't have it because I've spent money on food, which my bank account shows. It's so intense to job search, work part-time, and do all the bureaucratic policies. I have panic attacks going through the paperwork because I need records of everything. They use the authority of depopulation—if you don't comply, you won't have anywhere to live. The panic goes through the roof. No surprise people get a shotgun and shoot people. When you're crazy, you're crazy. When you receive a letter saying they'll take your house, people shoot their family because they see no point. That's what happened to me. Thank god I saw the new point, but these people go and shoot.
Can you tell me a bit about these people who are part of the movement, who you've come across as a result of your discovery?

My new view of the world is very similar to the people I've connected with through the truth movement. They're all over the world; I socialise through social networking. The truth movement really started from 9/11—I thought it was an inside job—and research about the new world government and control. I've connected with people doing that research, and they're my new friends. Once you're taken away from wanting success because you've been shown it's a con, you just want to work for one purpose: to expose and participate in global projects. I don't want to go shopping or talk about celebrities any more. I was never really interested in that. I'm more intellectual; I find meaning in those things.
Is there anyone from before that you've stayed friends with, friendships that have survived through this?
Yes, there are those people, and I'm getting involved in events now. I'm sure I'll meet more people and get local friends. That's one part of my friends, and it's really nice.
Are friendships developing?
