Actually yes, it's really supportive and developing. The other part is friends from before. Take my mum—she's always been my friend, but it's tricky because of family stuff. I've always been upset with her. In terms of normal friends, I haven't seen them for almost two years. When I do see them it's really weird, but I keep in touch. I've lost all my friends. Nothing connects you. Friendship is about a meeting of mindsets. You can hang out and not talk, like with a mate or a husband, but otherwise you've got to talk.
I wonder what part of you wants to stay in touch with them? It takes effort to maintain contact even without seeing them. Why do you do that?

It is an effort, and every time I get quite hurt. They dig into my previous attempts at worldly success, suggesting I look for a certain job or take investment courses, reminding me I was doing so well. I'm not interested in them wanting me to get money. I don't care about money anymore. I'd rather talk about things that have nothing to do with money, about life as they've never known it. But people don't know, they just want to go shopping. So it's hard. What part of me wants to keep in touch with these particular friends? I can't think of anything. I just want to keep in touch because I think I can still socialize with them on their level, although I haven't been because I'm so busy working part-time and doing all the stuff I'm doing. Now and then it's really good. Two weeks ago I met up with a friend from [Previous Employer]; I used to work with her. That was really difficult and challenging. She's very tired all the time, and I found it challenging because I've always been prompted about my worldly success when I'm not really interested in that anymore. I am successful. I am doing what I want to do. I'm not homeless, I'm fine, I've got food on my table. I actually deem that as a success, but worldly friends like these always want to know what I've achieved. There's always got to be something that's more than just you. And sometimes it feels like fake stuff.

Thinking about the new friends you're discovering from the development of that knowledge, you've got that group of people you're in touch with but you're not getting a lot out of that relationship at the moment and that feels quite difficult when you see them. Is there any gap in your friendships? Is there anything you would like to be there that's not in terms of friends?

Yeah, I would like people to just consider what I'm saying. Just consider me, that's all. Because they want to consider me in the way that they want to consider me. I want them to consider me in the way that I am.
More openness to what you're presenting?

Yeah, not wanting me to be something, but just not judging. If anything, what I would like to be there that isn't there in my friends is consideration. Just to consider what I am trying to tell them when I'm speaking. What I'm talking about, my new me in my kind of research and in my findings that money doesn't matter. I've done the job, I've worked for, you know, I've done everything that they have wanted to do and they're still doing, and this stuff just seriously doesn't matter. The work, I'm just bored with everybody wanting that. Just consideration, that's what's not there in my friends, not accepting. Acceptance, consideration.
Thank you, it's good to hear some really interesting views.

case_summary: The participant describes a period of profound personal upheaval following job loss and family separation, leading to a spiritual awakening and a radical re-evaluation of societal values. They express a deep disillusionment with materialism, corporate culture, and superficial friendships, and have found a new sense of purpose and community within a global 'truth movement' focused on exposing hidden systems of control. The participant's stance is one of a truth-seeker who has transcended a 'dead' societal norm, though this has resulted in social isolation from old friends and significant emotional distress.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: So what I'm interested in hearing about is people in your life who you see socially, who you would consider to be friends. Have you got any people like that at the moment?

Not many. It's mainly more family members than friends. I've had more friends in the past but I don't know if it's because I also had depression for a long time before my psychosis. I always felt like I couldn't really speak to people, didn't answer my phone and didn't really want anyone to come and visit me. I was quite a recluse. I didn't really want to go out and only did what I absolutely had to. With the psychosis, people are a bit reluctant to call and invite you when you're depressed anyway, and when they visit and you're not talkative they act like something's wrong with you. I mean, there probably is, but not like that. It's like they say 'what's wrong with you, you're not talking' or I think I'm doing something wrong. Most people I told about my nervous breakdown kind of look at me. Friends wise, I've got one really good friend who understands and is sympathetic but not in an annoying way, in a helpful way. But I've had friends in the past take advantage of me because they know I'm a bit sensitive. Do you know what I mean?
What sort of thing, can you give me an example?

Yeah like, just taking the piss out of me when I'm actually sitting there. Do you know what I mean? If I question them about it they say I'm paranoid, but you're doing it right in front of me. I'm not that paranoid.
Showing up your weaknesses and trying to get to you?
Yeah, yeah.
Has there been a friend that's been around through the whole thing, that you have stayed friends with?

No. Well, yeah, one of them, but we hadn't seen each other that regularly. She's got her life and I've got mine. We're best friends because of how long we've known each other and we still call even if we haven't seen each other for like a whole year. But my other friends saw me as weak, so that's why friendships are distant. I feel like someone who might just tag along but not really be that sociable.
The sort of things you want to do with friends now, is that the same as you would have done before the problems that brought you here?

No. My personality has changed a lot through the depression. Some of the things I might have liked to do before I got sick, if I suggested them in the past, I just got shouted down. Then it made me more withdrawn and quiet. It's like a vicious circle.
What sort of things was that, that you would have thought of doing but wouldn't have said about?
I dunno. Things I thought were fun.
And would you do those things more now?

I might, but I find I've got to do a lot of stuff on my own. Not on my own exactly, but no-one's really interested in art galleries and the things that I am. My cousin has a new girlfriend who does actually, but that's only recently that I've found out. My other friends wouldn't have done dance with me, but now I realise it's because she feels self-conscious, yet she would take the piss out of me. Now I realise these people have their own issues, where they could mock me because I wasn't strong enough to defend myself, kind of having a laugh.
So your contact with those people has become less and less? Do you think that's because you've been getting in touch with them less or do you think they're getting in touch with you less?

I had to distance myself because when you become somebody to tag along, people can tend to use you. When I was telling them the way I felt, they acted like there was something wrong with me for feeling that way. Not just with depression, even with how they were acting towards me. So I distanced myself.
So you made that decision yourself. Is there anyone in your life at the moment who's a newer friend or who has come about since or during your symptoms?

My friend [PERSON], I've known her about three years. I knew her through the depression. She lives at my Nan's and when I had the breakdown I went to stay there, and I knew her well because she lives on my Nan's estate. We've become much closer since the breakdown. I don't know whether it's because of my medication or what. I think it's a lot to do with the medication; I'm not as fragile as I was and I can now see that I was in a vicious circle with those other people, so I don't need to miss them. She knows about everything I've been through. She's a more supportive one.
What sort of thing does she do for you?

I don't know. She's just there all the time, either to talk or if I felt I didn't want to stay on my own. She was there for me but not in a judgmental way. If I was thinking of my old friends and what I was going through mentally, I know they would just think, they wouldn't think 'maybe you need to see a doctor', you know what I mean? They're just different types of people.
So she's more of the sort of person that you want to be around now?
Yeah definitely. I trust her, which is a big thing for me.
The sort of things you do with [PERSON], what sort of stuff would that be?
We've been raving together, we sit at home and drink tea, smoke cigarettes and chat, but you know just run of the mill stuff like go shopping or she comes up mine.
Is there anyone else like that at the moment?

Yeah, I have a younger cousin, and I'm really glad we've gotten closer lately because she's about to go through some of what I experienced. We talk a lot about those things—I can share what being depressed felt like, and she's happy we're having similar experiences so she knows she's not alone. When you're really depressed, you can feel like you're the only one in the world who feels that way, and you don't realize how similar the symptoms are in other people. That's another reason I kept things to myself; I felt something was wrong and I didn't know how to fix it. It stopped me from socializing and being with men a lot. My other friends always seemed to have a boyfriend, and I'd go long spells without one. They'd act weird, like they assumed I must be a lesbian—not that there's anything wrong with being gay, I'm not homophobic—but they'd think that just because I didn't have a boyfriend. Some people are just... you have to ignore that.
So it sounds like you were managing two ends of the scale: you have [friend 1], with whom you can talk about things without judgment, and you help your cousin too.

What she's saying makes me think of when I was 15. I went through such a period of self-loathing with this depression, feeling like, 'What is wrong with me? How do I fix it? How do I just become normal?' I just wanted to be normal. I feel like I've missed out on a lot because of depression.
What sort of things do you think you missed out on?

I missed out on being a normal teenager. I was so hard on myself because I thought my shyness and inability to talk was just shyness, not depression, so I'd get angry at myself. I just never felt good enough. I feel like I could have had a lot of friends and learned how to have friendships better if I hadn't gone through all of that at a time when I was already changing.
It's a really difficult time when you're a teenager anyway, isn't it?
Trust me. Let alone with the stuff I've been through.
So, with all of that in mind, do you think there are things you're having to practice now that other people might have already done when they were younger, or do you think you're there?

No, not at all. I'm practicing meeting new people and putting my barriers down. Even though my cousin [friend 3] and his girlfriend live around the corner, I'm the type of person who... we're talking fine now, but if you suddenly took an interest in me and wanted to come see me, I'd struggle. Small talk is something I can do recently, but it's so hard for me to keep a conversation going. It's also uncomfortable being in other people's houses; I feel like I don't know how to entertain. I grew up in such a sociable household—even though my dad used to hit my mum, there was also a good side and we did have fun. I've just been through so many changes, so much confusion, and feeling at a loss for so long about how to deal with things that it's kind of changed my personality.
And when you first started making those efforts, practicing small talk and things like that when the symptoms were starting to get a bit easier, how did that come about?

Well, I don't know. To give you a metaphor, it's like a tray with loads of glasses full of water, and another tray on top of that, piling up, and you've got to keep the water in all these trays while you're walking and running. Keeping the trays balanced is something I constantly have to concentrate on.
And that's how it felt?

That's how it feels now sometimes. Before, I just wouldn't try. I never felt happy and spent a lot of time suicidal, wishing I weren't here. Not in a morbid or dramatic way, but in a way that felt like that would be the best decision, the best option.
So being around people and developing relationships takes a lot of concentration and effort from you all the time?
Yeah, loads.
So we're hearing that [friend 1] is quite a different sort of person compared to your friends before?
Definitely, completely different.
What sort of qualities would you be looking for if you were trying to make more friends?

I'm looking for a down-to-earth person who's not judgmental and quite open-minded. That's why with [friend 4], even if we don't see each other, we're cool—we're both really open-minded and don't judge each other. She lives quite a radical life. One thing that's kept us close for this long is that we can confide in each other without judgment. I forgot what you asked?
About qualities in friends; that's a good example.

Someone with a good sense of humor, not judgmental, with a level of maturity and intelligence—not like they have to be a member of Mensa, but so we can have a reasonable conversation if I feel comfortable enough to converse. I do have a lot to say, and when I write stuff, I notice I am quite intelligent. What else... I wouldn't need them to be caring and loving straight away, because I don't get close to people quickly anyway. Just someone you can talk to who's not judgmental. I find that most people are, really.
Do you come across that a lot?
Yeah.
Do you talk about what you've been through to people quite early on when you've met them, or do you wait until you know them quite well?

When I was really depressed, I could sometimes talk about depression more easily if people started talking about it. I was in a hostel with 10 girls—a couple of them I knew from primary school, one from secondary school, and one from a dance class when I was at primary school. So when we started talking, I went through a stage where I was so lost I would just tell people easily what I was going through, but it had the opposite effect. Telling people things too quickly—I was unstable.
Thinking back to those older friendships, it sounds like you had a quieter, background role and were sometimes pushed around. What role do you play in your newer friendships?

Even though I was pushed around, I'm actually quite strong and can be defensive or even aggressive, so it was always done in an underhand way and they'd deny it. As for my friends now... what did you ask again?
What sort of role do you play in those friendships?

I'm a bit of a contradiction. I give a bit of everything when I'm ready, but when I'm not... I've learned to keep more to myself, because people don't understand you anyway. I play different roles. My two good friends can confide in me. I can be comical around one of them and make people laugh. People say I'm nice and warm. Because of what I've been through, I don't judge people straight away or try to make them uncomfortable, so maybe that's why some people like me. But I like keeping people at bay because of that. It's a varied role.
Thinking about the people in your life now and what they give you, is there anything missing or a gap in what you'd like from friendships?
Yes, there is a gap. I would like a man. But men are a different kettle of fish altogether, aren't they?
So that's something you'd like, a partner of some type?

Yes, like when you're a teenager in school and you have a best friend, but as you get older that gets replaced with a man. I haven't moved on to that bit yet. I've had relationships but they haven't lasted long and I've had big gaps in between.
So that best friend, companionship role? And would that be someone you'd want to talk to about your symptoms and what you've been through?
Yes, someone I could trust not to judge me or think I'm nuts. Being mentally ill isn't the same as being mad; there are loads of different types of mental illness.
Was there anyone who helped when you were going through the worst of it?
My mum and my brother. I trust them 100%. They'll always be there for me no matter how much we argue.
What did they do that helped?

They believed me. When I said I was feeling that way, they didn't treat me like I was mad or back off from me. My mum said I had to go into hospital and I just felt like crying, saying 'no, I'm not mad, I don't need to go to the hospital,' but...
Perhaps they showed you what you needed to do.
Yeah.
Is there anyone outside the family who was around throughout all of that?

A friend. After it happened at my mum's house, I was scared to go out at first, so I started staying at my nan's. Then me and this friend became closer through that time, and I would go and see her in the evenings.
So if she hadn't been around, do you think things would have been different?
Probably. I probably would have felt more alone than I did.
Is there anything the service did here to help with the social side of things?

I went to one forum, a group of us talking about how best to raise awareness of mental illnesses, and they were all saying the same things as me. Even though I'd talked to my cousin [PERSON] when I was having those experiences, and I know other people have days like that even without depression, listening to all these people saying they isolated themselves and stuff like that helped.
Did you see any of them afterwards socially, or was it just that one occasion?

Yes, which is why it was really interesting to see how similar it is for other people. Some of them had psychosis that seemed to come out of nowhere. It is frightening. I still feel like it actually happened, that's the thing. The stuff I experienced, I felt like it was actually happening, and to think that it wasn't is just nuts. It was hard to deal with. I can't believe it happened to me.
Is there anything else you would have wanted the service here to do to help you with being around people, socialising, or anything like that?

I've been referred to a behavioural specialist, I can't remember the exact title, but I should hear from them soon because the last person here referred me. As for the service here, I think it's good. My care coordinator is really lovely and easy to talk to, and the medication is helping so much, so I think they're doing everything.
Has the way you make friends changed now? I was thinking about how you met your old friends versus how you might meet people now.

Well, two of my old friends, one from primary school and one from secondary school, are the ones I distanced myself from because they were no good. But I still talk to another friend, and we've been friends for three years, though we only became much closer recently. The way I make friends would have to be different now, but I haven't really made new ones.
And your other friend is your cousin, isn't she?

Yeah. My brother's girlfriend is cool too. I can go see my brother, see my friend, and other girls from the estate come up and we chat, but I don't know. It takes me a long time for a friend's friend to become my friend. I don't know how I'd make friends now. It would definitely be different because I'm different, but I haven't really made any new friends.
Do you have any ideas about where you might go to meet new friends?

You know what? I am completely at a loss about how to make new friends. There were definitely girls I met at my first proper job in a call centre. We got on really well, but it's hard for me to make friends. And if they are my friends, they don't become my friends until long after we met, you know?
Just to check, have you always been like that? Do you think it's always taken you a long time to get to know people?

No, that's more recent. Some people might think I make friends easily, but I don't know. I just seem to find myself in situations where people are taking the piss and talking about me behind my back. Maybe I'm too sensitive, maybe that happens to everyone.
Why do you think people say you make friends easily?

Thinking about it now, when I moved into the hostel I met two girls I used to know and we became close quite quickly, but that ended badly. My friend from secondary school, for the last two years anyway, because I changed schools and left all my old friends after we fell out, that changed how I made friends a lot. I became so defensive. I wasn't letting anyone take the piss again like they did at my old school. I mixed with a harder lot of girls, they used to smoke weed and stuff. Even though I became like that, I wasn't quite like them, so I'd kind of be the weaker one.
Were you smoking weed with them before?

I smoked it very, very occasionally at school, not during the week or anything. But my friend's mum used to go out on the weekend and leave the kids at home, so a lot of kids from the estate would come over. I used to go there because there were a lot of boys around. I was a tomboy in my old school, but going through what I went through made me so self-aware that I started to become girly, doing my hair and stuff. I didn't know I could be attractive because I was always a tomboy, hair back in a bun, always in trousers and trainers. But when I moved, I suddenly became more girly and got attention from boys, and that was really hard. If we were at my friend's house on the weekend and her brother and his friends came in, I would be just mute, because being around men was different in the way they would take an interest in me, you know?
Okay. Do you think the way friendships have been for you has impacted how well you've been?
Yeah, I do actually.
You mentioned a vicious cycle, which obviously wasn't helping. Is there anything else that wasn't helping?

Well yeah, somewhat I'd say. But also, I don't know, I think they kind of fed each other. The trouble with the girls and friendships might have been because I was ill, you know? It might be why I got the reaction I did, but I don't know. Ask me the question again?
It was about whether the friendships around you impacted your symptoms, made them worse or better.
Yeah, I think they did feed into each other.
Is there anything else you wanted to add about your friendships and your experiences?
Just that, I don't know, I can't really make new friends, but yeah, I really want a guy I can trust.
Thank you.

delusion_points.summary: The participant maintains that a past psychotic experience felt completely real and struggles to accept the clinical view that it was not, finding the idea that it wasn't real to be 'nuts'.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant acknowledges the alternative perspective that the experience was not real, describing this as 'hard to deal with', but her subjective conviction remains strong.

case_summary: The participant discusses the impact of long-term depression and a psychotic episode on her friendships. She describes a history of feeling socially withdrawn, being mocked by past friends, and struggling with trust. She contrasts these negative experiences with a few current supportive relationships, including a close friend and a cousin, and expresses a desire for a romantic partner. She notes ongoing difficulty with socializing and a lingering subjective sense that her past psychotic experiences were real.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I’m interested in hearing about people in your life you see socially, people you consider friends. Does anyone come to mind right now?
I used to have a few friends before I became unwell, but I don’t see most of them now. I just talk to neighbours sometimes and family.
What sort of things did you used to do with those friends?
They would visit, we’d go out, exchange gifts, talk about our families and things like that.
How did you meet them?
I’d known one since I was a teenager. She lived with me and my mum for a while, then went back home, later came here and got married, and we reconnected. We’ve known each other a long time.
Was it the same for the other friends?
I think I lost them before I became unwell, or I was already unwell but not diagnosed. I just wasn’t nice or polite to them anymore, so we lost contact. I changed my number.
At what point do you think those friendships faded out?
I think I was feeling under too much pressure with things, and then I couldn’t cope with having to live up to those friendships.
So there was something about not feeling able to do things with them?
Yeah. Or thinking I didn’t have time to do things with them. I felt under pressure.
And when you started to feel better, did you start seeing them again?
I called one of them. She said she’d come to see me and I said okay, I’ll call again to arrange a date, but then I didn’t get back to her because I don’t want her to come.
Why is that?
Because she’s going to ask me questions and I’ll just be under pressure. She was going to bring her little girl, and I just felt under pressure.
What might she ask questions about?
About my health.
Would you want to talk to her about that?
No. She’s a qualified nurse though. I told her a little bit on the phone, and she already knew my brother had it so she was alright with it, but I just don’t want to talk more about it.
What about the other friends you had before? Did you have any contact with them after your symptoms?
No. One of them had a baby and I was going to approach her, but then I changed my mind, so I didn’t talk to her.
What made you change your mind?

I thought I was being bullied by her, but I probably was, because I was very weak when I was ill. Then I thought she might start coming round to my house again and that could start again, so I didn’t.
When you say being bullied by her, what sort of things was she doing?

She essentially took over my home, staying there for very long hours, day and night, bringing friends in. I had to go upstairs with my daughter while she used the downstairs. There was drinking, drug use, and things like that.

You decided not to contact her because you didn't want that situation to return. Was there anyone who was around for the whole time you were feeling unwell, or who was still around when you started to feel better?
No. There were many people I was avoiding, so basically no one was around. A few neighbours, but they were also avoiding me.
It sounds like when you became ill, people were avoiding you—friends and neighbours?
Yeah.
Was there anybody you talked to during that time?
Just my family.
Are you close to your family?
Yes.
If you were going to talk to somebody about what you'd been through, if you were feeling worried or frightened…
I would talk to my family.
I'm thinking about this friend you thought you might contact but then decided not to because of the pressure. Can you tell me a little about that pressure?
About the one who was going to come to my house?
The other friend, the one you thought you might call—the one you were going to call back with a date.

I just felt that she's going to come and my house won't be tidy enough. There are too many little things. Food should be ready, and I won't be able to manage. She will ask me too many questions, whys and things, and I might not be able to cope with it. So I didn't want her to come. But I will maybe.
What would have to happen to make it easier to call her?
I think, for a while, we should just speak on the phone and she shouldn't say that she will be coming.
So it's nice to talk to her, but the thought of her coming to your house is difficult?
Yes.
How would you feel about going to her house?
I wouldn't like it. It's too far. It's in [PLACE] and I would have a problem travelling over to her, and then I don't think I would feel comfortable.
Have you done that journey to [PLACE] before?
Once, when she had a baby. I went with my brother to see the baby.
I'm just wondering if travelling is harder since you've been unwell?
Yes, it's really hard, and if the environment is different then it's quite uncomfortable.
So you prefer to be at home with your own things?
Yes.
Do you think it would have helped if a friend had been around when you were having your symptoms and feeling unwell?

I think the symptoms were such that only a doctor would understand; a regular person wouldn't get it. Even I couldn't understand it when I was ill. The doctors kept saying I was sick, but I didn't believe them. Then after they gave me medicine and things started coming together after a few weeks, I thought, 'Oh, I must have been.' So the symptoms were only something a doctor or nurse would understand, not ordinary people.
So if there had been somebody around they might not have understood anyway?
No. My husband was telling my family that I was ill, but my family didn't believe him. I looked really bad. I lost a lot of weight, but they thought it was good because I was big before.
Your husband was somebody who was around and quite supportive during this time?

No, because I used to tell him to go away since I was frightened of him, so we separated and he moved out. I accused him of doing things which I believed he did, but they weren't true; I was just feeling that. He kept saying that I wasn't well, questioning what I was saying, and my family didn't... Some parts of it they probably did believe, but not all.
When you started feeling better, were you able to speak with your husband about what happened?

Yeah, I spoke with him, but I didn't explain everything I said because it's a bit painful. He said it's okay, don't worry about it, but it's still quite difficult being together after all the allegations I put on him. It's quite difficult at the moment. He's okay, he understands some things but not all of it.
The two of you are working to see if you can put things right?
Yes.
Which bits do you think he doesn't understand?

My sleeping pattern's a bit weird. He doesn't understand it, and sometimes he's nice and some days he expects more than I can do. I don't like that, because it's very difficult for me to manage. Some days he's quite helpful towards my daughter and some days he's not helpful at all. He says 'let's go on holiday' or something, but then when we go on holiday I don't have enough energy to hang around a lot, and he doesn't understand that.
It sounds like the pressure you described when people come to your house—people expecting you to do more than you're feeling up to. Is that right?

Yeah. I feel pressure with him as well. He's not with me at the moment, so he visits regularly. I feel the pressure, but if he were living with me it would be much worse. He would expect his clothes washed and ironed, the house tidy and clean like a normal home, the way I used to manage everything. But now I can't do it all. I can see what needs doing but my motivation and concentration are quite low. You know why I was late today? I fell asleep after taking painkillers for a toothache.
I'm sorry to hear that. Is it still sore now?
Yes, I have to go to the dentist after this.
Let me know if you need to take a break.
No, I'm okay.
I'm just thinking about having some new friends in your life. How do you feel about the idea of making new friends?

I wouldn't like the idea because it's very hard to trust people now. I've made one new friend, she's from [Asian country] and not a very close friend, but she visits sometimes and we talk a little. Occasionally we tidy up together, not much, just a bit. She's okay. That's the only person I've sort of befriended. She actually called yesterday to say her father passed away, so she was quite distressed. I think the friendship is good, though not very close. She's welcome to come and sit, but she doesn't expect too much because I told her I'm not well. So she's okay.
This friendship feels a bit more manageable because she hasn't got too high expectations?
Yes.
How did you meet this friend?

I went to buy clothes at her shop. It's just around the corner from my house, and she sees me dropping off and picking up my daughter every day, so she's seen me for a couple of years. After I shopped there a few times, we started talking, and I invited her to my house.
You made an approach to her to become your friend and she took you up on it?
Yes.
Was that easy or was that hard?
It was very hard. It took me about six months to think about it, and I really wanted to speak to her, but it took me six months.
It was very brave. I'm just thinking about your new friend; did you look for different qualities in your new friend to what you might have wanted before?

My mum was looking for help with her home, personal help. That's how I approached her. I said, 'Look, Mum's looking for help, so if you know someone, I see you in the shop all the time, so if you want to come to my house, it's good.' She came, and we spoke more about my mum. Now, once or twice a month, she goes to my mum's in [PLACE] and spends time with her. She's a nice girl, 26. Sometimes she comes to my house too. We were meant to meet on Sunday. She doesn't smoke or anything, so she's quite different from me, but she's okay with everything. We were meant to meet on Sunday, but my uncle died, so I had to go away. I phoned her and said I can't meet this week, maybe next week.
I wonder what it is about her that makes her a good person to be around, or easier to be around than other people?

I think I feel safe. Even my money and jewellery are out in the open, and I don't feel worried. Some relatives are coming from [COUNTRY] to stay with me in December, and I'm not happy about them; I'm very tense. Every time I go in the bathroom, I think I have to move my things from there, and from the living room. I have to move my things because if something goes missing, I can't say anything because they are relatives. It's a lot of burden, and I hate it. I lie in bed thinking about how I'm going to manage, because it's four adults and three children—quite a lot. The children are small. My house has hazards for smaller children, like cupboards and pushing things and falling. I have to sort things out before they come. It's too much pressure, arranging the space for them to sleep and getting a new mattress.
How will that be, being around other people so much?

Yeah, and my house is upstairs and downstairs, but there won't be any privacy. That's why I spend most of my time in the kitchen, and they can be there. I don't know how I'll cope. I spoke to my husband's sister about not being happy with this. I'm not too well to cope with such big pressure, and she was not understanding at all. She said, 'Look, you married into our family and you haven't done anything for ten years.' I said, 'I can't really.' She said, 'Look, it's only 4 or 5 days, you should do this.' But I don't think it's going to be 4 or 5 days; I think it's going to be longer.
How about making conversation, talking and being around people socially, what's that like for you at the moment?

It's really hard. I don't mind speaking to professionals like you or the dentist, because they understand me and support me, but I can't speak to everyone about what's going on in my life or how I'm doing. I'm quite... hiding things.
Do you manage to talk to people about other things? To distract yourself or is that hard?
I don't approach them, but if somebody approaches me, I'll say, 'Yeah, it's a nice day,' or something general, basic things, but not much.
Thinking about your new friend, the lady from the shop, is the sort of things that you would do with her different to the friends that you had before?
Yes. She's quite down to earth, but my other friends were very posh-posh. It's quite hard to cope with that.
Which bit was hard – the down to earth bit or the posh-posh bit?

The posh bit, because I used to be like them before, but not anymore. I've changed quite a lot, so it's very hard to fit in with their expectations. There's a lot of difference between my friends and her.
If you were looking to make some more new friends, do you have any ideas how you would do that?
No, because I'm not going out anywhere, and it's very hard to trust people, especially if they're not in the field of a professional.
Are there any particular qualities that you would want in a new friend? What would you want them to be like?
Polite and understanding, and not expecting a lot from me. But everybody sort of expects quite a lot, so I feel a bit of pressure.
I'm just thinking about your current friendships..

I talk to neighbours. They sometimes come by briefly, like to drop off a child to play with my daughter, or when I had a party for her. But I didn't speak to them then; I was mostly serving food in the kitchen.
What would need to be different for you to call those neighbours friends rather than neighbours?

They're not really my friendships, they're mostly my daughter's. We only speak because the children play and visit each other's homes. The adults don't come over much, just the children. I try not to have too many children in my house, just one at a time.
Would you want any of these neighbours to become closer friends?
I think no, because where I live is arranged around a central green with flats all around, and there's so much gossip. Everybody knows everybody's business.
You would be worried that the neighbours would talk about your business?

Yeah. One of my neighbours recently approached my mum and asked how I was doing, saying I'd seemed really depressed for the past few months. My mum said I was fine. I think the crisis team was visiting and they saw the NHS car, so they figured it out.
How do you feel about that? People knowing what happened to you?
Not happy, not nice, because there are quite a lot of rumours and things like that.
What would you be worried that people are thinking or saying?
Like I'm mad and things like that.
Is that the same reason that you don't talk about your symptoms with anyone but your family?
Yeah.
In case people think you're mad?
Yeah, or that I have a behaviour problem or something like that, because that affects my daughter as well. People will keep their distance from her too, and their children, so it's not fair.
Some of keeping yourself to yourself is to protect your daughter?
Yeah.
I'm just thinking about your friend who you were talking about, who you said you would ring back. What's going to need to change before you feel ok to make that phone call?

The pressure has to reduce. I'm really pressured about the family coming from back home, so that has to go. I have to be a bit more free in my daily responsibilities. My sleeping habits should settle down a bit. It's quite a lot to manage at the moment.

So there will be less pressure when the family visit is over with, when you're feeling a bit more rested perhaps, sleep may be more back to normal, everyday chores that have got to be done will feel more manageable?
It's getting there slowly. Before, my house was very dirty and messy, but slowly, slowly it's getting there. It looks clean but the cupboards are very untidy.
I remember you saying that your friend from the shop had helped you tidy round sometimes.

Yes, she helped me tidy sometimes. She likes my cat and my daughter. I don't like her to do too much, but if she wants to help I let her. When we cook together she washes up, or after we eat she clears the table and carries the dishes back, just small things. She also helps my mum but gets paid for that.
But she doesn't get paid to help you?
No.
It sounds like your new friend is more supportive and helping you to take care of things that old friends would be?
Yeah. We used to just eat, make a mess, and that was it.
So having someone who helps out reduces the pressure a bit in terms of what they expect when they visit?

Yeah. She doesn't come very often, once or twice a month for an hour or maybe two — that's good enough. If I really wanted help and was willing to pay her, maybe she would accept, but I haven't discussed it.
In a friendship, what sort of thing would you like to do for your friend? Do you like to be the joker, make them laugh, or be the listener, or the one with advice, or…?

I think I would be a good listener. I wouldn't advise because I don't want them to think I'm judging. I would help with physical chores. When my uncle died and I went to my sister's, we all had to do chores because they had all the guests coming. It was mostly her family, but I helped her arrange it and prepare food for 25 people; pouring food into big bowls and serving it.
So you're very good at helping with practical tasks?
Yeah. Especially when my mum tells me to.
How about friends for you — which qualities do you like in them?
Just support, actually. I don't expect them to help me a lot unless they created the mess, but being supportive and polite.
Is there anything you'd like to change about the friendships you have at the moment?

Not with friendships, but with my family I would like them to come to my house a bit less, because every day somebody's there, and that's quite… not good. But my daughter likes it, so I can't really complain much. When they're not there she is more lonely and keeps saying she wants to go to her friend's house, so sometimes I call her friend over, and sometimes I send her there.
So one thing you'd like is fewer family members dropping in all the time?

Yeah. All of them come together; it's extremely difficult. I physically feel so tired, and mentally as well, but it starts with mental tiredness and then I start getting aches and pains and then I'm sleeping very deeply for 14 hours or something.
Would you like to have more friends around, or does that not feel manageable at the moment?

I think I would like to have more friends to go out with, shopping. But I do my shopping online since I fell ill, so it's not that I need to buy things, but sometimes I go to [PLACE], like once a year or something. If I had somebody to go with I would probably go a bit more often.
Shopping is a good social activity, isn't it?
Yes. I do it online for weekly things, mostly for my daughter. She always needs clothes because she's growing in size.
Ok, so you'd like friends around to do more things like shopping. Is there anything else you'd like to be doing with friends?

I'd like to go to [PLACE], for doing my home shopping, but my brother takes me, so that's quite good. If he didn't take me I wouldn't go. Before, I wasn't going at all — they were bringing the shopping to me — but now he takes me.
What is it about [PLACE] that makes it difficult without your brother?
Carrying the things, and watching my daughter because she's going to run around everywhere and I'm so scared of losing her.
Keeping your mind on all those things at once is tricky. Does anybody here ever talk to you about friendships?
No, no one's ever spoken to me.
Is there anything you would like the service here to do to help with social things?
They offered me some groups, activities and things like that, but I don't want to because then everybody knows your condition. I didn't want to go to it.
Tell me more about that. The groups would be everyone who comes here, they'd have a similar condition. What worries you about them knowing?
Even if they have a similar condition, I feel it's not good for them to know I have it too. In a way, it also relaxes you to know you're not the only one.
So it's a sort of pro and con from coming to the groups here; a good thing might be that you wouldn't be the only one, but a con might be that people would know that about you.
Yes. I would be really worried about someone seeing me who was from my area and then they would gossip, and then I don't want people to keep away from my daughter.
I can understand why you would worry about that.
And if life was really good, exactly as you wanted it, would you be seeing more friends, or the same?

Maybe more. If I was healthy I would probably still be with the friends who I've been avoiding. I won't be smoking cannabis again but I did sometimes smoke before. I think I shouldn't be doing that, it's not a good idea, I realise that. It's quite bad in the long run, even financially and being around for the children.
Is that one of the reasons that you don't see them, because you don't want to smoke anymore?
Yeah.
So if you saw them there would be a chance that you would end up smoking?
Yeah, if it's in front of you, you can just be very intimidated.
So one of the reasons is that you choose to avoid that situation?
Yeah, they are encouraging you so.. Before this I wasn't smoking that before I met them, for many years.
Is there anything else that you'd want to talk about in relation to friendships or socialising that we haven't touched on?
Not really, no.
Thank you.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believed her husband was doing harmful things to her, which she later recognized were not true.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant explicitly states the accusations were not true and attributes them to a feeling she had at the time.

case_summary: The participant describes a significant reduction in social contact following a period of illness, during which she lost touch with most friends. She discusses feeling under pressure from social expectations, leading her to avoid reconnecting with old friends. She recounts past beliefs about being bullied by a friend and making false accusations against her husband, which she now recognizes as untrue. Currently, she has one new, low-pressure friendship and limits social interaction due to difficulty trusting people, fear of gossip, and low energy.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: I’m interested in hearing about people in your life who you consider to be friends, or who you do social stuff with. Is there anybody like that at the moment?
Yes, there is.
Can you tell me about them?

I met them at college and through an early intervention service group. I got to know a couple of people, got their numbers, and we started meeting up and socializing. I tend to prefer having just one or two close friends rather than a larger group. I like to explain things to them, like what I've done.
Let's talk about the friends from college first. How long have you known them?
About four or five weeks now.
Quite new friends?
Yeah. I'm actually going out with one girl after this. I've gotten to know her really well.
These people from college, are they in your class or..?
Yes, they're mainly in my class. I haven't really interacted with people from other departments. If someone was from a completely different course, like biology, I probably wouldn't relate to them.
These people that you've recently met from college, what sort of things would you do with them?

We're thinking of going paint-balling as a group. With the girl, we're going out today. Usually we talk, go out for lunch, grab a drink or a coffee, or play sports like football or badminton together.
Are there any friends in your life at the moment who were around before you became unwell?

Yes, there's one. A friend from university. We recently went on a holiday to [PLACE] for four days. He's a really close friend. Basically, nobody knew about my illness apart from my family: my mum and dad. I hadn't told anyone else, and I'd like to keep it that way. I don't like talking to other people about it. I think people get the wrong idea, they just walk away, they don't listen. They think there's something wrong with you and that you're mentally unwell. They might think I'm harmful to society, but I'm not. I'm not a violent person. I've never acted or talked that way. People just think differently—they wonder what you did wrong, or if you're taking drugs, but it's nothing like that. You can't talk to people about this sort of stuff. It's really confidential and difficult for me. I don't like talking about it, and when I do I get really upset. So it's a secret. The easiest thing is to just say I had depression. I don't mention psychosis or anything.
This friend, what do you think it was about him that meant you guys have stayed in touch, stayed good friends?

He's a good mate. He's not stingy with money, and he doesn't make jokes at my expense that are really bad. He's someone you can talk to. He can be funny, but he doesn't go over the top or show off. His family background is really good; he's an only child with very supportive parents. He's similar to me in that way; my parents are like that too. Some parents break up and the kids act out, going clubbing all night, but he's really responsible. I can rely on him; we support each other. I've known him for nearly three years. I used to have one really close friend in college, but I fell out with him because I felt like he was using me. Every time we went out, I paid for everything and he never gave anything back. Even when I asked, he'd just say he'd pay next time. He shouldn't have treated it like that. So far, my friend [PERSON] has been great.
Is there anybody who, like [PERSON] perhaps, that you've been friends with for a long time and you've lost contact with when you became unwell?

No, I've always been independent. There was one guy from school I lost contact with, but most of my friends from the past weren't serious about their work. I used to be serious in class and do my work, since we were in different academic levels. Outside of class, I'd hang out with them and it was more fun. If you only hang around with study-type friends, it's boring. I like to keep my studying in class and my friendships separate.
So when you left school, did you gradually lose touch with these people when you went to university?

I became more independent. In college, I was on my own most of the time. I didn't have any really close friends I could speak to. I was really stressed doing my A-Levels; it was two years of hard work on my own. I didn't have any insecurity about myself or my studies, it was just work as it came. I didn't have time for going out, apart from maybe playing football. I put on a lot of weight as well. When I got to university, I had practically no close friends. Then I met [PERSON], but we weren't that close at first. After we left university, we kept in touch through social media and phone calls, and eventually we met up and became pretty close. But apart from that, at university I had no proper friends. It was just casual hellos.
So more like acquaintances?
Yeah.
When you were unwell, and the time when you were starting to get better as well, do you think that would have been different if there had been more friends around?

No, I don't think so. Even if I had someone to turn to, they probably wouldn't have understood a single thing. The only people who would understand are my family, my mum and dad. They're the ones who supported me. Even if I had friends, they probably would have just spread rumors or talked about it with other people. I didn't feel like I could talk to any friends then, and I still can't now. I don't want to tell anyone. Never.
So your new friends that you've met at college, how did these friendships start? You're in class with them…

I went to college not just for the professional course, but to meet people because I didn't have anyone to hang out with. I went in with a smile, talking to everyone. My dad used to say be more aggressive—not really aggressive, but get out there and show who you are. In the first week, a girl I'm dating now didn't believe I could cook, so I cooked for the whole class. I brought traditional food, and it was a good introduction. Afterwards she started sitting next to me, and I met a few other people and got their numbers. I went in with two aims: make friends, maybe get a girlfriend, and get my career. It's been really good.
It sounds really good. How was that for you? It's scary on the first day, making new friends and getting your face known—did that happen naturally or was it hard work?

When I aim for something, I make myself work hard and I actually do it. If I'm too optimistic I probably won't do well, but if I'm negative I know what to expect. People might not have the same attitude—some might be quiet or have their own problems. I was cautious. It wasn't too easy, but I found that speaking a bit louder than normal got other people's attention and they'd turn and ask questions. Also, in class the first question was to introduce yourself. When she asked me to cook for the whole class, I thought it was a good way to meet more people and learn what they're like. What I did was, rather than try to know everyone, I focused on remembering three or four people.
It sounds like a pretty good strategy that worked. When you were in your first few weeks, was there anything you looked for in new friends? Any particular qualities?

I don't really look for qualities, but I do look for a couple of things: not being rude or arrogant, being friendly, smiling, polite, listening to someone, not going over the top talking about themselves all the time or what they've been doing at the weekend, like drinking. There's one girl who constantly talks about what she drank and her personal problems. I don't like it. It's like they know what kind of person I am and then they show what kind of person they are. Some people talk too much about themselves and what they've achieved. I don't like that kind of person.
And do you think that now, since you've been unwell, you look for different things in friends than before, or is it about the same?

When I was unwell I wasn't looking at friends. I was lost, insecure, frightened. I was even paranoid with my parents that they hated me. I didn't trust anyone. When I got better gradually, I wanted to make new friends but I couldn't because I wasn't at college or working—I was in all day. So I talked to my cousins and hung about with them more. One of them pushed me away because of work, so I looked to my parents, and that's what pulled me out. I don't know who else would go through that and help me. After I was well, my head was clear, I had support every week with my coordinator and did social activities at the EIS. I just wanted to do something to make new friends. I went to a coastal town a couple of weeks back, met a couple of people, and it was really fun.
Ok. I'm going to ask you about your friends from here in a minute, but I just wanted to check: do you think you're now back to how you were before in terms of socialising and being around people?

I feel much better than before because I've got less stress. Rather than just focus on uni and coursework, my head's in the right direction. I've got a balance now with my social life. I know for a fact that because of depression, studying just built up. I know my health is worth more than grades. There are people who don't go to uni and end up working in a bank or whatever, doing good things and they're really happy with families. I feel it's time I've picked my career—I'll follow that path with not a lot of stress and have a relationship on the side, go out with friends. I'm young, so before I was like an old man thinking work, work, work, money, money, money. Now I want to go abroad more. A couple of days ago I went to Barcelona with my friend. Before that I hadn't been on holiday since 2008, and that was with my parents when I was unwell, just to get me away, so it wasn't really a holiday. Apart from that I haven't been on holiday for six or seven years. So now I'm thinking every single year I'm going to go on two or three holidays. I don't care where the money comes from.
So it's shifted your priorities a little bit?
Yes. It's like, go out socialising more, and when you're at college just do your work, but don't go over the top with the study like before. I was addicted.
It sounds good. Thinking about your friends from the EIS groups—you went to the coastal town—have you done any of the other activities?

Yeah, badminton, been to the cinema, missed the Christmas dinner, but went to a couple of other places. We went to the zoo and things like that. It's been really good. At first, when I started going to the activities, I wasn't making many friends. The last trip, the seaside trip, kind of woke me up, because it was by the sea, away from fumes, stress, and traffic. When I went there, it was just peace. I was with some people, joking around. I saw a guy, a friend, I can't remember his name, but he was chatting and asking about girls. I met another girl in the group, got her number, but I only texted once and didn't call. I thought, I don't know if she's okay with this.
When you were going to the groups, was it the same idea you had for college, like going to meet friends, or was it different?

It was different. It was to see different things. In college, you're there twice a week and see the same people every day. But the social groups are one-offs, maybe once a month. The seaside trip was once a year. It's not very frequent. Some people in the groups don't talk. I don't know who I talk to, but some are alright. Most just keep to themselves. I understand, because I was like that too. I didn't want to. I don't like to hassle them because I know they've had similar experiences. I know their situation, so it's completely different. College is like, you can speak to everyone and not tell them that stuff. In the EIS groups, it's not like that. You can go out and enjoy it, but don't get too close. That's how I felt.
In the EIS groups, is there anything good about the fact that you've all had similar experiences?

Yeah, it is good, but I don't like talking about it. I don't think others in the group like talking about it either. It's difficult. The thing is, you enjoy yourself. You meet new people and can talk normally, but you can't get too personal and tell someone everything, or most of it; it's like 25%. But at college, you can tell up to 50-75%.
Why is there that difference?

I think the difference is, first, it's difficult to explain, and second, people get... I get emotional when I have to explain. It's difficult because when you're talking personally about the experiences you've had, it's really hard to explain, even in the groups. Even if they've gone through it, they might not have the exact same experiences. In college, you don't have to say anything about it. You just talk like normal people. But talking about your own experiences is a personal thing. It's really difficult in the social groups.
So in the social groups, because people have had similar experiences, they are expecting you to talk about that?

Yeah. Even if you did explain it, even if they had a similar experience, it's just... When I explain it, I get really emotional; I can't explain it. It's difficult to talk to people when you're the one who went through it.
I'm thinking about when you were unwell and the people around you. Is there anything that would have helped in terms of friends, having someone to talk to?

Difficult question. I think what would have helped was someone who could make you go out more, to get well. Just going to the cinema, just getting things out of your mind. The thing is, the care coordinator already talks to me and that helps, and medication and all that is already there. You just need someone to help you go out more, like to the cinema. A friend you can go out with, not a health professional. Like a normal friend, an ordinary person. You don't have to tell them your personal experiences, but someone who's just there and you can get support to go out and do stuff, like play football, like a really close friend.
Who can perhaps take your mind off things?
Yeah, take your mind off things. That's what it is.
That's a useful point. So you've started college, you've got a new group of friends, you've still got [PERSON] from before. Is there anything you think is missing in terms of friendships?
What do you mean, like...?
In an ideal world, if things were exactly as you want them to be, would it be different to how it is now?

Not having too many friends is not good. But having the wrong friend is even worse. Like, I know a guy who's alright but he tries to act too clever. He thinks I'm not seeing what he's seeing. I'll give you an example. He's going out spending lots of money on cars and stuff, probably gambling as well, and he's taking other people's money to do that. He's a student, not working or anything. Those types of friends you should stay away from. Or if you're friends with them and have any money involved, just get out as quick as you can. There are other friends who try to take your money, make you spend, spend, spend when you're with them, and they never do anything about it. There are other friends who lie to your face, and later you find out. I've experienced quite a few friends like that. I think in an ideal world, you'd want a friend with the same characteristics as you. Similar characteristics. I don't mean a relationship. Even a mate with a similar background, like working class, someone you can get along with, who doesn't joke too much, doesn't go over the top, isn't into themselves, not a bad boy or too nice. Someone who's genuine and not taking advantage of you. There are a lot of people out there who do that. I think that's the most ideal friendship. Someone who really cares for someone. Doesn't play with your emotions.
These 'bad' friends, these unhelpful people that you describe, have there been many of them in the last year or two years?

Basically, because I pick my friends, I'm really careful about making friends. I only make one or two. I have had that experience, but it's been my mistake in the sense that I shouldn't have helped them out. It's been my mistake. I should have thought about it, or got advice from someone else before I helped them. I should have found out more about what kind of person they were, rather than just taking their word. So there have been one or two.
Are those people from before you were unwell or after?
Before.
Do you think you're more cautious since you were unwell?

I think, after I've been unwell, because I've had two targets: one to get an accountancy job, and another to make new friends. Because I'm focusing on making new friends, I feel I'm more cautious deep down than before. Before, I was more into my studying and had my mind on work. I was more stressed then and less stressed with friends. Now it's like 50-50, so I actually see what's going on.
So rather than being more cautious, you can pay more attention and put more time into it?
Yes.
Do you feel you have enough new friends now, or are you still looking to add more?
I don't mind. I'd probably like to add more, but having too many, maybe more than seven or eight in a week, would be too much.
Is there anything about friendships that I haven't asked you about that you'd like to mention?
No.
I'm curious about starting college and your decision to use that as an opportunity to make friends. Did anyone suggest that to you or talk to you about it?

No, I realized I needed to. I don't want to be alone for the rest of my life. I didn't take the chance at school or in college. I moved far away from my school's area to escape the atmosphere and the bullying. I felt I had to leave that crowd and go to a good college to meet new people, but I ended up isolating myself. I already had a couple of school friends, and I questioned why I didn't go to a nearby college with them. Still, I made the right choice for me because it cleared my mind and let me focus more on my studies.
Thank you for taking part.

case_summary: The participant discusses their approach to friendships, contrasting a period of social isolation during past mental health difficulties with a current deliberate effort to build a small, carefully selected social circle through college and an early intervention service. They express a strong preference for keeping their mental health history a secret from all but family, fearing misunderstanding and rejection, and describe a past state of paranoia and mistrust that has since resolved.
no_delusion_point_reason: The candidate point describes a past feeling of paranoia ('believed his parents hated him') which the participant explicitly frames as a symptom of a past illness that they no longer experience. This is a retrospective account of a resolved symptom, not a currently held belief about external reality, and therefore does not meet the criteria for a delusion point.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: Okay. I'd like to hear about people in your life you see socially or consider friends. Do you have anyone like that right now?
I do.
Okay. Can you tell me about them?
Someone I see as the most memorable, the closest, is someone called [PERSON]. I've known him for about four years I think.
Okay.
And he's a very close friend of mine.
How did you and [PERSON] meet?

We met through a friend. I used to do GCSEs with someone who became a friend, and then we moved onto A-Levels and separated. I mean, in terms of A-Levels, we went to different colleges. But we stayed friends, and at the college he went to, my friend from GCSEs met [PERSON] and we got introduced.
Okay. And what sort of things do you and [PERSON] do together?
We used to go to parties and stuff together, but he stopped that. He was taking drugs a lot and I was as well, and he just decided that wasn't for him anymore. He stopped without any real problems.
Okay.

Maybe he had some mild negative, very slight depression or something. Then he stopped, but I had to stop because I had other problems. When I had psychosis, I still did them. He was one of the very few who… I used to go gardening with him every week and that was quite helpful. Now we just meet up and go to a bar.
Okay, so when you were feeling quite unwell, perhaps worse than you do now, [PERSON] was around to do stuff with you?
Yes. I mean, [PERSON] was quite helpful and I got a lot of support.
What was it that he did that helped?

We just generally preferred to… We did something together. Just us, alone, we spoke and sometimes brought it round to my problems and discussed it a bit. That helps as well. He would try to help me in that way.
Okay. Are there any friends who you've lost touch with or are not in contact with anymore as a result of being unwell?

There are, yes. It's mainly those who—even though [PERSON] was the one who first took us to this psychedelic trance club where we started taking drugs and moved onto psychedelics. For some reason I didn't have this fear of anything like that. There were other people I used to see after [PERSON] had stopped but I was still taking drugs. Those were the ones I took most drugs with. When I had a bad trip—which happened twice—they were the people I saw first. It was the first time I'd taken acid in a negative light. After the first time, I was fine. I had some weird thoughts but got over it. When it happened the second time and it was full on psychosis, I fear them a bit and still sometimes think I wouldn't necessarily want to see them.
Okay, so, because they became associated with that time they became frightening; is that too strong a word?

It did at the time, yes. And also, especially one of the girls. I guess during that kind of psychosis, when I lay in bed to sleep, there were mental images in my head where she would be playing games with me. They were with me for quite a while, so I just didn't want to be associated with her.

Okay. Thinking about the difference between [PERSON] and those people and why your friendship with [PERSON] has survived, what is it about [PERSON]? What qualities does he have that makes him such a good friend?

Once you get close to him, he's very warm-hearted and just a very warm person, nice to be around. He tends to be quite positive and our conversations are free and natural. We feel we can talk about all sorts of stuff together and he's quite open in our relationship. It's kind of his character and my character—maybe I'm not like that with other people and he's not like that with other people, but we kind of connected somehow.
Okay. Were there any other friends who were around beforehand who are still your friend?

No. I wouldn't call them friends so much now because I don't see them that much. When I was at my most ill, I stopped seeing most people, but as I'm feeling better, I keep some kind of contact with them. We don't see each other that much. Not necessarily because I don't want to, it's just… A few new people have appeared and it's kind of steps, the concept of a group of friends. But there is one other guy and my ex-girlfriend who I knew before it happened to me.
Okay. And were they around like [PERSON] was when you were finding things really difficult and starting to get back on your feet?
Well, my ex-girlfriend was the most involved because we met about two months before anything happened.
Right.
Or the second time it happened. We got together a month before it started, and she stayed with me through the whole thing, so she was very important.
And was that helpful or unhelpful, or what?

Yes, it was helpful mostly. I mean, mostly I say because I guess she would talk to me but at the same time she would get quite depressed as well and every so often we would argue, which I guess was not helpful in some ways, but yes, in general I think…
Okay. And how about that other friend? Because you said your ex-girlfriend and somebody else. Who was that?
Yes. The person who introduced me to my ex-girlfriend.
Oh, okay.

This guy was called [PERSON] and my ex-girlfriend was called [PERSON]. So [PERSON], he's less of a serious guy, I guess. He's not very serious. But he was still not far away from me and we still kept in contact and we spoke sometimes. The best place for me was my house, so they would sometimes come over and stay. I think I was seeing him less than [PERSON].
Okay. And are the sorts of things you do now with friends in general, that you do for fun, is that different?
Yes. I mean, before I would be taking drugs and now I don't do that.
Okay. So does that mean going to different places as well?
Not necessarily, no.
Okay.

Psychedelic trance parties, which are a kind of evolution of raves, used to happen in clubs but now are mostly in warehouses. I went maybe two or three times over the past two years, so I don't do that anymore. I've managed to connect or talk—I think I need to be less self-conscious—and I can talk to different people once I find common ground. Usually I go to this place in [local area], and the people who go there tend to attend these psychedelic trance parties, so that part didn't change much. But they go to other places too. Most end up going to these. It's like a kind of home for me. It's nicely made, everyone kind of knows each other, and they've shown good…
Okay, so it has to be sort of somewhere familiar, that kind of thing.
Yes.
Okay. Regarding discussing your symptoms and the period when you were unwell, who would you talk to about that? Are you quite open about it? Would that be with most people?
I'm quite open, yes.
Okay. Who's the most—who would be the first person you'd talk to if you wanted to?

It would be my ex-girlfriend and my mum. My ex-girlfriend not so much now because she's got a new boyfriend, which I don't mind at all. But my mum, if only very slightly something feels a little bit strange, I'd kind of—because it's nothing that bothers me that much, it's not making me feel really, really depressed all the time as it used to, but things can happen sometimes but it's not having a huge effect on me. She thinks that—it's true that I feel much better—and she's very happy about that, so I don't want to put—because of these little things that can happen sometimes—I don't want to put extra burden on her.
Okay.
With some other friends maybe I can… [PERSON], for example, or my twin brother.
Were you worried about that burden on [PERSON] or do you think he's better able to manage it?
No, I think he's better able to…
Okay. And thinking about new friends; have you made any new friends since you were unwell?

Yes, there's a very nice girl from my university I've become friends with. It hasn't been long, but she seems like a genuinely kind person and I'm free at the moment, so if something develops... I enjoy talking with her generally, and also about this stuff if it comes up.
Okay. Is there anybody else?
It depends. Like I said, I'm quite open, so I'd share that with most people and try to get some answers from them for myself—not everyone, but most people.
Okay. When seeking friends now versus during your illness, do you aim for different types of people, or the same? Do you value different traits now?

I don't think about it that much. Usually I don't have strong opinions or a clear 'I like that.' It's more a feeling—maybe in the moment I'd think about it, but afterwards it's not really about words. Just someone very nice and warm, who isn't judging me.
Okay. And if you wanted to make new friends now, if that was something you wanted to do, where would you do that or how would you go about that?

I wouldn't overthink it. Maybe I wouldn't even think about new friends at all. Even if I did, I wouldn't take a specific approach—just let it happen naturally. Not going to a particular place to make friends. Just making friends as they come, that's all.

Okay. Do you think being unwell has changed the way friendships are for you? I mean, for example with [PERSON], do you think that your friendship has experienced change to how it was before or is it the same?
With [PERSON] it's different. The psychosis actually brought us closer together, and I feel it's more positive now. We're a lot closer and able to talk about loads of stuff.
So how about [PERSON] and [PERSON]? Do you think those friendships have changed? I suppose [PERSON] has in a way because now she's your ex-girlfriend and she was your girlfriend.

Yes. After we broke up, we stayed sort of friends. I think it was harder for her than for me. I used to call her a lot—not trying to get back together, but because I'd been so dependent on her before. Maybe I was attached. Anyway, she has a boyfriend now and doesn't want that so much. She's tried to be a bit distant, but we're still friends. And [PERSON], after I got better I kept seeing him, but now he's busy, doesn't come out as much, and lives quite far out so he travels less.

Okay. We talked a little bit about how friendships might have been affecting you when you were starting to get better. Do you think that there was anything that you'd have wanted friends to do more for you when you were trying to get better?

Maybe—I don't know. Maybe more talking about this. Actually, I can't remember exactly. My mum would be quite strict in a way, spending a long time explaining why I was having these experiences, saying it was because of the drugs I'd taken and that's why I felt like that. She'd say, 'Don't be silly, you've heard from so many others how it is.' She was always very reassuring and supportive, always saying I'd get better. I didn't get that as much from my friends.
What sort of messages did your friends give you?
I don't know. I guess the same goes—I wouldn't find they'd explain things as much. It used to happen with my mum and my ex-girlfriend too, saying 'you're going to get better.'
Okay. But do you think they were reluctant to talk about your symptoms with you? Do you think they were a little bit unsure?
Yes, sometimes. Not all of them.

Okay. If you were going to change something about the friendships that you've got in your life at the moment, whether that's to get some more or to have less or different sorts of friends, what would it be for you?
I don't know. I don't know.
Okay. Do you feel there's anything at the moment that's missing from your friendships?
Yes, I guess—I mean, I don't think so...
Okay, so it feels quite kind of content with how you..
Yes, it's fine, yes.
Okay. Good. Does anyone here ever talk to you about friendships and social stuff? Anyone at the intervention service?
Yes. Mostly with my care coordinator. It was mainly about my ex-girlfriend, since I'd mentioned her before. Not so much about other things, but maybe a little.
Okay. And did you ever attend any of the social events they organized here? Any groups or activities? Were you offered them?
Like badminton and things?
Yes.

Yes. At the time I wasn't keen on getting involved with other people. I think that's fine. Now I'm very open and usually welcoming. But a girl I spoke to told me I was too open again, and that I should be more cautious about people.
Right. Do you think you've always been like that, quite open, or is that something new?
It's something new for me.
Okay. And what did you think when this girl said that? Did it ring true for you, or was it a surprise?

I kind of accepted how I was. I thought if I was with [PERSON], it might be too much. I don't know. But I like to think she told me that in the sense that you can't always trust people. It's more about the general thoughts people might have about others. But my more psychotic thoughts connected to my fears might be hinting that I should be careful because... I haven't really thought about it much. I was just trying to be open, so she could also be saying, 'Okay, you're very open, but be careful,' because people could be going against me and stuff.
Okay. I'm just wondering what it is about being unwell that's made you more open and welcoming to people? Do you know? It's hard to say, I know.

Well, I don't know, because I don't think about this. Maybe it's just this fighting element—we usually have this thought that we have to fight things in our life. When we've got problems, maybe we're working subconsciously to try harder and overcome them. And being open might be another way of looking at it, like when you feel everyone is nice to you. I haven't consciously thought about it, or maybe sometimes I have and realized how much effect it's had. I've told myself over time, 'Don't be silly, people are fine,' which at the time didn't seem to change my moods much. But maybe it made some kind of difference.
Okay. So to compensate for the power of the frightening thoughts, you compensated by forcing yourself, not necessarily consciously, to be very welcoming and open with people?
Yes. And also, that was at the time. Things that happen now I think have come naturally. And maybe because I've aged and become confident again talking to people.
Did you notice after you were unwell that you had a drop in your confidence? Some people tell me this, but not everybody.
A drop in my confidence...
In terms of being around other people socially?
