I don't know whether it's confidence or not. It was more a kind of fear of what they want. Not necessarily how I look or anything. I don't really think about that stuff much.
Okay. Has anyone reacted badly when you've talked about your symptoms and been open about your illness? Has anyone reacted negatively to that?
Not really, no. Everyone's been really supportive.
Okay. Let me just check if there's anything I've missed. Do you think there's anything else services could be doing to support you in friendships? Is there any need you have that's not met?
I can't think of anything.
Let's think about perhaps the friendship with [PERSON], the sort of role that you play in that friendship.

I guess I'm always there to talk to him about whatever he likes. I'd like to give advice whenever I can, if I'm able. I do sometimes. And if he needs any help at all, I'd be willing to help as much as he wants, as much as I can. Or just in general, going out with him and having a good night out.
Is that the same for [PERSON] and [PERSON], do you think?
I think so, yes. Again, help is something I'd be very willing to give both of them. Talking with [PERSON] is perhaps less easy now, but yes.

Okay. Regarding the roles they play as friends to you—you've mentioned you're there as someone who listens, talks, supports, that kind of thing—do you need the same from them, or do they give you something different?
They do give me that, yes.
And do you think your role or any of those roles changed since you were unwell, or have they always been the same?
In the period that I was unwell or now? Is that—

I'm just wondering; some people find that after they've been unwell, the things they need from their friends are a little different or the things they give to their friends are a little different, and again, not everybody. I don't know if that's the case for you?
I'm not sure.
Okay. Is there anything else you can think of? Any comments about friendships in relation to your illness before or after?
No.
No? Okay.

delusion_points.summary: During a period of psychosis, the participant experienced persistent mental images of a specific girl playing games with them while they were trying to sleep, leading them to avoid association with her.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant frames this as occurring 'in my head' and describes it as part of a 'kind of psychosis', indicating insight that it was an internal experience.

delusion_points.summary: The participant acknowledges that psychotic fears can involve a sense that people might be going against him, and that a friend's warning to be careful could be interpreted through that lens.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant frames this as a past or potential psychotic thought, not a current conviction, and notes he hasn't thought about it much. He also accepts the friend's advice as general caution.

case_summary: The participant discusses their social network and friendships following a period of drug-induced psychosis. They describe a close, supportive friendship with [PERSON] that strengthened through their illness, contrasting it with friendships lost due to fear and association with bad drug experiences. They are open about their mental health, value non-judgmental warmth in friends, and note a new, natural openness with people, though they acknowledge past psychotic fears about others' intentions.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: Okay so do you feel that you've got any friends in your life at the moment?

Yes. Just on Facebook. I'm in touch with my friends and cousins, I write to them and they write to me but I don't see them day to day. I only see one friend from college once every two or three weeks because she works at her dad's shop so she's not always free. Apart from her, I was seeing a boy but I ended it with him.
Okay.
I'm not seeing many people at the moment.
Why's that?

Because I write to them on Facebook, they write to me but they never suggest meeting up. Most have married, some have kids, some don't, but they're working and built a new life after marriage. One says she's busy all the time since her life changed, and she didn't give me her new phone number on Facebook after her holiday when I asked. And my step-mum, who knows the girl's mum—we're distant relatives—might have told her mum that her daughter shouldn't see [PERSON], or something went wrong. My instincts say my step-mum might be involved.
Okay, so was it…
My step-mum and me didn't get on so she might not want my friends to be around me.
I see, okay, okay.
She might want to leave me alone.
And did you lose touch with this friend—has that happened since you were ill or was that before you were ill?

After I was ill, about a year ago. Six months before her wedding I stopped visiting because she never called. She'd say she was busy preparing and not running away from me. After marrying she says she's busy with guests and visitors, her life changed, and she hasn't got time to meet. She claims she doesn't see her other friends either, just writes on Facebook.
Okay, okay. So you feel like…
Maybe she's lying.
Okay I was going to ask you do you think she's being truthful or not, it's hard to know isn't it?
Yes.
Okay and how about your…

And her husband might have thought I was a bad influence and didn't want her to be friends with me. Maybe he told her not to meet me. He knew me before and we spoke as friends—he's a good person—but he may just not want me around her.
Okay, what would make you think you're a bad influence do you think?

Well I went to [PLACE] and got engaged to someone without telling my dad. I met the boy on MSN, spoke for three and a half years, then got engaged there. My aunts got involved and told his parents I was being used to go to [PLACE], saying if he were serious he'd visit my uncles in [PLACE]—it's cultural, you need permission from parents or uncles. So the boy didn't want me. That friend bought my ticket to [PLACE], but she only knew I went to one part of [PLACE]; I went to another part myself. I never told my dad and step-mum. My dad and cousin blamed whoever bought the ticket, so my dad was upset with her mum. That could have affected my friendship because she got blamed for buying it.
I see, okay, and that's why her husband might not be happy.
Possibly and her mum as well.
Right, okay. Tell me about your friend from college who you see every few weeks.

She's a very good person, we get on and enjoy our time together. We go out to eat, sometimes the cinema but not often, mostly just meet and talk. I tell her about my relationship—when I split up and got back together with my boyfriend. She listens and tries to give a little advice, but she says she won't really advise me anymore because I take it the wrong way and don't want to listen, so she mainly just listens now.
Right okay. What is it about your friend that you like? What are her good qualities?
She listens, she's a good listener, she cares about me, she wants the best for me, she thinks about me.
And how long have you known her?
Since college, [DATE].
Okay, a long time.
Eight years.
Was she around when you were ill, when you were unwell?

Not right next to me, but I was still seeing her. There were times I wasn't seeing her though. I was living in a hostel and wasn't seeing her that often, then I started seeing her more. She knows my illness as depression; I didn't tell her it was psychosis. She doesn't know that I hear people calling me names in the street when I walk past them. I don't hear voices when I'm on my own at home or anywhere, only in the street when I go past strangers. I think they're putting down my appearance. I'm insecure about my appearance. In the hostel they were calling me monkey, chimpanzee, and since then I haven't had much confidence in myself.
Right, okay. Is there any friend you've told about what happened to you?
Sorry?
Are there any friends that you've told about psychosis?
I told my boyfriend about it and he was supportive.
Right.

Who else have I told? I told the boy in [PLACE] when I got engaged. I told his mum and dad. I told his dad and his dad told him, but I told them I had schizophrenia, so then they didn't want to know me anymore. He didn't say 'I don't want to know you,' he said, 'Don't think I never loved you, I loved you but it's not working, things are not working, your aunts got involved.' He got upset that my aunts got involved and said he's only using me to come over to [PLACE]. He lives in [PLACE], that's my ex-boyfriend. I got through a lot of hard times, a lot of heartbreak.
Yes, it sounds like it.

I wanted the truth to come out so that in the future if we got married, if he found out he wouldn't leave me or get angry. So I told him from the start, and then it didn't lead to marriage. We ended up not getting married. I spoke to him for three and a half years on MSN and on the phone, and then I saw him for 10 days and got engaged. The first time after three and a half years I went and saw him, I'd never seen him before that. That was after he came back from the army in [PLACE]. After that I went for seven days, so basically in 17 days of seeing him face to face I was ready to marry him. Now when I look back I think it was a stupid idea. If we got married it would have ended in divorce. But it was because I was so much in love with him, and he said he had a lot of feelings for me as well.
Okay, so do you think that the relationship split up because you told him you were not well?
Yes.
Okay.

No, that wasn't the whole reason. That was part of the reason. He said, 'Your aunts got involved and said that I'm using you to go to [PLACE],' that was another reason. Another reason was after I came back from [PLACE] the first time, I was all jealous and paranoid of him, saying I saw in my dream that he was seeing another girl, he was seeing girls and I want it to end. He said, 'I can't take your jealousy and your paranoia anymore, you're too much.' After that I went out with someone else here in [PLACE]. Before I went to [PLACE] the second time, he made me admit if I went out with him or not and if I slept with him or not. I told him the truth. When I went to [PLACE] he said to me, 'Your aunt is saying that I'm using you to go to [PLACE], it's just an excuse.' What he means is that I was unfaithful to him after we just split up for just one month. After I went out with someone else, he still called me back to [PLACE] for the marriage. He said, 'I forgive you.' I don't know whether he had really forgiven me or he just thought, 'Let me get my own back on her, let me go and get married with her and then leave her when I get my leave to remain in [PLACE].' I don't know what he thought. He just called me back and I went back because I cared about him so much. Obviously I didn't show him that I cared about him too well by going out with someone else.
Okay, and when you were…
I've basically made mistakes in my life.
Yes, everyone makes mistakes, don't they, and things that they regret perhaps. When you were feeling really unwell, at its worst…

Yes, they kept calling me monkey and chimpanzee. I had arguments with around 20 or 30 girls in the all-female hostel. In the mixed-gender hostel I hadn't experienced psychosis. I was only diagnosed with psychosis last year, in January or February of 2009, but I had been going through it before without realizing. My hostel manager referred me to the GP, who then referred me to the mental health team in North city, and that's when I got the psychosis diagnosis. That was in my second hostel, the all-girls one. I moved between hostels trying to get a flat. I didn't have psychosis in the first, mixed hostel, so I didn't hear things there. But in the all-girls hostel I felt they were ganging up on me. They all called me names, and I called them names back. The hostel reported to the council that I was the one who started the name-calling, that they never called me names. I don't know.
Okay, so at that very worst time, when the psychosis was really strong, were there any friends about for you then? Was there anybody who…?

I wasn't seeing my friend from college. I was seeing my friend, the one who got married, and she didn't give me her number. I was seeing her but I never told her my illness was psychosis, I said it was depression. I didn't used to tell her that—I think I did tell her a little bit that they were calling me names and I was calling them names, but I don't remember very well if I told her or not. I think I did tell her. Yes, I said, 'I've got problems with girls in the hostel, I'm arguing with them too much,' that's what I said.
And was there anything she did that helped?

She was just there for me, a good friend when we were together. She was fun, made me laugh, and was really good at joking and imitating people in a playful, teasing way, not mean. She'd make fun of her aunts and others, sometimes without them knowing, but she's a really funny, charming person.
Okay, so she helped by taking your mind off things.
Yes, we've been good friends since we were about 12 or 13, right up until now.
And the friend from college, you said at that time you weren't seeing her much. Why was that?

I don't really remember. I might have seen her sometimes, but I think I was more occupied with the people there because I liked some of them. I was spending time in the girls' hostel, listening to music, watching old comedy films from my home country, and arguing with the girls. My mind was too busy with them.
Okay, and when you started to get better, since things have been improving but are still hard work...

Yes, I'm still hearing voices sometimes, but I'm not hearing the monkey or chimpanzee anymore. I just hear them say things like, "Look at her, look at her figure, just look at her, oh no," things like that.
Is there anything friends do now to help you with that?

No. My friend doesn't know, and my boyfriend knew. He was supportive, but I'm not with him now; I ended it. I've been ending it over the last two weeks, saw him yesterday, but ended it again today. He was supportive, but I realized something was wrong. He was on the internet with a friend back in his home country. He posted a love song on his Facebook, and his friend commented, "Don't listen to such heavy sad songs, everyone lives with what they do." He replied, "Yes I know, I did something wrong myself and I'm having to live with it, don't worry about it." I felt this meant they were talking in code about a relationship he had back home, since he's only been here eight months, arriving in March of this year. So I told him yesterday and today, by text and face-to-face, "You never loved me, you still love one of your exes and can't forget them. You only feel sorry for me and that's why you went out with me. You cared for me but you didn't love me." That's what I think.
Why do you think someone would feel sorry for you?

Because I told him my parents got divorced, I didn't grow up with my mum, I grew up with my step-mum. My grandma looked after me, then my step-mum and my cousin. So I feel like he sees I haven't had a stable, good life, that I've had a hard life. I just think he likes me as a person and cares about me, but underneath he doesn't love me. Even though he says he loves me and cares a lot, with tears in his eyes when I mention separating, I still don't trust him. I've lost my trust in people.
When did you lose your trust, do you think? Is that from having the psychosis?

That could be part of it, or all of it, I don't know. But it's not all of it. There's more. The boy I went out with before this one came to me and said, "When I was going out with you, I was going out with other girls, and now I'm next to you, she doesn't know I'm next to you, I've got a girlfriend now." And then after that, this last boyfriend spoke to a girl on the phone right next to me in my house, saying, "You're the only one, you're different from everyone else, you're the only one in my life." He said he never saw the girl, that it was someone his cousin randomly gave his number to, and she was abroad or somewhere, and he never met up with her. He says, "When he came to your house you walked outside, so I should also not be trusting you. Why don't you trust me? Because I spoke to a girl on the phone once, I never met up with her, I never lived anything with her." And I say, "I can't trust you because of what that boy said to me before you, and after what you did, speaking on the phone next to me." Now I've lost my trust in people, in men.
Do you think if you were looking for friends now, you'd be looking for something different? Would you want to be friends with different sorts of people, or the same as always?

I like my friends from secondary school and college, but unfortunately they're all working or married and working. So I would like to have people in my life that I have a good time with, who make me laugh and joke and help me forget my worries. I'd be happy to make new friends, but the place of old friends is always different; you can never replace them.
Yes.
If you have memories of them since childhood.
Yes, definitely. It's nice to talk about all the old times when things happened that made you both laugh.

Yes, and laughter, sadness, tears, joy—all the mixed feelings I went through as a teenager. My friend who's married now and didn't give me her number, she lived through it all with me. I would tell her everything, let it all out so it wouldn't hurt me. I would share with her and get advice about how to talk with boys, or I would advise her. Maybe she was the one who listened to me, because she only went out with one person and ended up marrying him.
So you really like to be open with your friends and talk about anything and everything.
Yes.
But that's been harder lately because your friends have been working or married, or you find them difficult to get hold of?

Yes, it seems like they're avoiding me. They like to know I'm okay and well, but they don't want to be part of my life. I can't blame every single one of them for my illness; that can't be the reason they're staying away, I don't think so. I think they all have their own circle of friends by this age. The ones I only used to see at weddings or at college now have their own friends from university, so they don't feel the need to be close to me.
Okay, and have there been any more recent friends after your friend from college? Because that was actually 2002, I think you said.
No, until now I was friends with her but…
Anyone you've met since then, any newer friends I suppose?

No. At the mixed hostel and the girls' hostel there were nice girls, I would talk with them, but after that I just left them there, I never swapped numbers. I just saw them while we were living in the hostel, I wasn't hanging out with them outside. I saw people from all backgrounds: Ethiopian, Somalian, black, white, mixed race, [NATIONALITY], mainly that's all.
All different nationalities?
Yes.
Okay and is there anything you'd like to…
So living in that hostel opened up my vision of the world, it made me see different people's cultures and ways of life, so I'm quite happy in that sense that I did move to the hostel.
Okay and thinking about your…

At school I mostly stuck with the [NATIONALITY] girls and didn't mix much with other races. We shared a similar background, so we were closer. I'd talk with the white, black, and mixed race girls in class but wouldn't hang around with them. Moving to the hostels let me see different people, but I never kept in touch with any of them afterwards.
Does that mean that your friend who lent you the money for the ticket and who got married, that your step-mum might know her mum?
Yes she does.
Does that mean that your step-mum knows the parents of lots of your friends from school, those [NATIONALITY] girls?
No. She knows the names of them; she knows the ones on my Facebook who are from the same village as me.
Right okay. I'm just thinking if she had any impact on how well you've managed to stay in touch with the other people but it's hard to know isn't it?
Yes, I wouldn't really know.
Okay.

People from secondary school and my village write on Facebook wishing me well, but I wasn't close with them. I'd just see them at weddings, say hello, chat briefly, and that was it—I never swapped numbers. They're more like acquaintances. My only real close friends were the girl who bought me the ticket, who's now married, and the one from college.
Okay, and if you wanted something to change about your friendships right now, would you prefer having more friends, fewer friends, or different kinds of friends? What would you want to be different?
Different types of friends and more friends. I wouldn't say less friends because I always have a little…
Okay so you'd like to have more people around?
Yes, I have little ones that I'm in touch with day to day.
And if you had more friends what sort of thing would you want to do with them?

Go to the cinema, go to nice places and eat together, and watch TV at home together, introduce the person I will be with in my life to them—a boy when there is one in the future—and make them become good friends, make them have a bond with them, and that's it.
Okay and would it be friends that you would want—would you want to be able to talk to them about everything or would it be more just for fun times?

I'd definitely want friends I could talk with about all my sadness, joy, and worries—everything. And at the same time have fun with them, like I did with my friend who got married. We could have fun and I could cry next to her, tell her about boys I had feelings for. When they liked me back I'd push them away—I did that with two boys at college. All those mixed feelings, not knowing what to do, all my teenage worries, I told her everything.
That's what you'd like again?
Yes.
And would you want to tell new friends about the voices, or would you keep that to yourself?

I would keep it to myself. I forgot to mention, there was a woman from the job centre years ago, when we were on a support programme. I became friends with her. I brought her to my place once and we had a drink. Later, when I told her my boyfriend got angry and called me schizophrenic, she stopped calling me after that.
Okay, so you think that was because of…
Yes, she probably thought this person isn't quite okay.
Okay. It sounds like you've been working hard on your illness and getting better. Is there anything friends could have helped with in that process? Do you think they could have made it easier?
If I had explained it to them, they couldn't have made the voices go away, but they could have just been there for me. I never told them about it.

I told a friend who got married that I went through depression and that's why the man in [COUNTRY] possibly didn't want to know me. She said it was my aunts' fault, that they shouldn't have got involved and messed it up, that he really cared about me and loved me. She got to know him because they became friends on a messaging platform. He was in [COUNTRY] and she was in [CITY], and they bonded well because she was my friend and his friend. Those days were beautiful. I wish I could go back. I only saw him 17 days, but I knew he liked me a lot and had deep feelings for me. But his aunt said the second time I went that he has a heart that jumps from one girl to another, that he falls in love easily and then falls out of love. I never forgot that, but I believe he had deep feelings for me. I just want to go back to those days when I was younger and more innocent. I wish I could make it all okay with him; that's something I'm longing for.
Okay. Do you think there's anything the Early Intervention Service could do to help you make friends and get more people in your life?

Yes, that would be really good. I would want to come to the groups they have here once a month, where they go to the cinema or bowling. I went bowling once but I'd never played before, so I didn't take part and just sat with them. Another time we played football at the park with a few people. I liked that a bit, but we never really bonded; we just played and went home. So I would like to meet new people.
But you'd like to have some time to talk to them?

Yes. I wouldn't want to give them my phone number and see them all the time right away. I would want to get to know them and trust them first, while bonding here or outside. Only the ones I want as true friends for life, or at least for as long as we're together and they're good to me, would I give my number to after getting to know them here.
Okay, and do you think it would be easier to talk about the voices with people who also come here, or would you still prefer not to?

I think I would like to talk about it because they're not already my friends or people in my life. It would be okay to speak with them if they've gone through similar experiences, and I think they have.

Yes, I think you're right. Let me check my list for anything I haven't asked. One other thing: what do you think it is about you that your friends like? You said you like your friends because they listen, give advice, and help distract you from the voices. What is it about you that your friends like?
Sorry, say that again.
What are your qualities that your friends like about you?

I'm funny, charming, I like to joke a lot, and I know how to have a good time. I'm not so good at that now because I went through depression. I think I'm quieter now, and I tell my doctor I believe I'm still depressed. I don't know how to enjoy life as much as I used to. I used to have a lot of fun and make jokes and laugh, but now I can't because of the bad experiences in my life. It made my enthusiasm to live die down.
So you think you're a bit of a different person with your friends now compared to before?
Yes, it changed me. I couldn't joke; I became more serious, just sitting down, and I couldn't laugh much at jokes. That's how I've become.
And do you think that's one of the reasons you see friends less as well?

But I'm not like that with my boyfriend. We joke and laugh and have fun together. But at the same time, I believed he didn't love me. Just recently, it's been a week since he wrote that message on social media, and I've been believing he didn't love me.
Is there anything else you'd want to add about your friendships, how they've been, and how they've changed?

There was another woman from the same support programme, from [COUNTRY]. I became friends with her while living in a mixed hostel. She later told me I was rude and sarcastic, that our friendship wasn't working, and it was best we didn't see each other anymore. She never called or wondered how I was after that. I saw her last summer or the summer before at a bus stop with her mum. I walked away to the next stop. They got on the bus and her mum told her to talk to me, but she said I didn't want to talk because I was walking away. I bumped into her again and saw her on social media and wrote a message. Then I saw her face to face on the bus about two months ago. I asked why she never called or worried about me after ending the friendship. She said she was too busy with university. I told her I wanted to be good friends because I'm not rude to her, and it hurt the way she spoke to me, you know, when you answer back in an angry way.
Okay, aggressive?

Not physically. She said okay, and I asked her to add me on social media, explaining I've changed and become much more sensitive to others. She never added me or called, even though I'd given her my number. I'd also visited her house earlier, but her parents said she was asleep. I left my number with her mother, but I'm not sure she passed it on. Basically, she wasn't interested anymore.
Okay, so you tried quite hard to be friends with her and she didn't make a response to you?
Yes.
Okay, well thank you very much, [PERSON], you've told me loads of really useful information.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes her step-mother may be actively interfering to prevent her friends from seeing her, with the intent to isolate her.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant expresses this as a suspicion based on instinct ('My instincts say my step-mum might be involved') and acknowledges she doesn't know for sure ('I don't know what possibly could have gone wrong').

delusion_points.summary: The participant suspects her friend's husband may have instructed her friend not to see her because he considers her a bad influence.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant uses speculative language ('could have maybe', 'maybe') and notes the husband is a 'good person', indicating uncertainty.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes strangers in the street are verbally abusing her by making critical comments about her appearance when she walks past them.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant distinguishes this from hearing voices when alone, linking it to her own insecurity about her appearance. She reports the specific insults have changed over time.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believes her boyfriend's Facebook post and his friend's comment were coded messages referring to a past relationship, which she interprets as proof that he never loved her.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant presents this as a firm realization ('I felt this meant...'). The boyfriend's alternative explanation is mentioned but dismissed.

case_summary: The participant discusses her limited current friendships, primarily maintained through Facebook, and her feelings of isolation. She describes a close friend from college she sees occasionally and a formerly close friend who has become distant since marriage. She attributes this distance to the friend's busy life, potential interference from her step-mother, and the friend's husband possibly viewing her as a bad influence. She recounts a past engagement that ended due to family involvement, her mental health disclosure, and her own jealousy. She reports hearing strangers in the street making derogatory comments about her appearance, a symptom she has not disclosed to most friends. She also describes ending a recent relationship due to a belief that her boyfriend's social media activity was a coded message indicating he did not love her, and expresses a general loss of trust in people, particularly men.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.

messages.content: Okay. Do you have anyone in your life who you see socially at the moment? Have you got friends about?
Yes.
Okay, where are those friends from? Can you tell me about them?
What, where I met them or…
Yes, where you met them, what sort of things you do together, how often do you see them..

Well, I've got one friend who's actually living with us now and I've known him since about [DATE], like a year before my episode. We live together, so we hang out and go out every so often for a drink. Then I made a really good friend around [DATE] and she's a single mum, so I don't see her that much. We try to do things together, like go out to eat or have a night in. Then I've got some old friends from about five years before my episode, and I see one of them more than the others, every so often, not as often as I used to. That's basically it. I don't have a massive group of friends. I've never really been like that anyway, never been one to have loads and loads of friends.

Yes, lots of people are like that. Prefer to have a few friends rather than a group. Okay, so the first person, the one you're living with at the moment, you've known him since [DATE], did you say? Yes. How did you meet him?

Well, I used to go out to a bar a lot and we knew each other through a friend. We used to say hi to each other and then I don't remember really, we just ended up starting to talk more. Then we started hanging out together and became really good friends.
Okay, and then the other friends that are older, the five or so - perhaps the one that you are friends with, was that the same sort of thing or did you meet them somewhere different?

I was going out with someone for a couple of weeks, and he lived in a house with loads of people because he was from [COUNTRY]. I made friends with about two girls who were living with him and then after they separated and moved into another flat with two other friends, I made friends with them too. So they were always together, and I was always with them. Then one of their friends moved from [COUNTRY] over, a guy, and I became very close friends with him. Then they lived separately and we all still met up and I still visited them all and we all went out. So yes, through someone else as well.
Yes, knowing friends through friends, that's the most common way I think, isn't it? How about the newer friends?

Through my friend that lives with us. He knew this girl, she's half [NATIONALITY], half English. He said, 'You should meet her, she's really nice.' We all met up one day and then we just clicked and continued talking.
Okay. Which of these friends, if any of them, were around when you were having your episode?

The older ones, which was mainly a guy and a girl. There were two girls and two boys and then one girl moved out and lived on her own with some guy and then the other guy moved in with the girl. So a girl and guy ended up living together for like two, three years from place to place. I was closer to those two. The other girl had a baby, so she wasn't going out a lot. So it was those two who were around when I had my episode.
Did you tell them what was happening to you? Did you talk about it with them?
At the time?
Yes.

To be honest I didn't really know what was happening myself, I just thought it was normal. So I didn't talk to anyone, even my family, about it. I think they knew that something was wrong, that I wasn't myself.
How severe had the situation become when you realized something wasn't right? And perhaps you then began receiving treatment here at this facility and similar steps?

Well, I got sectioned. So after about a week or two of being sectioned, being inside, I started acknowledging and understanding what actually happened. It was in the mental health centre that I was starting to understand that what happened wasn't normal. They would come and visit me every so often but I was still a bit midway, didn't really kick into it properly. Then after I came out I sort of lost – I don't know, they weren't my life anymore, sort of thing. Weird.
Why do you think that?

Well, when I came out I still had a bit of my episode and I went to [COUNTRY], where they're from, their village. They've got a friend there who now lives here and I asked him if I could come and see him. So I went to see him and over there I was acting really weird as well and I got arrested by the police over there. It was a really small village and it brought shame on them. Everyone knew what was happening, all the families know each other, it's like that in [COUNTRY]. So then they found out here in [CITY], and they just stopped talking to me.
Right, okay. Was there anybody else with whom the same sort of thing happened or not? Not the exact same circumstances but that you lost touch or the friendship ended as a result of your episode?
Well, my partner at the time. That ended when I went into the mental health centre.
Which bit of it caused that to end, was it the fact that you'd been sectioned or was it the way that you behaved or…

When I was hospitalized, he visited and I tried to kiss him, but the staff said we weren't allowed physical contact. He never came back after that. He told me he was hospitalized for two days because he was hallucinating too, but I'm not sure if that's true. His mother was very preoccupied and might have told him not to see me again. Honestly, I didn't want him to come. I had broken up with him before I went in. After I was discharged in February, he kept trying to get back together, but I couldn't do it. It was my decision; I was the one who chose to lose touch.
What made you feel that way?
I think that was part of what led to my main episode.
So the decision to lose touch might have happened anyway. I wonder if the relationship could have survived if you hadn't become unwell?

It's hard to say. Sometimes I think he might have brought it out in me, making me realize I shouldn't depend on anyone. Maybe he brought this to the surface, and that was part of me getting better. If I had stayed with him, perhaps nothing would have changed.
What was it about him that makes you think he might have stopped you from getting better? Was it something about his behavior or what he did?

I felt like he used me a lot, especially financially. It just didn't feel right. It was an instinct; there wasn't any concrete evidence. He wasn't hitting me or anything like that. Just little things that made me think, 'This doesn't feel right.'
So it sounds like you decided this person wasn't going to be good for you. As you said, he didn't do anything concretely wrong, but he wasn't going to help you get better.

He also grew and smoked a lot of cannabis at the time. I'm not blaming anyone, because you make your own choices. He smoked every day, and since I was at his place almost all the time, he'd suggest we buy some and I'd smoke it. I felt I had to because he was. So I ended up smoking all the time. Yes, maybe he wasn't good for me.
Was there anyone around who helped you during that time? Someone who helped you find support or talked to you when you were starting to get back on your feet?
After I was discharged from the section?
Yes.
It's still quite blurry. I was trying to fit back into society, so I wasn't really going out anyway. No, just my family.
So you chose to talk to your family?
Yes.
Okay.
I had the partner I'm with now, but that was it. I had lost touch with those friends I thought were really close. They were really the only people I used to hang around with.
You were relying on your family? Is your family here in [PLACE]?
Yes, they are. I live with them, so they saw what happened to me. My mum visited me every day I was in the mental health center. So yes, it was basically just them.

When you started to get life back on track, going out again and things like that, what was that like for you? After you'd been in the mental health center, that transitional period when you were maybe not quite back to normal but getting there...
Like the transitioning?
Yes.

It was quite hard. I would try to see if anyone wanted to go out—not close friends, but acquaintances I used to go out with, like to the market or for a drink or dancing. I tried to find people like that, or if someone asked me, 'Are you coming out on Friday?' I started going out a bit. It was a bit weird being around people again, but slowly, slowly, I just got used to it.
What was the weird part about being around people?

I think it was grasping that everyone was just doing their own thing. During my episode, I was hearing loads of voices and it seemed like everyone was looking at me all the time. So when I was out, looking around and seeing that people were not looking at me was a bit strange, because I hadn't experienced that since before it happened. I think that was the weirdest part.
So, when you did start going out again? When the part of the illness that was making you feel paranoid had been resolved, so you didn't have those thoughts?

No, because I just felt that that was only when I was, sort of, hallucinating and hearing things. It wasn't like hearing threatening voices, it was just normal people speaking, hearing a conversation. Yes, thinking like everyone knew me, the grandiose part of it. That had been resolved when I was in the mental health centre because they medicated me. Then when I came out it was just getting back into realising that you're not someone that everyone knows. Because that's what I was thinking.
Okay, and do you think having close friends around during your section and after discharge would have changed things? Did you miss that then, or were you focused elsewhere?

Well, I'd met my partner that February and spent so much time with him that I basically cut my friends off. I wasn't depending on them then. So afterwards I didn't think, "Oh, I need my friends to talk to," because my family was there and they knew me better. I get why others might want friends around, since many aren't in my position and lack family support when they come out.
Are you really close to your family?
Yes, very close, yes.
So, you've got your mum. Who else is there?
My dad and my sister.
Okay, and they're all around?

Yes, my dad doesn't really talk about things a lot. I'm not saying he's not emotional but he sort of mentions something and then it's just like, "[PERSON], are you okay?" It is just like, "Yeah," and that's it, we won't talk it through. My mum worries and talks about things a lot. My sister wants to face things but she has a threshold she reaches. Like if she keeps telling you something and you don't do it, then that's it.
Is your sister older than you?
Yes, 39.
Okay. Did the illness change the kind of people you want to be around, or are the friends you'd make still the same as always?

It's a tricky question actually. I'm not sure because even before, when I was younger, I was very – everyone liked me and I liked everyone, I got on with everyone but I could never really rely on my friends. So, I wasn't really searching for that perfect friend I could tell everything to. Then friends have come along that I've really been able to tell everything to and connect with, but I don't think it's changed my thinking on being careful who your friends are because you never know. Looking at what happened and those friends that then just stopped talking to me because I thought they were really close friends, but obviously they weren't.
Yes, so that's quite disappointing in a way?

Yes, there was one guy who when I met him out didn't really want to talk to me and he said, "I think we should wait a good amount of time until you get better." So, I waited a couple of months and then he said after that we could go out for a coffee and talk about it, so that's what I did. He was scared of what happened and how to deal with it. He was really understanding and then slowly we started building up again and now we're really close and see each other every couple of weeks. The girl has never talked to me again. I've spoken to her a couple of times on the phone and seen her once but she totally just cut me off.
How did you make sense of that? What do you think is going…

I think she's very family orientated and she looks at how everyone sees her. She has to represent. It's a cultural thing, like if something goes wrong, if someone brings shame on you, it's like, "Oh my god. What is it going to look like."
Okay, and she perceived it as you brought shame on her family when you…

Yes, and he was also gay. So, the majority of gay people don't really care what people think of them. That's my perception because they do their own thing and just want to be who they want to be and not conform to society. He was more understanding and he's more detached from [COUNTRY] than she was.
Almost more like open minded, do you think?
Yes, more open minded. I think that's why I then understood more and wanted to build my friendship up again because we were really close.
Do you think that when you see friends now, you do the same sort of stuff that you always did or – I mean you mentioned smoking before; do you still do the same sort of stuff or is it different?
Smoking I cut off. I still drink and stuff with friends and go dancing. Yes, nothing's really changed apart from the manic stuff that I used to do during an episode. Like crazy stuff.

How about the sort of role that you play in friendships? People I've spoken to say they've seemed to be a particular person in their friendships. Like with some people they're the joker or maybe the one who listens to all everyone's problems, all different roles. I just wondered if that's changed since you've been unwell and become something different? I don't know what sort of roles you think you play with your friends?
Is this just friends or family as well?
Friends.

No, I've always been someone who listens to people, but the people I've listened to have always listened to me as well, friend-wise. I've always found people who can give back what I give. If I listen to someone a lot and when I'm talking they don't, they're not really going to be my friend at the end of the day. No, it hasn't changed. I always joke around people and that hasn't changed either.
Okay, and is talking to your friends quite openly and being able to share stuff quite important to you; that kind of openness?

Yes, maybe not all my friends, there are specific ones who I tell everything to and then there are obviously some things that I don't tell anyone. Maybe just things for me - like if I'm feeling a bit manic, obviously I'd tell someone that but other stuff maybe, feelings towards someone. Maybe I might not tell that person that thing because it might affect them. Yes, I say what I think as well, if I think it's wrong.
Yes, and is that ever affected by your paranoia, for example, saying what you think?
What do you mean?

Well, some people have said that if they've experienced feeling paranoid about people, they found it more difficult to talk openly with people because they worry that although they are not feeling paranoid anymore, there's still a slight bit of mistrust or concern about…
I used to do that during an episode.

Yes, anyone really – I'm not familiar with your symptoms or your file, so I don't know if you felt paranoid about particular individuals or locations, but sometimes when people have been paranoid about certain persons, they found it hard to interact with them after recovering. Do you see what I mean?

Right, I understand. See, it wasn't a targeted paranoia, I've got more general. So, there's maybe a few crumbs along the road as well, like it wasn't a brand new thing. I didn't think, 'Oh, that person's talking about me.' Then I think if that would have happened, it would have been – like the girl one that, obviously after it happened I thought she is probably better off without me as a friend, because then some of her friends that I knew didn't want to talk to me anymore either. Then I just basically cut her off, not that I didn't care but I just thought, 'Well, sod off,' sort of thing. So, I wouldn't have been that much affected by it, if you know what I mean. It wouldn't have affected me that much but I understand that some people it might affect.
Okay, that's fair enough. Thinking about now when you're at home, is there anything that you think that's missing in terms of your friends or your social side?
I miss going out and just talking to loads of people and knowing I'd be walking past them and then, 'How are you?' sort of like knowing them like that because I haven't done that for ages.
Why is that?

I don't know, I just started thinking maybe I shouldn't be that known to everyone because I was quite promiscuous at the time. I thought perhaps being widely known isn't actually a good thing. They might be – so yes, it's maybe the knowing – like in the gay scene, everyone knows your business and you sleep with someone and they know, and the person you know slept with them. So I felt that maybe I should stop doing that.
So, you decided to get a bit of a lower profile really?

Yes. Obviously it's a bit of a confidence thing, like everyone knows you, it's like, 'Oh-o,' but then obviously that can't go on forever. I miss also getting drunk and not having to think about anything or think about your actions, which is obviously what got me here but do you know what I mean?
That carefree kind of thing?

Yes, and not having to walk down the road maybe, be careful, like want to walk in – like say there's a group of boys walking towards you and having to cross the road because I never used to be like that, I was very - like I didn't care, sort of thing.
Why do you think that changed?

Well, I got mugged, so that's probably caused it as well. I don't know, maybe having to – realising that I can be that way. I can be carefree but then I have to be quite careful what I do as well. So that it doesn't just lead me off the path of where I want to go. So, just to get a direction in life, it's difficult to explain.
Yes, I know what you mean, it's all a bit…
Grown up, sort of thing.

Yes, and dealing with something that requires you to take medication and reflect on things. It does make you grow up quickly and then they have to – they lose the carefree teenage, 20s period because suddenly things become a lot more…

Yes, because that's the thing, because I had to take medication at the beginning of [DATE], I had HIV. So, then I started in [DATE], [MONTH], so since then I was like ten months before my episode. So, I started, I already had that, like take every day my medications, I needed routine in my life, I can't just not care – I can't just be carefree anymore, I have to care for myself. Then in the end I got with a guy and just went a bit off the rails.
Okay, last couple of things. What qualities would you look for in friends and people you want in your life right now?

I wouldn't want all my friends to be the same. I'd like positive people, but also some who are more negative, for balance—so I remember you can be happy but also have problems and be sad. I like friends who share their problems and I can, what's the word, not guide…
Support them.

Yes, advise them, but not to the point where I'm doing too much and they rely on me heavily, which was happening before my admission. My family would always share their problems and I'd suggest what they should do, but then I'd keep everything bottled up inside. So I want friends like that, but who also listen to me and offer advice—maybe not telling me exactly what to do, but suggesting different approaches. Friends I can go out with for a meal or a drink. I need to avoid those who go out constantly, getting drunk every weekend.
Do you think that shift is because of being unwell, or something you would have done anyway as you got older?

It's quite a gay scene thing. You start going out at 16, drinking, sleeping around, always needing to look good. I think it was the environment I entered. It was about trying to separate yourself from everyone else. Nowadays things feel more integrated, though back then it was somewhat integrated but less so. You still have young people on the gay scene wanting to fit in. So yes, I think it would have happened anyway.
Maybe it's about finding your identity and getting comfortable with who you are. Your identity has become much more than just that aspect, I don't know.
Yes.
Did you ever attend anything here at the centre, like the groups or social activities?

I went to one when I was sectioned, I think they had snacks. But I haven't been to any others. I don't want to discriminate against mental health, but I don't want to be labelled as a mentally ill person. I really dislike the idea of socialising with people who've been through the same thing. It feels a bit weird—not to be horrible, but you know what I mean?

That's interesting, because people seem to fall into two groups. Some, like you, don't want to be reminded of what they went through. Others really want to talk to someone who's had the same experience.

Maybe some people come out understanding why it happened, having talked it through and found answers. On the other side, there are those who haven't been able to do that and are still asking why it happened to them, feeling it ruined their life. Those people might want to connect with others who've experienced it, to learn how they reached a better stage. I always try to find the positive in things, even the bad stuff, and in a way I move on. I don't want to be around people who remind me of what happened.
That's fair enough. Do you ever discuss social stuff or friends with [PERSON], or does that not really come up?
She's always suggesting groups, and I'm not really interested. She does ask if I'm going out with friends and what we do, yes.
She checks in?
Yes, she checks whether I'm going out and meeting people. I think I'd tell her too if I wasn't feeling right, you know?
So if you started feeling a bit deflated or less confident, you'd feel able to mention it to her?
Yes.
Okay. Is there anything the service here could have done differently to help with friendships while you were recovering?

I would have liked maybe an hour a week, when I was settling back into home life, with someone who had been through what I had—a kind of mentor on the sidelines. Someone who understood, who could just come round and talk, not interrogate me like a doctor or social worker. A buddy who could draw things out that formal questions can't. [PERSON] and the doctors are great, but they're very focused on what happened and how to prevent it recurring. It would be good to talk to someone with lived experience, because you can study forever but you don't really know what it means until it happens to you. Yes, a buddy.
I think that's a really good idea. Some others I've spoken to have wanted similar things, though not expressed as clearly as you just did, but touching on the same concepts.

It's obviously very hard. Some people just want to forget and never engage with mental health services again, maybe because of a bad experience. And there probably aren't enough people who could do that role, given how many are discharged. But even one person visiting two or three people a day, Monday to Friday—so a caseload of about 12 a week—and paying them really well.
Loads of money!
Yes! If that ever becomes a real thing, once I've sorted myself out, I'd be happy to do it. I wouldn't mind helping out.
Okay. Is there anything else about friendship or social life that's been important for you in the last couple of years that I haven't asked about? We've covered quite a lot.
Just maybe – yes, no not really.
Okay, thank you.

delusion_points.summary: During the episode, the participant believed that everyone was looking at them all the time.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant describes this as a past experience during the episode and contrasts it with their current, more accurate perception that people are not looking at them.

delusion_points.summary: The participant believed that everyone knew them, which they identify as a grandiose part of their illness.
delusion_points.uncertainty_or_counterevidence: The participant states this belief has been resolved through medication and they now realize it was not true.

case_summary: The participant discusses their social life and friendships before, during, and after a psychotic episode that led to hospitalization. They describe having a small, close group of friends, some of whom they lost touch with after the episode due to their behavior while unwell. The participant reflects on past symptoms like paranoia and grandiosity, their recovery process, and their current preferences for friendships, emphasizing a desire for balance and avoiding reminders of their illness.

provenance.source_citation: Huckle, Lemmel, and Johnson (2021), Experiences of friendships of young people with first-episode psychosis, PLOS ONE 16(7):e0255469.
